#6696. All About Bonnie-Chance Roberts, Beanie Feldstein’s Wife

Beanie Feldstein just shared a major life update: She and her wife, Bonnie-Chance Roberts, quietly welcomed their first child. “She is genuinely beyond my wildest dreams. I really did dream her,” Feldstein told People of their baby girl in November 2026.

In May, the actress announced her pregnancy on Instagram, writing, “Limited Edition Scouse Beanie Baby coming soon!! 🎀🍼.”

The announcement comes nearly two years after the couple married in a camp-themed celebration in upstate New York.

Feldstein often keeps the spotlight on her work, but when it comes to Roberts, she doesn’t hold back. Over the years, she’s shared glimpses into their relationship, from how they met on set to building a life together.

So who is Bonnie-Chance Roberts? Here’s everything to know about Feldstein’s wife and their life as parents.

Originally from Liverpool, Roberts works behind the scenes in the entertainment industry as a producer.

Her credits include projects like Mary Queen of Scots, Bridget Jones’s Baby, and How to Build a Girl—which she worked on as a producer while Feldstein starred in it.

Feldstein and Roberts first connected while working on How to Build a Girl. Feldstein told Vogue in June 2023 that they initially met over Skype during the casting process. “Bon had been developing Caitlin Moran’s book How to Build a Girl into a movie for over five years when they finally started the casting process for Caitlin’s fictional proxy, Johanna, a 16-year-old girl from Wolverhampton, England,” Feldstein said. “With a dash of luck and a push from the universe, they ended up being open to meeting a Jewish girl from Los Angeles.”

Their working relationship quickly shifted. As Feldstein recalled to Vogue, “From the moment we first kissed, we both knew we would get married and months after that, Bon had announced that when the time came, she wanted to be the one to propose to me.”

The relationship grew steadily from there. By 2020, Feldstein publicly celebrated Roberts on Instagram, writing in a birthday tribute, “I’m pretty convinced you’re actually made of magic. The girl with the warmest heart, the most expansive imagination, and the most exceptional brain. I love you so much. Happy birthday, bubba!!!”

The couple didn’t keep things private for long. In September 2019, they stepped out together at the Toronto International Film Festival for the premiere of How to Build a Girl, marking their first red carpet appearance as a couple.

Roberts later posted about the experience on Instagram, writing, “They say it takes a village to build a girl, and they are right!”

Roberts took the lead when it came time to propose. Feldstein announced their engagement in June 2022, sharing photos from the moment on Instagram and captioning them, “I do, Bon.”

Roberts later described designing the ring during a long period when the couple lived apart due to the pandemic. “The dream was for the ring to look as if a shard of magic was frozen in time,” she told Vogue in 2023.

The couple tied the knot on May 20, 2023, at Cedar Lakes Estate in New York’s Hudson Valley.

The theme felt personal. Feldstein told Vogue, “I grew up going to summer camp for 10 years, and my parents and both sets of my grandparents met at summer camp, so camp is a lineage of love through the generations of my family. Even though we met in London and fell in love on a film set, to get married at a camp was a truly beautiful emotional homecoming.”

Roberts wore a tailored bridal suit for the ceremony, while Feldstein opted for a vintage-inspired Gucci gown.

Looking back on the day, Feldstein shared on Late Night with Seth Meyers in February 2024, “[My wedding] went so swimmingly,” she said. “Like, I’m such an anxious girly. And I was more calm at the wedding than I am, like, brushing my teeth, at the supermarket. I was so calm. I just got to look at her and hear her vows, and it was perfect.”

“We wrote our own vows, and it actually rained a little the day of our wedding, and we handwrote the vows and the trees sort of shook and dripped on my vows,” she continued. “And I was like, ‘Oh, I hope I know them by heart.’ But it was fine. It was actually all going perfectly.”

In May 2026, Feldstein and Roberts announced they were expecting their first child.

The couple shared the news with a joint Instagram post featuring a series of photos, including one of a cake decorated with pink bows and the message “B+B are having a baby!”

The announcement marked a new chapter for the couple—and a years-long dream realized for Feldstein. In 2021, the actress told Bustle, “Sixteen years from now I hope to be living in New York City or London, married to my girlfriend, and have babies and puppies running around while we both make movies, shows, and plays that feel meaningful and exciting and profound.”

Feldstein quietly welcomed her and Roberts’s baby girl. In a November 4 interview with People, she opened up about parenthood for the first time. She did not share her child’s name or birth date but marveled about life with her.

“She is genuinely beyond my wildest dreams. I really did dream her,” Feldstein said. “I always wanted to be a mom, and I always wanted a daughter. I look at her every day, and I’m like, ‘You’re just beyond anything I could have even tried to imagine.’”

“I love getting to watch her take in the world; it’s just the greatest gift. And getting to be a mom alongside my wife is the greatest gift,” she added. “She’s such a good mom, and it’s so special to watch. Motherhood is unbelievably beautiful.”

She reflected on one milestone she saw a few weeks before her interview. “There’s nothing like the first smile,” she said. “I could feel her soul from the moment she was born. I remember people told me newborns are little blobs and they don’t really come alive until 6 weeks. I disagree with that completely. I could feel her soul from the moment I met her, but when you get to see that externalized in the smile, it’s so magic.”

Feldstein doesn’t shy away from expressing how much Roberts means to her.

Speaking to People in February 2024, she said of married life, “My favorite part of married life is everything, but I think the big thing that felt different was saying ‘my wife.’ [It] has more power than like ‘my girlfriend’…you know, it’s like ‘my wife’ is like ‘oh, this is legit.’”

She added, “Oh my god, I just want her with me every second of every day.”

In her November 2026 interview with People, she touched on her gratitude raising a child with Roberts. “I don’t think anyone that has had a baby can look at their child and not just feel the most gratitude to the universe,” Feldstein said. “I feel very grateful every day that I get to be her mom and mother alongside my wife and watch her with my whole family.”

The accessory, introduced for the Fall/Winter 2026 season, was crafted from black leather, with a rounded shape and top closure. Gold hardware detailing and a matching chain added a little pop of shine, and for some contrast, Lively selected a pair of silver Brent Neale bow earrings and mixed-metal rings.

The actor added a pair of red-bottomed PVC Christian Louboutin heels with a black cap-toe accent, ankle strap, and ultra-high stiletto. And of course, she finished things off with her signature bouncy blonde blowout, parted at the side. ’Tis the holiday season!

#6693. 16 Best Automatic Watches for Men 2026, According to GQ Watch Nerds

A budding “watch guy” most likely starts off their collection with an assortment of quartz tickers (and let’s be clear, there’s nothing wrong with that). But as your interest in watches grows, it’s only natural for you to want something on your wrist you can brag about, which inevitably pushes you towards automatic watches.

Inside the case of an automatic watch is a weighted rotor that spins as you move your arm, a few little flicks of your wrist throughout the day keeps the internal mechanisms running long enough to keep that minute hand tick-tick-ticking across the dial.

But automatic watches also have a reputation for being finicky or costly. And while that can be true, the beauty of watches is the wide price scale in which the industry operates. From stunners for less than $250 to ones you’d have to mortgage your house (and maybe your parents’ house) to buy, here are the top automatic watches on the market today for any budget.

While not impossible to find a great watch at the $250-mark, you are going to be limited. Given the many internal pieces and complicated mechanisms needed to build an automatic watch, many brands have to charge a bit more for a quality automatic. Even so, brands like Orient and Seiko lead the way on well-made (and well-designed) options.

Orient’s range of inexpensive watches punch well above their weight-class and the Symphony III is no different. With its classic, clean design and movement that promises 40 hours of power reserve, this is a watch that’s made to be a daily driver without breaking the bank.

Timex’s Waterbury is a staple in their line-up and the extremely stylish Metrograph has an Art Deco-style case and dial that’s pared-down enough to keep things simple, but without looking boring.

The Seiko 5 is something of a cult favorite for the Japanese brand – and for good reason. It’s a perfect daily driver and a budget-friendly alternative to the Rolex Datejust. Best of all, it clocks in at just 37mm, which is the perfect case size for nearly any wrist.

As ever, Timex provides maximum bang for minimum buck with this classic "Pepsi" bezel diver.

At $500, the doorway starts to open up a bit more – but only a creak. The usual suspects like Timex and Casio, are populating this price point, Bulova and Sternglas are great alternatives who will give you a little more street cred among collectors.

Undoubtedly one of the best looking watches in the sub-$500 category, the Timex Marlin in this particular shade of green strikes the perfect balance between classic and modern.

Heavily influenced by motorsports, the Edifice is a bit of a departure from the digital, retro-charm of many mainstays for Casio. The integrated bracelet keeps it sporty, while the patterned dial makes it a little more interesting than other options on the market.

At 45mm, 200-meter of water resistance, and 42-hours of power reserve, the Bulova Marine Star ticks all the boxes for a great dive watch at a reasonable price – the two-toned bezel is just a nice bonus.

This fan favorite hits the bullseye of the style-quality-price nexus, and looks especially fetching with a bright yellow dial.

A thousand bucks is a perfectly reasonable budget to have when you want to upgrade your watch game without completely breaking the bank. Here, I’d recommend looking at smaller, or more indie brands to find some interesting designs not seen by more household names.

You’d be forgiven for not knowing their name, but Kuoe is starting to gain traction in the U.S.. The Japanese-based watchmaker produces high-quality, well-designed pieces that harken to a more classic watch style. The OLD SMITH is based on the military field watch, but with a slightly more refined design language.

A reborn grail from the Studio 54 era, with a vintage-correct 35mm case.

UNIMATIC uses the basic field watch as the springboard for their Modello Due, which strips it back to its barebones to make something a bit bolder, a bit more modern, and eye-catching.

Paulin is a Glasgow-based microbrand that’s known for colorful, unique, and whimsical watches, often playing with color to make their designs all the more interesting.

Needless to say, if money isn’t an issue, the sky’s the limit. Not all watches are created equal and buying just for the name recognition alone doesn’t always make for the best watch for the money. Instead, look for a price point that’s commensurate with the movement, design, and materials used, and you’ll never regret the decision to spend the big bucks.

Taken from a 1924 archival design, the Brunswick’s cushion case, clean lines, and mother-of-pearl dial may all feel a bit “precious”, shall we say; but this is a workhorse watch that’s destined to be a daily driver for anyone who is looking for a little eye-candy on the wrist.

The IWC Ingenieur is a masterfully made ceramic watch (and matching ceramic bracelet) that will no doubt get you a few compliments every time you wear it to the office.

Not many watches can be mistaken for a Bell & Ross watch with its larger proportions and signature square case shape. The BR-05, the brand’s most popular model, is a sportier, slightly bolder answer to Cartier’s Santos.

It’s hard to narrow down one Grand Seiko to choose, but the White Birch is subtle and versatile enough to dress up or use as your daily driver. Most impressive about this particular model is the Caliber 9SA5 movement, which promises a whopping 80-hours of power when fully wound – nearly twice that of many others on the market.

Mechanical watch movements fall into two basic categories: hand-wound and automatic. Before the invention of automatic wristwatches in the 1920s (and long before the invention of battery-powered quartz movements in the 1960s) all watches were hand-wound. That meant you needed to manually wind up your watch every day to keep it running. An automatic watch (also called a self-winding watch) doesn’t require this because it winds automatically with the movement of your body as you wear it.

Most automatic watches wind themselves via a weighted rotor, which you’ll be able to see if your watch has a see-through case back (it’s the half moon-shaped piece right on top). When you wear the watch and move around, the rotor winds a spring, which turns the hands, date wheel and everything else that moves on a watch.

To keep your watch from stopping when you’re sitting still (or when you take it off at night) automatic movements also store excess energy and slowly release it over hours or days while the rotor is stationary. This is called a “power reserve,” and it typically ranges from 40 to 80 hours, with some going as high as a week or more. They’re useful if you don’t wear a watch every day, and don’t want to have to reset the date and time every time you put it on—particularly with annual or perpetual calendar models that can be complicated to set.

It’s not a downside, per se, but they do require some upkeep. Unlike a quartz watch that requires nothing more than a new battery every few years, a mechanical watch is a finely-tuned machine consisting of many tiny, precisely calibrated parts. Watchmakers have made huge advances in shock-and waterproofing over the years, but there’s still only so much abuse a mechanical movement can take. And that’s the thing: repairs to automatic watches can be expensive.

If you stick to the manufacturer’s recommended service schedule (it’ll need an overhaul and lube every 4 to 10 years, depending on the brand and model) and don’t make a habit of wearing it in the sauna, you’ll probably be fine. Whether it’s a $200 Amazon special or a $200,000 grand complication, automatic watches are designed to be worn, so the best way to take care of your watch is to wear it as much as possible.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

Dakota Johnson and Machine Gun Kelly have yet to define their relationship publicly, but the two stars have been spending plenty of time together.

The actress and musician were first linked in September 2026, when they were photographed together in New York City. Days later, a source told People that Johnson and Kelly, whose real name is Colson Baker, “have been hanging out and seeing each other under the radar for months now.”

The two stars had known each other before, but according to the source, they became closer after attending Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce’s wedding in July.

Since then, Johnson has watched Kelly walk the runway in Milan, and sources have shared more about how their connection developed.

Below, everything we know about Johnson and Kelly’s rumored relationship so far.

Johnson and Kelly both attended Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce’s July 3 wedding at Madison Square Garden in New York City.

The two stars already knew each other, but a source close to Kelly told People in September that they “hit it off” at the wedding.

On September 28, a source gave Entertainment Tonight similar intel, telling the outlet that Johnson and Kelly “really connected at Taylor and Travis’s wedding.”

On September 12, Johnson and Kelly were photographed together in New York City, getting out of the same SUV and entering Swift’s Tribeca apartment.

Four days later, a source close to Kelly told People that Kelly and Johnson “have been hanging out and seeing each other under the radar for months now.”

The source explained that Johnson and Kelly “started off as friends and were texting often, but now they’re spending more time together.”

“It’s a very new start, but they’re smitten with each other right now,” the insider added. “They haven’t put a label on their relationship yet. They are just seeing where spending time together will take them.”

A second source characterized things as “super casual” at that point.

On September 22, Johnson and Kelly both traveled to Italy for Milan Fashion Week and attended the same event.

Three days later, Johnson addressed the broader attention her dating life receives during an appearance on Vogue’s The Run-Through podcast, though she never mentioned Kelly specifically.

“Even if I go to dinner with my manager or my lawyer, it’s like, ‘Seen with mystery man,’” she said. “I also don’t care.”

When asked whether she ever feels compelled to correct speculation about her personal life, Johnson explained why she prefers not to engage with it.

On September 28, a source shared more about Kelly and Johnson’s relationship with Entertainment Tonight: “Dakota was the one who made the first move. He’s very shy around her, but he likes her a lot. It’s still new, but they’re having fun and seeing where things go.”

The insider added, “Dakota has been a fan of his music and has always found him cute. He likes her a lot, too.”

On October 19, a source close to Kelly told People that he and Johnson were spending more time together. “They have been out on dates that people don’t know about because there aren’t any photos.”

The insider said that they’re in the “dating phase,” and “aren’t ready to go official yet.”

“They both really like each other and have been seeing each other more frequently,” the source shared. “They haven’t put a label on their relationship yet, but they’re growing closer every time they hang out.”

In the past few months, they’ve especially connected over their “same dry and dark sense of humor,” the source said. “[They] make each other laugh.”

Days later, Kelly and Johnson were photographed out in Los Angeles on October 23. They first left a music studio together, riding off in Kelly’s red Maserati. That evening, they were seen together again, leaving the Chateau Marmont.

A source close to Johnson gave People an update on their dynamic on October 28. “She’s happy and enjoys spending time with him,” the insider said. “There’s a lot of chemistry and she’s been going to the studio with him while he works. For now, it makes her happy.”

On November 3, Kelly and Johnson were photographed leaving a restaurant in Calabasas, California, after a dinner date. They were smiling and talking to each other in the shots.

#6689. Exclusive: The All’s Fair Cast Held Court in Couture at the Season 2 Premiere and After-Party

“This season is just more of everything,” Kim Kardashian told Vogue, as Sarah Paulson shrieked “Yes!” in agreement, adding, “More drama, more sex, more fun, more fashion, more shenanigans.” They were talking, of course, about All’s Fair, Ryan Murphy’s panache-packed Hulu series following high-powered divorce attorneys with silver tongues, scores to settle, and exceptionally good wardrobes to do it in. On Monday, the cast gathered on Manhattan’s West Side for the New York premiere of season two, the third installment of their whistle-stop publicity tour.

Much like in the series itself, there was no shortage of drama at the Highline Studios: white velvet ropes, marble, and an infinite amount of gold. Add to that the parade of couture emerging from black cars, and suddenly the first Monday in November seemed as glamorous as a certain Monday in May. “This is All’s Fair! You either go big or go home,” quipped hairstylist Sharif Poston while giving Niecy Nash-Betts’s hair a final once-over with a shiny metallic comb.

The show’s costuming certainly sets the precedent for such excess. Fred Leighton brooches, Balenciaga gowns, and no shortage of Birkins. “The show’s wardrobe has the biggest budget I’ve ever seen,” revealed actress Denise Richards. “I was actually quite impressed by it.” (And that’s coming from a former Bond girl.)

For this red-carpet outing, some went the lawyerly route, while others dialed up the haute factor. Teyana Taylor managed to tick both boxes in an architectural Nicholas Oakwell Couture pantsuit, festooned with a giant bow below the waist. Her summation of the evening was the same as hers of the second season: “It’s drama and suits!” Similarly, actor Nyle DiMarco nodded to the legal theme in a Paul Smith suit, “straight off the runway.” And Nash-Betts’s Louis Vuitton look had multiple acts. “This dress turns into three or four different things—so keep your eyes on me.” Sure enough, the next time I saw her, the gilded halo that initially framed her was nowhere to be seen.

“She looks so good,” director and executive producer Anthony Hemingway said as Kardashian arrived in a lace-up Ashi Studio gown with a sweetheart neckline and a snatched bodice, accentuated with lace, croc embossing, and ribbons. Everyone seemed to stand a little straighter as Kardashian walked in—but sure enough, as soon as she started chatting, the room relaxed.

“I’m excited for people to see how funny we are,” Kardashian said. “There’s a lot more comedy this season,” Paulson added, hooking a thumb toward Kardashian, who leaned right into it. “I’m the funniest,” she teased. Paulson had her own theory: “Kim did a movie with all these comedy geniuses in between seasons one and two,” she said, explaining that her co-star came back to set brimming with notes. When Paulson said she’s still waiting for Saturday Night Live to call, Kardashian chimed in with an idea of her own: “Should we do it together? Please!”

Though there were photos to take and interviews to give, the cast still stopped mid-carpet for a catch-up. Glenn Close, in Matières Fécales, had missed the first two stops on the press tour. “I’m excited to see my friends,” she said, holding hands with Kardashian through an entire interview. Taylor, who’d been busy wrapping up another project as director, felt much the same. “You have to understand the FOMO I’ve been having.”

“We had long TV days that lasted up to sixteen hours sometimes,” Naomi Watts added. “It’s a grind, but we somehow find a way to laugh in between takes.” She credited Murphy with putting together a group that clicked. “There’s not an outsized ego amongst us.” For Taylor, that sisterhood mattered especially on the days she turned up feeling less than her best. “Everybody’s got their silent battles,” she said. “Come to work with them, and with this cast, you just know that you’re going to be surrounded by love.”

For reality TV regular Dorinda Medley, who plays Loni and worked mostly with Glenn Close, taking on a scripted role was a chance to try something new. “All these little steps in your life move you a little closer to who you are,” she said. “For so many years I was Dorinda someone.” She ticked off the surnames she’d gone by and the roles she’d played offscreen. “Mother, wife, widow. Now, for the first time, I’m just Dorinda. There’s incredible freedom in that.” Medley, in an embellished Gucci dress that she jokingly called “very casual,” already had a pitch for her next collaboration with Murphy. How about setting American Horror Story at Blue Stone Manor, her home in the Berkshires?

“We rarely get a chance to rock together. We’re always working,” Hemingway, the director, said. He was looking forward to a chance to “hang out, have a cocktail, even do a little two-step, and just laugh.” And at Crane Club nearby, there was ample opportunity for all four. Around the red velvet-draped dining room, servers made the rounds with truffle arancini and caesar salads, a giant ice sculpture of the show’s initials presided over the raw bar, and the DJ was good enough to make you forget it was a school night.

If the carving station said wedding reception, the cocktail menu said divorce. Bartenders whipped up drinks named Contested Assets, with habanero-spiked mezcal number, and Alimony, which came with gin, vodka, vermouth, sake, and a little cucumber. Taylor had a special order in mind. “I need a real big margarita,” she told Vogue. Her favorite? “Passionfruit. Sugar rim. There—you’ve got sugar, spice, and everything nice,” she said, dancing as she delivered the recipe.

For a cast that had reserved tables ringing the room, they sure spent little time in their seats. And who could blame them? Ash Hodgkinson was doing magic tricks for a knot of guests, while Murphy, in ochre-tinted aviators, made duck faces for the camera with Paulson. When the DJ put on “Plain Jane,” there was Nash-Betts, dancing with her girls. “I love those moments,” Hemingway had said. “That’s living.”

As for any flak the show had received, Anna Delvey, who knows a thing or two about mixed press and courthouse fashion, had a thought. “It says a lot about people, how they take it,” she explained—stating that some people “are too serious about it.” In her view, anyone busy cataloging the show’s excesses was liable to miss the joke. “They obviously know what they’re doing,” she said of the silliness.

#6688. Simu Liu’s First Favorite Brand Was Abercrombie & Fitch

Simu Liu is no stranger to fashion’s biggest night, so, when I met him at his hotel in SoHo Monday night, he figured the Council of Fashion Designers of America Awards show should be a cinch. “I think everything’s a little bit more chill than the Met Gala,” Liu says. “So I’m looking forward to having a little bit of a more relaxed environment to talk to fashion houses and meet people from the different brands and also just to see friends.”

We speak just a few hours before the 37-year-old actor is about to make his first appearance at the Oscars of fashion and it’s hard to tell that he just hopped off a plane from Los Angeles this morning. The Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings actor has had a packed year, from making his Broadway debut in Oh, Mary! between February and April to getting married back in October. He’s preparing to start promotion for the highly anticipated December release of Avengers: Doomsday, in which he’s set to reprise his role as the superhero Shang-Chi. Marvel fans haven’t seen him on the screen since his record-breaking film debut in 2021. “It’s been a long, long time,” he jokes.

For now, he’s clad in a robe sitting barefoot on the sofa, swiping a metallic device across his unblemished, glowing face. “I think it’s like a gua sha, but it’s cold,” he speculates. (His makeup artist, Alex Keating, confirms that it’s Shark Beauty’s Depuffi, a hot-and-cold contrast therapy gua sha that basically “gives you a full facial.”) A room service trolley is sitting inches away from him, allowing him quick access to a plate of chicken tenders and fries. And a Diet Coke. Don’t forget the Diet Coke.

Keating makes good use of Liu’s wavy locks, hairspraying a Superman-like curl into permanent place on his forehead as he sips his fridge cigarette. The actor’s dad cut his hair until he was 18 and he says it took him a while to learn what worked for his own mane. He envied the typical stick-straight Asian hair others had, but through his work with groomers learned the power of salt sprays to lean into his hair’s natural texture. It admittedly took a while for Liu to develop his own fashion sense as an adult, too.

“When you grow up working class and you grow up with parents whose purchasing habits were just the furthest thing from luxurious, I think it just takes time for you to learn about fashion,” he says. “The first brand that I remember really caring about was Abercrombie & Fitch.”

Tonight, though, Liu has moved far beyond the mall. He’s attending the CFDA Awards on behalf of White Rabbit Trust, an organization that supports AAPI creatives and entrepreneurs. It's hosting the award’s Emerging Designers Table, which allows industry leaders—this year, Jason Wu—to mentor AAPI designers who create custom looks for the muse of their choosing. In Liu’s case, he’s been dressed by Asian-Canadian designer Haoran Li of the brand Private Policy.

The look for the evening was a matching set made from black silk jacquard woven with bamboo paired with a shiny new silver wedding ring and a Rolex Batman GMT-Master II. His cropped trucker-style jacket, accented by hand-knotted Chinese buttons, sat over a crisp frayed-hem white button-down with wide-legged pants that draped over low-profile black shoes. “In Chinese culture, bamboo is one of the Four Gentlemen, a symbol of integrity and resilience,” Li says. “It bends in the storm but never breaks. That felt like Simu, who has spent his career pushing through doors that weren’t built for us.”

I ask if he’s ever bothered by the responsibility of representing the Asian diaspora. “Right around the time Crazy Rich Asians came out, it was the first studio Asian movie in 25 years,” he recalls. “Then Shang-Chi was the first Asian Marvel superhero movie. For a while it was just like first this, first this, first this. So I felt like innately the stakes were high and I put pressure on myself. I don’t regret doing that. I just remember looking around and not really seeing anyone doing that. So I thought, well it might as well be me.”

To that point, this isn’t the first time Liu has used his name to promote an indie AAPI brand. At the the premiere of Shang-Chi in 2021, he spotlighted Singaporean-British designer Chelsea Scott-Blackhall’s label Dzojchen, wearing the brand’s silk kimono tuxedo.

Prominence in Hollywood has meant more to him than giving him the opportunity to wear really nice clothes. He’s decided to take more agency in his career, he says. Last year, he starred and executive produced the spy thriller series The Copenhagen Test, which despite favorable reviews was cancelled after one season. That hasn’t slowed his aspirations for new creative outlets: "I think actually right now I’m really excited by the idea of becoming a director."

But before we get to see “Directed by Simu Liu” on the big screen, the star has an awards show to attend—and a plate of tendies to devour. Just as quickly as he’s touched down here in New York, he’s off again to Hong Kong tomorrow.

#6685. The Only 9 Pieces You Need for a Chic Winter Capsule Wardrobe

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Getting dressed is hard enough on an ideal day, but add frigid temps and icy conditions into the mix, and I’m constantly on the verge of canceling my plans to stay in bed all day. As a fashion editor, one thing that I’ve found immensely helpful in this struggle is having a winter capsule wardrobe, replete with versatile staples that lend themselves to mixing and matching. It really takes the guesswork out of my mornings.

In case you can relate, I’ve decided to share my winning formula here. To maintain style while staying warm, you’ll need foundational pieces like a good coat and boots, plus a few winter accessories and, of course, a healthy dose of shearling. You’ll notice this list doesn’t include a pair of pants. This isn’t an invitation to go pants-less this winter, but rather a reflection of the fact that there aren’t any seasonal staples in the category. Utilize your jeans, trousers, or a pair of satin pants for a more holiday-friendly look.

Below, find nine key building blocks for all your wintery outfits and shoppable options that transcend trends. Good luck out there, friends.

Out of all the available outerwear options, I’ve decided that a wool coat is the first and foremost necessity. Every winter, I’m reminded of the importance of stylish jackets that can make or break my cold-weather ensembles. One of these will keep you warm, and if you shop smart, it will last for years.

The entrance to my high school was a long, uphill ramp, and I have many embarrassing memories of near or total wipeouts. I shudder at the thought of walking on an icy sidewalk. So, as an adult, I’ve traded my boat shoes for lug-sole styles (though they would not have been uniform-compliant) that offer more traction. I recommend a weatherproof option that can withstand rain, snow, and ice. As hard as it may be, avoid suede.

Turtlenecks are the heroes of winter layering. Whether you’re bundling up before hitting the slopes, adding warmth under a sweatshirt, or shielding your skin from that scratchy sweater, your winter capsule needs at least one of these bad boys.

I know cashmere can be costly, but it really is worth it. Plus, getting dressed for work during the colder months is so much easier when you have a trusted lineup of sweaters and knit tops.

A personal favorite, I confess! I adore a full-length, long-sleeve dress for the winter months. At a time when I can hardly be bothered to change out of pajamas, slipping into a dress can have a transformative effect. And there are so many delectable options to be had.

Everyone has their own opinion on furs—faux or real. Regardless of where you stand, this is the one time of year when you can lean into this look. Here at ELLE, we have a policy against real fur, so you can rest assured that these options are all faux.

If you want to do après-ski correctly, you’ll need a bag with a touch of shearling. Options abound this time of year, so feel free to be selective. I’ve rounded up a few favorites here.

#6684. Cemeteries Are the Unsung Hero of Travel

I was flipping through old journals recently and came across an entry dated December 31, 2017. I was in Todos Santos and had risen early to watch the sunrise over the Sierra de la Laguna mountains. There were scribbled goals for the new year, and reflections on what I wanted to leave behind. But the part that stood out most was a slice of the surrounding atmosphere—rooster crows echoing in the streets, and sunlight spilling onto a colorful cemetery in the distance. It reminded me that for as long as I’ve been traveling, I’ve always sought out the local cemetery. And it’s always left an indelible impression.

If you’re not a fellow taphophile, allow me to make the case. Spending time in cemeteries invites you to sink in. It sticks your mortality front and center and reminds you that you won’t always be here (stress!). It’s also a reminder to appreciate today, and remember those who aren’t around anymore. And as it pertains to visiting the dearly departed while traveling, cemetery strolls offer a distinct way to familiarize yourself with the local people. How a culture approaches death conveys a great deal. (In the case of Mexico, graveyards are not somber, but rather, awash in rainbow colors and elaborate decorations. Very lively!)

On a less morbid note, cemeteries are also really lovely for architecture and natural landscapes. History, too. And with the spooky season in full swing (which I’d argue lasts well beyond Halloween), there’s never been a better time to become a cemetery convert. Below, nine destinations worth planning a trip around.

I’m very lucky to live less than 10 minutes from this world-famous cemetery in Brooklyn. Green-Wood was founded in 1838 and is now a National Historic Landmark. Its paths stretch across 478 hilly acres, winding beside tombs belonging to iconic figures such as Jean-Michel Basquiat and Leonard Bernstein. It’s also a Revolutionary War historic site, and a haven for birdwatchers (over 260 species have been spotted).

When I lived in Los Angeles, outdoor movie screenings at Hollywood Forever Cemetery were a common occurrence. But despite being one of the trendiest ways to spend a Saturday night, this cemetery dates back to 1899. It serves as the final resting place for numerous Hollywood legends, from Judy Garland and Cecil B. DeMille to Eve Babitz. There’s even a cenotaph marker for Toto from The Wizard of Oz for fans to memorialize the adored cairn terrier.

Established in 1821, this breathtaking cemetery features an array of architectural styles, including Neo-Gothic, Neo-Maya, and even Art Deco. Its tree- and mausoleum-lined avenues are home to over 25,000 burial sites, including Felipe Carrillo Puerto (a progressive champion of human rights who was assassinated in 1924). Leading up to Día de Los Muertos, there is a festive procession called Paseo de las Ánimas that begins at the cemetery.

I’ll preface this with the unfortunate fact that Lafayette Cemetery No. 1 is currently closed to the public (reopening is still TBD). But that doesn’t stop me from declaring it my favorite in New Orleans. This 19th-century cemetery has appeared in films such as Interview With the Vampire and can still be enjoyed with a stroll around its scenic perimeter—which is punctuated by towering Spanish live oaks whose massive roots pry the concrete curb upward into a wonderfully spooky, uneven pathway. (If you’d like to go inside a New Orleans cemetery, don’t miss voodoo practitioner Marie Laveau’s tomb in St. Louis Cemetery No. 1).

This is the cemetery I’ve probably returned to the most over the years (and arguably the most famous in the world). It’s huge, so you’ll need to set aside an entire afternoon to explore its 110 acres that play host to thousands of burial plots. Also in the thousands: trees (about 5,000), making this landscape exceptionally beautiful as the leaves change colors. Don’t miss the highlights—Jim Morrison, Frédéric Chopin, Oscar Wilde, Édith Piaf—but also give yourself time to wander without a destination.

This is one of my favorite day trips from New York City this time of year. Hop on the Metro-North and get off at Philipse Manor Station. From there, it’s about a 10-minute walk to this 19th-century cemetery where writer Washington Irving is buried. After meandering around 90 acres of landscaped grounds, join a special event like an adaptation of Irving’s Bracebridge Hall complete with traditional carols and holiday cheer.

This cemetery was designed to resemble a city (rather than a burial ground) and is world-renowned for its neoclassical gates and beautiful maze of tree-lined paths. There are just under 5,000 burial vaults (all above ground), which include imposing mausoleums made of marble. La Recoleta Cemetery is the final resting place for dozens of Argentine presidents, as well as Nobel laureates and cultural figures.

Located a quick stroll from Hampstead Heath—my most beloved green space in all of London—this legendary cemetery is home to a fascinating mix of cultural figures ranging from Karl Marx to George Eliot (Mary Ann Evans, author of Middlemarch). Travelers can explore both the east and west sides of the cemetery without a guided tour, but why not book one for your first visit to get the full lay of the land? Highgate was modeled after Paris's Père Lachaise Cemetery and now operates as a historic park, nature reserve, and active burial site.

On a peaceful bluff of the Wilmington River, Bonaventure is one of the country’s most gorgeous cemeteries. Live oaks draped in Spanish moss hover above Victorian sculptures and timeworn tombstones belonging to famous figures such as John Muir. (Fun fact: during his thousand-mile walk to the gulf, Muir ran out of money and ended up sleeping in the cemetery, which he later wrote about in a famous chapter titled “Camping Among the Tombs.”)

#6680. Coperni Closes Following Relationship Breakdown with Distributor

Following months of trying to resolve its conflict with its distributor and shareholder, Tomorrow, Coperni has ceased operations, the brand revealed today.

In a personal memo shared with Vogue Business, co-founders and creative directors Arnaud Vaillant and Sébastien Meyer said they had been unable to fix an ongoing dispute involving unpaid sums.

“These eight years have been extraordinary,” the Coperni duo shared in a personal email. “Coperni has always been a collective adventure, and we are immensely proud of what we have created.” The company thanked the Fédération de la Haute Couture et de la Mode (FHCM), stores, buyers, press, celebrities, models, and other industry figures who had supported them.

“As the world becomes increasingly challenging, particularly in the fashion industry, we believe there is still so much to create and reinvent,” they said. “Innovation has always been our passion and a priority in everything we do. We look ahead with optimism and plenty of ideas, and cannot wait to share them with you.”

In June, Vogue Business reported that Coperni had secured protection from the Paris Court (France’s equivalent of Chapter 11) to help Coperni continue operating. At the time, Vaillant told Vogue Business that the support followed several months of pending payments owed to the brand by Tomorrow, its exclusive distributor and majority shareholder. Additionally, Coperni shared that Tomorrow had terminated its licensing agreement in place.

Complicating the issue, Tomorrow Ltd was sold to Progetto 11 in March. As previously reported, Progetto 11 is the holding company for Italian e-commerce platform The Level Group, which has worked with brands including Palm Angels, Herno, and Off-White. Former CEO and founder of Tomorrow, Stefano Martinetto, stepped down after the sale was completed.

Since then, the Coperni founders had been attempting to buy back their brand from Progretto 11. “Our view is based on what we found when we arrived [at the] end of March: a business already in the middle of a broader dispute about ownership and governance, lacking funding, also resulting in the cancellation of the last fashion show, and founders seeking to reacquire control,” Progetto 11 said in a statement at the time.

In June, Progetto 11 clarified that Coperni has been controlled by two entities: holding company Coperni UK Limited, which holds the license with Tomorrow, and subsidiary Coperni SAS, the main French operating company that oversees day-to-day operations and employs the teams.

Tomorrow acted as a licensor and distributor across its portfolio of brands, receiving all revenues and paying royalties to brands based on their individual deals. Tomorrow would also reimburse brands for costs incurred outside of design — like producing fashion shows or campaigns — but as Tomorrow’s wholesale business faltered due to challenging industry circumstances, Coperni claimed the company ceased paying Coperni’s revenue share and reimbursements.

In fiscal 2024, Tomorrow’s turnover fell 34% to £8.4 million, while gross profit margin decreased from 76% in 2023 to 41% year-on-year. And the company’s operating losses were mounting, up 28% year-on-year to £7.5 million. (Tomorrow had not submitted its fiscal 2025 earnings to Companies House by the time of the sale.)

Tomorrow’s issues first emerged when Coperni abruptly canceled its Fall/Winter 2026 show at Paris Fashion Week. In March, Martine Rose (also in the Tomorrow portfolio) shared a statement noting that she was unable to produce her upcoming collection due to reasons outside her control.

#6679. Ralph Lauren’s 17 Best Outfits of All Time

On Monday night, the Council of Fashion Designers of America crowned Ralph Lauren as its menswear designer of the year—his 12th win since the show’s inaugural ceremony in 1981, minting him as the most decorated designer in CFDA history. The council even has a tradition of creating awards in Lauren’s honor, as they did with the Fashion Legend Award in 2007 and the CFDA Members Salute in 2018.

At age 87, Lauren is the consummate businessman of American fashion, and he’s still producing masterclass-caliber collections that build upon his label’s established codes. In addition to his business savvy and keen eye for tailoring, the designer remains as relevant as ever in 2026 because of something far more ineffable: a deep-rooted sense of personal style. For Lauren, clothes aren’t just a wardrobe; they are identity. His own relationship with getting dressed, from his deep and abiding love of Westernwear to his knack for blending Waspy blazers with rugged workwear and military pieces, has always been at the core of everything he does. Here are some of his best looks from the last 50 years.

Technical hiking gear was a relatively late addition to the RL oeuvre, but the man was wearing hikers in the city long before hipsters discovered Salomons.

Like a skilled party DJ, Ralph Lauren has an uncanny knack for combining unlikely elements—like a yachtsman’s sweater and a pair of worn-in blue jeans—with complete ease.

There’s black-tie, and then there’s RL black-tie. There’s no doubt that Lauren can wear a pair of tuxedo pants and patent leather shoes as well as anyone, but he is much more himself in jeans and cowboy boots.

A two-year stint at Baruch College in Manhattan was the closest Lauren came to the Ivy League, but that didn’t stop him from adopting repp ties, Oxford collar shirts, and other hallmarks of the East Coast elite. The juxtaposition of oversized aviator shades with this solidly trad look is quintessential Ralph.

Think a funky belt can’t be the defining element of an otherwise understated fit? Lauren would respectfully disagree.

Few people will ever look as good in a biker jacket as Ralph Lauren did at age 70. The difference is in the details—the flannel shirt unbuttoned and tucked, the crisp white henley—and the confidence.

Lauren is a master editor, but the magic of his greatest looks is in details like a vest tucked into trousers, a knotted belt, and a pair of precisely rolled sleeves.

Yacht club up top, honkey tonk downstairs. Another Lauren signature.

Ralph Lauren never learned how to sew, but he has an instinctive understanding of tailoring. By blending the stiff silhouettes of Savile Row with the breezy swagger of American ivy style, he created a look that was all his own.

Style is all about understanding the rules before you can break them. Lauren certainly does, and that’s why this ensemble—from the wide-spread collar and slim tie combination to the double-down on stripes—works as well as it does.

There’s perhaps no more challenging look to pull off than “office cowboy,” but Ralph Lauren makes it look easy.

Leather pants and a denim shirt under a tweed jacket is another decidedly advanced maneuver, but (if executed correctly) a potentially powerful one.

In recent decades, Lauren has increasingly swapped his signature cowboy boots for La Sportiva hikers, anointing gorpcore in the process.

Lauren has always revered the look of traditional British tailoring, from safari suits to Savile Row, but he’s just as likely to pair his flannel suits with cashmere turtlenecks and cowboy boots as neckties and Oxfords.

#6677. 21 Easy Weeknight Dinners for November

As daylight dwindles and the November chill settles in, dinner calls for something cozy. Think chicken thighs nestled into caramelized onions, pasta slicked with brown butter, and hearty soups that practically demand a hunk of crusty bread. It’s time to lean into comfort food.

The good news? You don’t need to spend your whole Sunday cooking to make dinner feel special, so you’ll have plenty of time for that When Harry Met Sally rewatch. These 21 easy weeknight dinners deliver all the comfort without the commitment. There’s a three-ingredient pumpkin soup, gochujang chicken that gets a quick blast under the broiler, and a smoky one-pan pasta made with pantry staples. Plus a few Thanksgiving-adjacent flavors—sage, stuffing, squash—because the holiday is right around the corner.

Greek yogurt tenderizes the chicken quickly, but the real weeknight win is the broiler: just 15 minutes under high heat, and you’ve got dinner.

Juicy chicken meatballs and crisp-tender sesame green beans roast on opposite sides of the same sheet pan, streamlining both dinner prep and cleanup.

This speedy stir-fry recipe brings together thin strips of boneless pork shoulder and crisp-tender bok choy for a satisfying, weeknight-ready dinner.

Savory ground beef, fluffy scrambled eggs, and crisp vegetables turn a bowl of steamed rice into a satisfying Japanese dinner that’s ready in 35 minutes.

Brushed with a sticky, sweet teriyaki sauce, then hurled under the broiler, this salmon develops a glossy, caramelized finish in a matter of minutes.

This easy sheet-pan dinner pairs tender cod with a savory chorizo topping. Big flavor, minimal effort, and only one pan to wash.

Canned chickpeas and frozen spinach make this richly spiced saag quick to prepare—and any leftovers taste even better the next day.

Nutty brown butter, crunchy pecans, and hot Italian sausage make this an easy dinner bursting with fall flavors. One reader reports, “Made me feel like a 5-star chef.”

Buttery, garlicky shrimp scampi meets pasta in this weeknight-friendly dinner. A splash of white wine and a pinch of red pepper flakes make the sauce sing.

Canned butternut squash purée (find it by the canned pumpkin!) makes this cozy, cold-weather recipe come together in a snap. Vegetable broth and certified vegetarian parm keep it meat-free, but chicken broth works if that’s what you’ve got.

Four ingredients are all you need for these grown-up buttered noodles. Toasted almonds and parsley are totally optional, but add welcome texture and zing.

Pumpkin purée adds richness, body, and a gentle orange hue to this speedy ground beef chili, letting the flavors of the spices and aromatics shine.

Roasted squash, crispy bacon, and crunchy walnuts turn chopped salad into a proper fall dinner. Use pre-cut butternut squash to streamline prep.

When dinner needs to get on the table pronto, a tuna melt is hard to beat: pantry-friendly, cheesy, and comforting.

This fiery soup has a shockingly trim ingredient list: curry paste (we like Maesri), a can of pumpkin purée, and coconut milk. Perfect for busy November weeknights.

#6676. Everything We Know About The Batman: Part II Thanks to… Heidi Klum?

If you’d told me even a month ago we’d get significant spoilers for The Batman: Part II, the next Robert Pattinson-led Batman movie, in a photo Heidi Klum posted for her annual Halloween costume, I would find that both weirdly specific and entirely unbelievable.

And yet, that looks to be exactly what happened this past weekend when prosthetics supplier The Makeup Armoury posted BTS photos of the work prosthetics expert Mike Marino (who also worked to transform Colin Farrell into The Penguin for the first film and subsequent HBO Max series) was doing for Klum. If you’ve somehow been off-grid for the last few years, you may have missed that the famed supermodel takes Halloween incredibly seriously, frequently donning costumes with extensive makeup and designs that make her unrecognizable. This year was no exception, but it might have gone largely unnoticed had that photo not accidentally revealed clues about the upcoming superhero sequel, which is currently in production with an expected release date of February 18th, 2028.

In the photo, Marino, who provided a helping, ahem, hand in Klum’s costume together for the year, had a number of molds lingering in the background, which have seemingly confirmed that Brian Tyree Henry will play Two-Face, Sebastian Stan will play Victor Zsasz, and that Part II will feature the famed Court of Owls.

Henry’s mold appears to show the Atlanta actor with a disfigured face that mimics the iconic villain. Some, including me, in this very outlet, have, speculated that he might be playing either Dent or Detective Harvey Bullock, a hardened Gotham City cop who frequently works alongside Jim Gordon. But this seems to confirm it. Considering writer-director Matt Reeves has cited Jeph Loeb and Tim Sale’s The Long Halloween as an influence on his version of the Caped Crusader, it’s not ultimately a huge surprise, but perhaps a slight disappointment considering Reeves had stated his intention to move the sequel into uncharted territory by featuring a villain that had “never really been done in a film before.”

Which brings us to Victor Zsasz, who Stan seems to be playing. There was some speculation when he shaved his head upon joining the production he might be playing the character, but the cast looks to confirm the speculation. While the serial killer—who carves tally marks into his body for every person he’s killed—shows up in Batman Begins as a minor enforcer in Carmine Falcone’s crew, he’s got a much larger role in the comic books themselves. In Long Halloween, Zsasz is hired by Falcone to assassinate Dent before he's intercepted by Batman. Might Reeves look to flip the script here and disfigure Henry’s Dent in the process? This interpretation of Zsasz would certainly fit the extremely grounded approach Reeves took in the first installment. But there’s also some confusion here, as Stan was rumored to be playing Harvey when casting first broke and even went so far as to say he’d be playing the role in an interview over the summer. The French publication Le Journal du Dimanche did, however, later retract his statement.

The last accidental spoiler is a big scoop for comic book fans. Simply labeled “Owl 3,” this likely confirms that the Court of Owls will finally make their silver-screen debut. Created in 2012 by writer Scott Snyder and artist Greg Capullo, the Owls are one of the biggest new additions to the Batman canon in recent memory. The Court is a clandestine criminal society made up of Gotham’s wealthiest and most influential citizens, whose power and influence stretch back to the city’s earliest days. They have immeasurable resources and frequently deploy assassins, known as Talons, to do their bidding. This tracks with the story Reeves told in The Batman of a Gotham beset by a history of corruption. Owls are also bats' natural predators; so that, too, is bad news for Battinson.

While this potential leak is exciting and unexpected, it also raises doubts about the identity of Scarlett Johansson’s character, as she was rumored to be playing Harvey’s wife, Gilda Dent. Either way, never in a million lifetimes could we have guessed that Heidi Klum would be the one to spill the beans about one of the most anticipated comic book movies of the next few years.

#6675. Pumpkin Bolognese

Classic Bolognese, with its multi-hour cook time, can be truly remarkable, if you ever have a stretch to make it. In this version, a scoop of canned pumpkin purée is the head-turning ingredient that gives it full-blown flavor and body, without the wait typical of a nonna-style sauce. Lightly caramelizing the pumpkin in the pot along with tomato paste gives it a nutty, savory edge. Milk is the other surprise ingredient here, especially in the quantity of a full cup. Think of it as a tenderizer, making the final sauce soft and delicate. Pay attention to the order in which the ingredients appear—the milk goes in first with the wine to follow. If you switch the order, the acidic wine will curdle the milk.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Heat 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Add 1 large white or yellow onion, finely chopped, 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. freshly grated nutmeg and stir to combine. Cover pot and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion and celery are very soft, 8–10 minutes. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until onion and celery are golden around the edges, about 5 minutes.

Uncover pot and add 1 lb. ground beef, preferably 20% fat; season lightly with salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until beef is very lightly browned but not crisp (it will still be pink in spots), 6–8 minutes. Pour in 1 cup whole milk and cook, stirring occasionally, until milk has evaporated and fat is pooling on surface of meat, 7–10 minutes.

Pour in 1 cup dry white wine and cook, stirring occasionally, until wine has evaporated, 6–8 minutes. Add 1 cup canned pumpkin purée and 2 Tbsp. double-concentrated tomato paste; season generously with freshly ground pepper. Cook, stirring often and scraping bottom of pot, until combined and pumpkin darkens slightly, 8–10 minutes.

Pour in 1 cup water, reduce heat to low, and cook, stirring occasionally, until mixture is saucy, 12–15 minutes. If meat seems dry, add an extra ½ cup water and continue cooking another 3–4 minutes. Taste sauce and season with salt if needed. Keep warm.

Meanwhile, cook 12 oz. fresh tagliatelle or pappardelle or dry rigatoni, in a large pot of boiling salted water. If using fresh pasta, cook about 3 minutes. If using dry, cook until very al dente, about 2 minutes less than package directions.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to pot with sauce. Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid and 2 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about 1 cup). Increase heat to medium, bring to a simmer, and cook, tossing constantly, until pasta is al dente and sauce is slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.

Transfer pasta to shallow bowls and sprinkle with more Parmesan.

#6674. The Vogue Business Funding Tracker

Introducing the Vogue Business Funding Tracker, a running list highlighting the most notable and intriguing investment and M&A activity in fashion and beauty. From emerging disruptors to legacy giants undergoing major changes, we spotlight the deals that are shifting the dynamics of the sectors we cover, including fashion, beauty, tech and sustainability.

Company description: Founded in 1889, Lee has made its marks as one of the biggest heritage names in denim. The American brand generates an average of $1.5 billion in annual sales across 73 countries, of which almost 40% comes from outside the US and Canada. New York-based Authentic Brands Group has successfully acquired Lee from Kontoor Brands in an effort to expand Lee into adjacent categories, including activewear and workwear, as well as lifestyle offerings.

Investor(s): Authentic Brands Group (portfolio includes: Guess, Juicy Couture, Reebok).

Investor comments: “We are thrilled to welcome Lee to the Authentic family,” said Jamie Salter, founder and executive chair of Authentic Brands Group. “Lee has the heritage, recognition and consumer loyalty we look for in a brand. By connecting Lee to Authentic’s global platform and the right partners in key markets, we see a significant opportunity to expand its reach through content, experiences and new product categories.”

Company description: Touted as London’s first functional smoothie bar, Elevate launched at the Royal Exchange in June 2025, before opening in Selfridges in April 2026. Founded by Julia Baldet, its bestselling smoothie, The Glow, made with collagen and hyaluronic acid, has grossed close to half a million pounds since rollout. Elevate has collaborated with brands such as Nike x Skims, Adanola, Ouai and Medicube, as wellness continues to crossover into beauty and fashion. The new funding will be used to open additional London sites next year, after finishing its first full year with over £1 million in sales.

Investor(s): JamJar (portfolio includes: Innocent Drinks, Deliveroo, Humantra), Active Partners (portfolio includes: Tala, Healf, Salad Project) Cassius, Soho House founder Nick Jones.

Investor comments: “Elevate’s proposition is perfect: delicious smoothies that look great while meeting real nutritional and wellness needs. It’s clearly working; loyal customers love the brand. But most of all, we’re backing Julia. She’s focused, ambitious, creative and commercial, and we’re thrilled to support her as she builds Elevate into a category-defining brand,” JamJar partner Adam Balon said in a statement.

Company description: Frasers Group has successfully taken control of Hugo Boss. Following a rejected takeover bid of €2 billion (€38 per share) in June, the British retail conglomerate has raised its stake to approximately 50.08% — an additional purchase of 198,666 shares, equating to €7.63 million, according to the stock market filing. The German fashion company will now become a subsidiary of the Mike Ashley-owned business.

Hugo Boss believed the June takeover proposal to be “financially inadequate”, urging its shareholders to reject. Though Frasers continued its efforts, gradually raising its holding once again to 48% in mid-August (up from 30.3% in June, alongside the initial takeover bid). Frasers Group CEO Michael Murray assumed the Hugo Boss chair position last month, after Stephan Sturm stepped down.

Investor(s): Frasers Group Luxury (portfolio includes: Flannels, The Webster, Harvey Nichols, Matches).

Company description: Frasers Group has adjusted its stake in Burberry from 7.4% to 6%. This comes after the growing British retail group raised its position in the company from 6.3% last week, after upping it from 4.2% at the end of September. This marks a potential pullback from its current luxury brand spending spree.

Investor(s): Frasers Group Luxury (portfolio includes: Flannels, The Webster, Harvey Nichols, Matches).

Company description: Frasers Group has acquired a 8.78% stake in US-based sports brand Under Armour, continuing a string of cross-category investments in recent months. Earlier this week, Frasers upped its investment in Burberry to 6.3%, having also taken on ownership of esteemed department store Harvey Nichols in August. The Frasers portfolio spans discount retailer Sports Direct through to The Webster, House of Fraser, and Flannels, as well as a strong stake in Hugo Boss — upped to 47.89% in August. Under Armour’s share price has risen since the SEC filing was made on October 1.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: Harvey Nichols, Sports Direct, The Webster)

Company description: Frasers Group has upped its economic interest in Burberry from 4.2% to 6.3%, with the British brand now part of a new luxury division launched in early October. Also part of the luxury portfolio, Hugo Boss — of which Frasers now owns almost 48% — continues to reject the retail group’s takeover bids; it may be looking elsewhere for potential acquisitions.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: Flannels, The Webster, Harvey Nichols, Sports Direct).

Company description: Activewear brand 437 was founded in 2016 by co-CEOs Adrien Bettio and Hyla Nayeri. Initially founded as a swimwear brand, 437 moved into activewear in 2023, which is now the core of its business. The Toronto-based brand is the top-selling activewear brand on Revolve, and has fast become a celebrity go-to.

Funding and round: $15 million CAD, minority stake

Investor(s): Revolve (portfolio includes: Alliance Apparel, Alexandre Vauthier)

Investor comments: “437 is still a small player, but is already outselling nearly every activewear brand on our site, including billion dollar brands. The brand is great and the aesthetic and products are great — it’s really just building on their core momentum and continuing to gain awareness. Hyla and Adrien had built something very special, but had also reached a point where they needed additional capital, infrastructure, and a thought partner who had been through the same journey,” said co-founder and co-CEO Michael Karanikolas.

Company description: Founded by former fashion executive Yasmin Sewell, Vyrao launched in 2021 as a fragrance brand blending aromatherapy and neuroscience principles. The brand was ahead of the curve tapping into the cross-section of fragrance and wellness, by offering customers something more than just a scented mist. Following the acquisition, the genderless brand will embark on its next development phase under its new owner.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Company description: Based in LA, Arey launched in 2021 under entrepreneur Allison Conrad and celebrity hairstylist Jay Small, offering vitamin, antioxidant and peptide-infused products to help delay and repigment aging hair. The funding will support Arey’s new product development, ongoing clinical research, and expansion through retail partnerships.

Funding and round: Series A, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Unilever Ventures (portfolio includes:), Greycroft, Female Founders Fund.

Company description: AI-driven discovery platform Slayd launched in Gurugram, India, in 2025. Targeted at Gen Z, the startup sorts fashion items from more than 300 marketplaces and brands by theme and curates personalized feeds that enable product discovery across multiple sites. Slayd claims to currently have more than 200,000 users, and can identify emerging trends through its proprietary tech software. The investment will help strengthen its team and accelerate the growth of its private-label business, Slayd Originals.

Investor(s): AJVC (portfolio includes: Midcase, Bubble Me, Trufides).

Company description: ISDIN is a product of pharmaceutical company Corporación Químico-Farmacéutica Esteve (CQFE) and beauty group Puig, who partnered to launch the skincare brand in 1975. Since then, both families have supported ISDIN’s evolution into a global dermatological skincare business focused on scientific formulation and innovation. In acquiring CQFE’s 50% stake, Puig will obtain complete ownership of the Spanish brand.

Investor(s): Puig (portfolio includes: Charlotte Tilbury, Byredo, Penhaligon’s, Dr. Baraba Sturm).

Investor comments: “Expanding our presence in dermocosmetics is a strategic priority for Puig. ISDIN is a unique company, with a strong management team, a clear strategy and a distinctive position in dermatology and skincare. Full ownership will give Puig the best platform to support its next phase of growth and continue investing behind the science and innovation that have made ISDIN successful,” Puig CEO Jose Manuel Albesa said.

Company description: Founded in 2021, Talm (“To All the Mamas”) initially focused on bodycare products during pregnancy and postpartum, however the brand has gradually expanded to offer sensitive skincare for all stages of life. It currently offers around a dozen products, operates in roughly a dozen countries, and reports double-digit revenue growth. This marks the first acquisition for Caudalie, which plans to accelerate Talm’s global expansion and product development by leveraging its pharmacy network, sales force and infrastructure.

Company description: Medici Brands, owner of David Protein and newly launched confectionery brand HallPass, will use its Series B funding to enter the next phase of growth. This includes expanding HallPass’s retail presence, alongside the remainder of its product portfolio — extending David into new formats and categories, advancing product innovation, and enabling the launch and scaling of new brands such as Rowdy.

Funding and round: $250 million, Series B.

Investor(s): Greenoaks (portfolio includes: Stripe, Canva, Discord, Robinhood), Valor Equity Partners (portfolio includes: GoPuff, SpaceX, BitGo), Peter Rahal, Iconiq, Imaginary Ventures.

Investor comments: “Two years ago, David Protein showed customers they no longer had to choose between great macros and great taste, and it became one of the fastest-growing CPG brands in America. Now, Medici is bringing that approach to the rest of the store, building a house of brands that delivers the taste consumers adore, without making the compromises they have grown to accept,” said Greenoaks partner Neil Shah.

Company description: Truly Beauty is a plant-based personal care brand founded in 2013 by Maxx Appelman. Known for its viral, Gen Z-focused bodycare and social media marketing, Truly Beauty combines high-performing active ingredients with a luxurious but playful aesthetic. It is headquartered in Los Angeles. For razor company Dollar Shave Club, this marks its first acquisition as it extends beyond grooming.

Investor comments: “By layering Truly’s fast-turn product engine onto our AI-driven inventory planning and backend logistics, we are building a high-velocity innovation model that legacy CPG conglomerates simply cannot replicate,” said Dollar Shave Club CEO Larry Bodner.

Company description: Scottish-born accessible luxury leather goods brand Strathberry has closed its second funding round, consisting of a growth investment from Soho Square Capital’s new Fund II, and marking the fund’s first investment. The funding comes on the heels of a strong year for Strathberry, which delivered 39% year-on-year growth in 2026 at $50.5 million. Soho Square’s investment will support Strathberry founders Guy and Leeanne Hundleby’s ambitions to accelerate the brand’s North America expansion.

Funding and round: Undisclosed minority investment valuing the company at approximately £100 million, second funding round.

Investor(s): Soho Square Capital’s Fund II.

Investor comments: “Strathberry is an exceptional brand with a rare combination of craftsmanship, a distinctive design signature and a genuinely international, loyal customer base. The label’s ‘high-end quality at accessible prices’ ethos is resonating with shoppers disillusioned with top luxury houses. Guy, Leeanne, and the team have created something special, and there is significant scope to grow the business internationally,” Soho Square Capital director David Steel said in a statement.

Company description: Thorne, the science-backed supplements brand founded in 1984, has entered into a definitive acquisition agreement with P&G. Thorne is currently owned by L Catterton’s Flagship Fund. It is now best known in the wellness space for its creatine product, leaning into the rise of the supplement and its various formats. The acquisition helps to further Thorne’s attempt at becoming the market’s most-trusted personalized health brand, as well as P&G’s aim to move its personal health business upmarket. The transaction is expected to close later this year, subject to regulatory approval.

Investor(s): Procter & Gamble (portfolio includes: Seven Seas, Oral-B, Pepto Bismol).

Investor comments: “Consumer interest in selfcare, prevention, wellness, and personalized health continues to grow, and Thorne strengthens our position in premium wellness with a trusted, science-backed brand that complements our existing portfolio,” CEO of P&G Health Care Paul Gama said.

Company description: Frasers Group has taken a 4.2% position in British luxury brand Burberry. Frasers, the company behind House of Fraser, Sports Direct and Flannels, is holding the position through put options, which gives Frasers Group the right to buy shares at a predetermined stock price. The company is also the second largest shareholder in Mulberry PLC.

Frasers Group has been on an investing spree of late, increasing its stake in Hugo Boss to 30.3% and offering a takeover proposal. Frasers Group also bought Matches for £52 million in December 2023, before it announced that it was going into administration; Matches was sold in December 2025 to form part of newly established luxury group Hulcan.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: House of Fraser, Flannels, Sports Direct).

Company description: Solomei AI, the company behind the Callimacus platform, has announced that it has entered into an agreement for an investment from Salesforce. The investment will “support Callimacus’s efforts to expand its engineering and AI research capabilities, accelerate product development, and scale commercial operations across Europe and North America.” In January 2026, Callimacus, whose chairman is Brunello Cucinelli, was used to build the new e-commerce experience for the designer’s eponymous luxury brand.

Investor comments: “Brunello has always believed that technology should elevate humanity, and that conviction is at the heart of Callimacus,” said Marc Benioff, chair and CEO of Salesforce. “The team has developed an innovative platform that reimagines AI-powered experiences — bringing together conversational AI, enterprise context, and real-time personalization to create entirely new ways for businesses to engage with their customers.”

“Three years ago, Marc Benioff and I began an endeavor with mathematicians, philosophers, humanists, and technologists, from which Callimacus was born. Our idea was to create a simple, intuitive product capable of speaking the language of human beings; a sort of new web, without pages, categories, or predetermined paths, able to accompany the intent of each individual navigator. I look with great confidence and hope for the path that Callimacus will pursue with Salesforce’s investment,” Brunello Cucinelli, chairman of Solomei AI, added.

Company description: Founded in 2021, Merit is a US-based beauty brand designed as an antidote to using multiple, trend-led products — collapsing everyday cosmetics into a curated, minimal line-up. The investment is led by Vasiliki Petrou, managing partner at Semcap Beauty & Wellness, who also founded the Unilever Prestige division in 2014, spanning Dermalogica, Paula’s Choice, Hourglass, K18, and more.

Investor comments: “Merit is one of the most thoughtfully built brands in beauty, a true icon in the market. I love the timeless brand aesthetic, the simplified and edited approach to beauty, and the focus on the millennial and Gen X consumer, which is a significant white space in our industry. I am thrilled to support the continued global scaling of the brand,” Petrou said in a statement.

Company description: Frasers Group has increased its stake in Hugo Boss to approximately 30.28% (up from 26.06%), which demands an official takeover bid in line with German legislation. The move follows Frasers’s €2 billion (€38 per share) takeover proposal in June, which Hugo Boss believed was “financially inadequate”, urging its shareholders to reject. Frasers, now Hugo Boss’s largest shareholder, said its offer still stands through July 27.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: House of Fraser, Flannels, Sports Direct).

Company description: Syntetica is a French startup that transforms textile waste into recycled nylon through a proprietary chemical method that allows the processing of fabrics containing multiple materials. The funding will help Syntetica build its first commercial facility in France, which will be able to transform hundreds of tons of post-consumer textile waste annually. While Syntetica already works with labels such as Victoria’s Secret and Etam, it also plans to scale its recycling efforts and partner with more fashion brands.

Funding and round: $30 million, Series A.

Investor(s): Ecotechnologies 2 (portfolio includes: Standing Ovation, Mantle8), Lululemon (portfolio includes: Epoch Biodesign, Samsara Eco, Zymochem), MAS Holdings (portfolio includes: Victoria’s Secret, Calvin Klein, Gap), Swen Capital Partners, EQT Ventures.

Company description: Founded in 2021 by Abhi Arora and Sanket Agarwal, Fleek is a wholesale vintage fashion marketplace. Fleek connects retailers and resellers with verified, secondhand clothing wholesalers worldwide, enabling them to source vintage inventory in bulk through a digital marketplace with integrated logistics and quality assurance.

Funding and round: $25 million, Series B.

Investor(s): Burda Principal Investments (portfolio includes: Vinted), Ebay Ventures, FJ Labs, H14, Andreessen Horowitz, HV Capital, Y Combinator, and more.

Company description: Whering is a digital wardrobe and styling app founded in 2020 by Bianca Rangecroft. The app enables users to catalogue the clothes they already own, create outfits, track wardrobe usage, and receive styling recommendations, with the aim of encouraging more intentional fashion consumption and reducing unnecessary purchases.

Investor(s): Ebay Ventures, Google AI Futures Fund.

Company description: Hair technology company Halo has developed its first product, HaloBraid. Launching in salons this fall, the device will be the first automated hair braiding tool that works alongside stylists to halve braiding time from as long as 10 hours per appointment. Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian’s VC firm Seven Seven Six is leading the investment into a business that was launched off the back of Yinka Ogunbiyi’s winning Harvard Innovation Labs pitch last year.

Investor(s): Seven Seven Six (portfolio includes: Anthropic, ElevenLabs, Flock Safety), Bling Capital (portfolio includes: Palantir, Gusto, Everlane), AlleyCorp (portfolio includes: ShopMy, Gilt Groupe, Business Insider).

Investor comments: “As an investor, I look for founders that see something broken that everyone else has accepted as fixed.
