Investor comments: “Earth Rhythm represents an exciting addition to our portfolio and presents an opportunity to expand our play in the clean beauty space, a category with immense long-term potential,” said Adwaita Nayar, co-founder of Nykaa and CEO of Nykaa Fashion.

Company description: H&M Group’s digital fashion outlet launched in 2018. Due to a lack of demand, the group announced that Afound would be discontinued in August, but it will integrate with Secret Sales under a December relaunch, offering over €5 billion in revenue sourced from 3,800 premium brands.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Secret Sales, an off-price marketplace within private equity firm Perwyn’s portfolio.

Investor comments: “Bringing Afound into the Secret Sales family reinforces our commitment to growing our premium off-price solution across Europe. This acquisition is another step towards transforming the off-price landscape,” said Chris Griffin, CEO of Secret Sales.

Company description: Manchester-based men’s streetwear brand founded by brothers George and Michael Heaton in 2011. The brand has scaled quickly with a compound annual growth rate of 64 per cent since 2020, delivering double-digit profit margins, and expects to generate around £100 million in revenue by the end of the fiscal year. In 2021, Represent launched its ‘247’ performance line and in 2024 it introduced its first retail locations in LA and Manchester, with a London store planned for 2025. The brand aims to use the funding to fuel retail expansion and improve operational capabilities.

Funding and round: Minority stake, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): True (Portfolio includes: Formerly Known As Haeckels, Boy Smells).

Investor comments: “Represent is a real success story for British fashion. The team’s track record of developing culturally relevant products and acquiring loyal customers to the brand, despite the challenging consumer environment, is remarkable,” said Ejike Onuchukwu, investment director at True, who has joined Represent’s board.

Company description: Paris-based lab-grown leather startup founded in 2021. Faircraft manufactures leather using cellular biology that replicates the structure and cellular composition of animal skin. The funding will be used to expand Faircraft’s team, recruiting more engineers and biologists to scale its operations.

Funding and round: €15.8 million, Series A.

Investor(s): Kindred Ventures (portfolio includes: Poshmark, Postmates), Cap Horn, BPI, Sake Bosch, Entrepreneur First, Alliance for Impact, Heirloom.

Investor comments: “Leather has long been the cornerstone of the fashion industry, valued for its timeless appeal and durability — but its production comes with steep environmental costs. Faircraft’s lab-grown leather is a breakthrough for brands and consumers who refuse to compromise between quality and sustainability, and we’re proud to support them as they scale operations and bring this revolutionary product to market,” said Kanyi Maqubela, managing partner at Kindred Ventures.

Company description: Founded in 2019, Clean Skin Club is a mass skincare brand known for its single-use disposable facial towels, stocked across Amazon, Target and Beauty Bay, among others. The brand was inspired by an aesthetician’s complaint about the bacteria in spa towels. The funds will be used to expand the brand’s bricks-and-mortar retail, new product development and grow the team.

Funding and round: $32 million, Series X.

Investor(s): Astō Consumer Partners, Amberstone (portfolio includes: Bloom Nutrition, Crown Affair).

Investor comments: “Clean Skin Club is ushering in a new era of skincare through reimagining the category and delivering straightforward, science-backed solutions that truly work. The disruptive brand has amassed a cult following, ranking as a bestseller on Amazon and breaking through the large, high-growth skincare market,” said Clayton Christopher, co-founder of Astō Consumer Partners.

Company description: Prestige haircare brand founded in 2020 and known for its promotion of haircare as a selfcare ritual. Crown Affair previously generated $5 million in Series A funding in 2022, also led by True Beauty Ventures. The Series B funding will be used to expand Crown Affair’s offering at Sephora, build out its team and scale marketing initiatives.

Investor(s): True Beauty Ventures (Portfolio includes: K18 Hair, Caliray, Maude).

Investor comments: “As a long-time supporter, I have witnessed Crown Affair consistently demonstrate the strength of its brand with a unique blend of elevated, clean haircare innovation, thoughtful hair rituals and authentic storytelling,” said Cristina Nuñez, co-founder and managing partner of True Beauty Ventures.

Company description: Beauty supplements and wellness brand, founded by influencer Tati Westbrook in 2018. Westbrook departed the company in August 2024 after settling a four-year legal battle in which her business partner, Clark Swanson, accused Westbrook and her husband of fraud, negligence and breach of fiduciary duty to Halo Beauty.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Investor comments: “We’re honoured to carry Halo Beauty’s legacy forwards by expanding its mission of clean, effective beauty and wellness. This acquisition marks a new era of innovation and commitment to empowering consumers with products that enhance both their beauty and overall well-being,” said the private investor.

Company description: Skincare brand known for peptide-infused anti-ageing products. The brand claims its signature OS-01 peptide can reverse the skin’s biological age ageing by preventing senescent or “zombie” cells, which are cells that are alive but damaged. OneSkin was founded by four PhD scientists: Carolina Reis de Oliveira, Alessandra Zonari, Mariana Boroni and Juliana Carvalho. The recent investment brings OneSkin’s total funding to $20 million.

Investor(s): Selva Ventures, Plus Capital, Unilever Ventures, Able Partners, Camila Alves McConaughey (Brazilian-American model and wife of actor Matthew McConaughey), tech entrepreneur Kevin Rose, plus previous investors.

Investor comments: “As a Brazilian woman, I am thrilled to invest in a brand founded by four Brazilian female scientists — my heritage is something I’m incredibly proud of, and I am honoured to support those who are executing this work. The OneSkin team has built a line of products that hold a unique space in the massive skincare market. I fell in love with the products the moment I saw the results on myself, and I knew I had to be a part of it! I’m so looking forward to seeing their future innovations and continued success with the help of this funding,” said McConaughey.

Company description: Wholesale vintage clothing marketplace founded in 2021 by Abhi Arora and Sanket Agarwal. The platform connects retailers and resellers to inventory from verified vintage wholesalers around the world.

Funding and round: £17 million total, £4.7 million in seed and £12.3 million in Series A.

Investor(s): HV Capital (portfolio includes: Depop, Zalando, Hello Fresh), Andreessen Horowitz (portfolio includes: Instagram, Pinterest, Roblox), Y Combinator (portfolio includes: Snap, Airbnb), Shopify president Harley Finkelstein, former Depop CEO Maria Raga.

Investor comments: “We are proud to invest in Fleek, a company that is redefining the secondhand fashion landscape. Fleek’s innovative approach to scaling the secondhand market globally reflects tremendous potential for growth. The marketplace not only addresses current industry needs but also paves the way for a more sustainable future in fashion. We’re excited to be part of this journey,” said Felix Klür, general partner at HV Capital.

Company description: Founded in 2005 in Stockholm by Jockum Hallin, Cristopher Nying and Richardos Klarén, Our Legacy is known for high-quality menswear with intricate design signatures. The brand has around 200 stockists and seven of its own stores, and has risen in notoriety thanks to buzzy collaborations with Stüssy and Emporio Armani.

Funding and round: Minority stake, terms undisclosed.

Lead investor(s): LVMH Luxury Ventures (portfolio includes: Aimé Leon Dore, Lyst, Heat).

Investor comments: “Our Legacy is the epitome of what we could call the ‘quiet cool’ tendency, featuring a unique blend of contemporary minimalism and creative subversion,” said Julie Bercovy, CEO of LVMH Luxury Ventures Advisors.

Company description: Californian premium athleisure brand Vuori was founded in 2015 by Joe Kudla. The brand is known for its unique fabrics and is certified as carbon neutral by Change Climate. Following this investment, the brand’s valuation has reached $5.5 billion, building on a $400 million investment by Softbank Vision Fund 2 in 2021, which brought its valuation to $4 million.

Funding and round: $825 million, secondary tender offer.

Lead investor(s): General Atlantic (portfolio includes: Gymshark, Sézane, Tory Burch), Stripes (portfolio includes: On, Reformation, Khaite) and existing investors.

Investor comments: “Vuori encapsulates everything we look for in a Stripes investment — the products are amazing and beloved by the consumer, the team is fanatical about quality and innovation, and the market for athleisure is global with durable tailwinds,” said Chris Carey, partner at Stripes.

Company description: Secondhand peer-to-peer marketplace founded in 2008 by Milda Mitkutė and Justas Janauskas in Lithuania. The platform is Europe’s largest clothing resale marketplace. The recent investment brings Vinted’s valuation to €5 billion.

Funding and round: €340 million, secondary share sale.

Investor(s): TPG Tech Adjacencies, Hedosophia (portfolio includes: Monzo, Go Puff), Baille Gifford, Invus Opportunities (portfolio includes: Coupang, Chrono 24), FJ Labs (portfolio includes: Farfetch, Uber, Klarna), Manhattan Venture Partners (portfolio includes: Discord, Epic Games, X), Moore Strategic Ventures.

Investor comments: “We’ve seen that consumers are increasingly choosing secondhand as a core part of their wardrobe, as sustainability and flexibility become top of mind for many people. Vinted’s customer focus, leading product experience, and sophisticated approach to logistics have made this market accessible to an even broader population,” said TPG partner Andrew Doyle.

Company description: Biotech-powered prestige skincare brand Reome was founded by beauty editor and acupuncturist Joanna Ellner in 2023. The UK-based brand is known for its sensorial products and is stocked in Space NK, Liberty and Moda Operandi among others.

Investor(s): Rianta Capital (portfolio includes: El Rayo, Home Cooks).

Company description: UK-based women’s shirt brand launched in 2017 by a former Vogue stylist and Tatler editor Pip Durell. The B Corp-certified brand, which is known for timeless designs inspired by men’s tailoring and British heritage, launched its first pair of trousers earlier this year and plans to expand further with blazers and knitwear at the start of 2025. With Nothing Underneath was named one of Walpole’s Brands of Tomorrow in 2022.

Lead investor(s): Pembroke VCT (portfolio includes: Tala, Me+Em, Bella Freud) and JamJar Investments (portfolio includes: Deliveroo, Oatly, Spoke).

Investor comments: “With Nothing Underneath (WNU) holds a unique position in the womenswear market. Pip and her team have built a fantastic brand around one staple item, the shirt — an essential in most women’s wardrobes. It has become a standout in the fashion industry and early growth metrics have given us conviction in the brand. This investment will enable this emerging British heritage brand to enhance its product range, assist with growth and support WNU’s international reach,” said Andrew Wolfson, CEO of Pembroke Investment Managers.

Company description: UK-based luxury retail platform that stocks a curation of independent brands. The retailer is known for its selection of vibrant eveningwear. Founded in 2019 by Nina Briance, Cult Mia initially received $3 million in seed funding in November 2023 led by Fuel Ventures, with participation from Morgan Stanley and David Wertheimer of the Chanel family.

Funding and round: $2 million, seed (bringing total seed funding to $5 million).

Investor(s): H&M Group Ventures (portfolio includes: Goop, Klarna) and existing investors.

Investor comments: “We are delighted to invest in Cult Mia on their mission to launch independent and diverse designers from around the world. We have been incredibly impressed by all that Cult Mia has achieved in such a short space of time,” said Nanna Andersen, chief of new growth and ventures at H&M Group.

Company description: Founded in 1997 by Dr Gregory Brown, Révive is known for its luxury serums and creams powered by bio-renewal technology. The brand was previously acquired by Shiseido in 2016, before it was sold to Tengram Capital Partners in 2017.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): S’Young Group (portfolio includes: Evidens de Beauté, Pier Augé).

#6672. The Clarks Wallabee Goes Gorpcore

Clarks has been on one lately. Over the past few weeks, Moncler worked up the British footwear brand's signature Wallabee, while A.P.C. took on the Desert Boot and the Weaver. Now, Clarks has called in Italian shoemaker Diemme to drag three of its biggest silhouettes up a mountain.

(In case you don't spend all day thinking about Italian hiking boots, here's a primer: Diemme was founded in Montebelluna, a town in northern Italy with a very serious footwear-making history. The brand is best known for taking the kinda boots originally built for mountains and making them nice enough to wear with your very best trousers. Every pair is still made at its factory in Veneto, and the upcoming Clarks collection is, too.)

The main event is the Wallabee, of course. Diemme reworked the familiar moccasin-shaped shoe and covered it in pale “champagne” suede from Charles F. Stead, the British tannery responsible for some of the nicest fuzzy leather in footwear. So far, so classic. But then you get the thick rope laces and rubber mudguard wrapped around the bottom. Underneath, the OG crepe sole has been swapped out for the chunky, lugged unit found on Diemme's Roccia Vet and Cornaro boots. It makes the whole shoe sit higher and gives it enough tread to deal with more than a slightly sticky pub floor. Your ’Bees are now ready to hit the trails.

There are two more styles in the cross-branded collection. The Desert Boot comes in the classic “cola” brown suede, only now it's been fitted with a heavy-duty sole. Then there's the Desert Trek, which has been transformed into a mid-cut boot and made from black full-grain leather. It keeps the signature center seam and little Trek Man logo, but it's easily the biggest and baddest of the three, with metal D-rings running up the lacing system and a beefed up ankle for extra support.

The Diemme x Clarks collection is set to drop on November 5, purchasable through Diemme, Clarks, and select stockists globally.

A version of this story originally appeared in British GQ.

#6670. A Diwali Menu That’s Full of Joy (and Sticky Chicken Wings)

Growing up, I remember a steady stream of guests coming in and out of our home in the weeks leading up to Diwali. The season would start with Navratri, a nine-night Hindu festival celebrating the divine feminine, Shakti, through the worship of Goddess Durga. Our celebrations were led by women, my grandmother, mother, and aunts, who would meticulously clean the house and spend weeks preparing snacks and sweets. They taught me the art of hosting and how to share the joy of food with our community.

I came to associate Diwali with that sense of abundance, care, and graciousness. There was always more food than we needed, and always room for more people. When I moved to New York, I started to miss that deeply, so I began a tradition to share Diwali with my chosen family here, many of whom were experiencing the holiday through food for the first time.

I’m the kind of host who likes to enjoy her own party, which means being strategic about the menu. I lean on dishes like my homestyle chicken kari, which can be made ahead and tastes even better the next day. And then there are dishes that bring a little theater to the table, like the creamy rice pudding which gets torched before serving. I want food that feeds a crowd, feels special, and lets me spend less time in the kitchen and more time with the people I love.

Guests always ask me for this crowd-pleasing app. Japanese sweet potatoes have a creamy texture that pairs beautifully with the spicy, crunchy elements of chaat. Best of all, the spuds can be cooked ahead, with the toppings added just before serving. One less thing for you to do on the big day.

Wings reign supreme when it comes to a party appetizer, and these tamarind-glazed ones deliver tangy punch in every bite. The marinade combines tamarind purée, fish sauce, brown sugar, red pepper flakes, and cumin, with extra glaze brushed on for maximum flavor and char. Be sure to finish with fried onions for bonus crunch.

This tastes like you spent hours cooking, but actually it comes together in less than an hour. The best part? It’s even better the next day, making it ideal for hosting. Gently reheat the kari before guests arrive, letting the warm, heady spices fill your home before everyone gathers around the table.

Mushrooms are an underrated ingredient in Indian cooking, and this creamy masala puts the earthy veg front and center. Sautéing them in batches gives the shrooms beautifully caramelized edges, while deglazing the pot captures all those flavorful browned bits. Serve the masala with rice or warm flatbread to sop up all the savory sauce.

No Diwali celebration is complete without something sweet, but dessert doesn’t have to be elaborate to feel special. This recipe transforms a handful of pantry staples into a rich, creamy rice pudding. For a playful twist, finish it with a crackly brûléed sugar crust and serve with a scoop of mango sorbet.

#6669. Pumpkin Enchiladas With Black Beans

Homemade enchiladas might sound like a laborious weekend project, but with a few clever tricks, this version made with black beans and pumpkin can be whipped up on even the most hurried of work nights. For starters, canned pumpkin creates the base of a quick sauce that requires no precooking. And because they are vegetarian, the filling—a combination of canned black beans, onion, and bell pepper flecked with cilantro—comes together in a flash. In lieu of baking the enchiladas, this version opts for broiling in order to brown the tops while also heating the enchiladas through in the same skillet you cook the beans in. A flourish of pumpkin seeds, sliced onion, cilantro, and fresh lime brightens up everything, although serving them straight from the oven would be just as delicious.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large broilerproof skillet over medium-high. Add 1 large white onion, finely chopped, and 1 medium green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, and cook, stirring often, until browned in spots and fragrant, 7–9 minutes. Add 4 garlic cloves, finely grated, two 15-oz. cans black beans, rinsed, and 2 Tbsp. chili powder and cook, stirring occasionally, just until combined and beans are warmed through, about 3 minutes. Transfer bean mixture to a large bowl; reserve pan.

Smash bean mixture with a spoon or potato masher until about half of the beans are mashed. Mix in juice of 1 lime and ¼ cup coarsely chopped cilantro; season with kosher salt. Set bean mixture aside.

Whisk together one 15-oz. can pumpkin purée, 1 tsp. Tabasco, and 1¼ cups water in a large bowl; season pumpkin sauce with salt.

Place 1 of twelve 6" flour tortillas on a surface. Scoop out ¼ cup (heaping) reserved bean mixture and arrange in center down length of tortilla. Scatter some of 4 oz. pepper jack cheese or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup), over, then roll up tortilla into a cylinder. Place, seam side down, in reserved skillet. Repeat process with remaining tortillas. Brush tops with oil.

Place a rack in upper third of oven; heat broiler. Broil enchiladas until tops are deeply toasted and charred in spots, 4–7 minutes (depending on your broiler; watch carefully as they can go from browned to burnt very quickly). Pour pumpkin sauce over enchiladas and spread into an even layer. Top with remaining 4 oz. pepper jack cheese or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup) and raw pumpkin seeds (pepitas; if using). Broil until cheese is melted and deeply browned in spots, 4–7 minutes (watch carefully). Remove enchiladas from broiler and top with thinly sliced white onion and cilantro leaves with tender stems. Serve with lime wedges for squeezing over.

#6668. The 9 Best Hotels in Vermont for the Perfect New England Getaway

Known for its picturesque little towns and scenic mountain views (and, equally importantly, its cheese), Vermont is worth a visit year-round—but it really comes alive in the fall, when the foliage is at its peak and the brisk chill in the air is still a novelty. From charming towns like Woodstock to lakeside cities like Burlington and outdoorsy havens like Stowe, the New England state doesn’t disappoint if you’re traveling in search of autumnal activities. And just like their surroundings, the best hotels in Vermont are full of charm.

Travelers looking for sleek accommodation with glitzy furnishings should probably go elsewhere: this is the time to lean into the rustic appeal of the region. Quaint bed and breakfasts, cozy inns, and inviting lodges are the way to go—so with this in mind, we pulled nine options from across the state. Cue the cider.

I recently spent a fall weekend at the Seminary, at a time when the surrounding foliage was in peak form and the brisk air made certain features—like an antique claw-foot tub and wood-burning fireplace—especially appealing. Each guest room has its own personality, outfitted with original artwork and vintage furniture (made modern with touches like Bellino Italian bedding and chrome desk lamps). There’s a cranberry-colored room with a matching velvet seating area; a moody blue room with a gorgeous antique room divider; a cozy little mauve room with ornate wooden furniture and marbled lampshades where I made myself at home. The real highlight, though, is the communal space. It’s hard to pick a favorite between the aqua blue kitchen, complete with a raspberry-colored zellige backsplash that could inspire even the most cooking-averse to whip up pancakes, and the colorful living room where sunlight streams through oversized windows; either way, this is a spot that encourages gathering the whole friend group together for a weekend away.

This 53-room Alpine-inspired spot is lodge living at its finest. Explorers book it for its prime location directly on Cady Hill Forest, which has multiple trails for hiking and biking. Spend your rest day alternating between the hot tub, sauna, and its two pools. The design leans rustic (give or take a couple of Togo chairs), with moss green paneling, tartan upholstery, and wood beams running throughout. It’s all centered around a Great Room, a multi-use space that houses both daily breakfast and a bar—the ideal spot to unwind by the fire after a day outdoors.

If you’ve ever wondered what a woodsy cabin would look like with a Wabi-Sabi-inspired overhaul, AWOL is the answer. The 35-room boutique hotel pulls inspiration from organic shapes and washed-out color palettes, resulting in a deeply tranquil space. If you’re visiting in the winter to take advantage of the nearby slopes, make sure to book a room that comes with ski racks—and bring a swimsuit for a dip in the cedar hot tub while you’re at it. (Your sore muscles will thank you after.) The complimentary breakfast, which is served daily in the light-filled lodge space, is another highlight. (It features an artisanal toast bar, which is frankly too intriguing to pass up.)

For a city stay that still feels tucked away, book a room at Blind Tiger. Originally a mansion built in 1881, the 14-room boutique hotel feels like staying at your eccentric friend’s country home in the best way; splashy decor and mixed prints characterize the aesthetic, and many of the pieces are handmade or one-of-a-kind. (Plus, as none of the rooms come with a TV, unplugging is heavily encouraged.) The central solarium is a great place to unwind with a book and a cup of tea in the afternoons, too.

Another Bluebird by Lark project (this one predating the Cady Hill Lodge by two years), Tälta Lodge offers itself up as a slightly more pared-back alternative. There are 51 rooms and suites, many of which come with balconies for soaking up the great outdoors. That’s not to say it skimps on amenities: the indoor pool is heated, and the bar lobby is stocked with local beer on tap.

Dating back to 1793, it’ll be hard to find a more historic stay in Vermont than the 142-room Woodstock Inn & Resort. The sprawling property has been updated many times—most recently in 2018—and today includes all the luxurious bells and whistles without sacrificing that old-school charm. Dine at one of the on-site restaurants for those days when it’s too cold to venture out; Richardson’s Tavern focuses on locally sourced ingredients with a contemporary twist, like a chanterelle-and-cherry tomato bucatini pasta or crispy quail served with pickled blackberries and poultry jus.

The very picture of a quaint New England B&B, this place has a small number of guest rooms that put on a charm offensive: some have working fireplaces, others have mountain views, and all have a distinctly old-school inn feel. In addition to a full country breakfast served daily in the dining room, the property includes a French-Vermont fine dining restaurant to book if you’re traveling to celebrate a special occasion.

Sitting on 112 acres of lush land that includes everything from a trout pond to apple orchards, this hotel has no shortage of activities (including pastry classes and archery lessons, if you need a break from all the hiking and biking and want to stay put for a day). In terms of accommodation, you have a similarly vast number of options. Stay in a Historic Inn room for farmhouse simplicity, a Coldbrook room for a more pampered experience, or the Carriage House for a group trip.

For a true country inn experience, stay at the Rabbit Hill. No two suites are remotely alike: in one, you’ll find a rustic cedar four-poster bed set against tartan wallpaper, while in the next room over, a California-inspired, honey-colored design scheme awaits. Start your day off with the free breakfast, pop in for afternoon tea, and end the night with marshmallow roasting at the fire pit or a martini in the British-inspired pub. When you’re not snacking, book an ATV tour of the country roads or try your hand at canoeing—the hotel can help you set up a host of activities, so you’ll never be bored.

#6667. Wildly Delicious Weeknight Dinners To Keep You Cozy All November Long

There’s more than just Thanksgiving to plan for.

November is the month when comfort food season really kicks into full gear. It’s the last month that really feels like fall before those pleasantly chilly evenings turn teeth-chattering, the leaves are still colorful and on the trees, and, of course, we can’t forget about Thanksgiving, so we’re not letting it get away without celebrating all it has to offer. Join us this November as we cook up cozy, comforting meals for both weeknights and special occasions. We’ve got 40 recipes to help inspire you to make dinner this November—one for every day of the month, and then some.

We’ve included a good mix of entirely new recipes, like our lasagna alla vodka skillet and our sheet-pan chicken tagine, as well as some old cold-weather classics like our chicken & dumplings, our broccoli cheddar gnocchi soup, and our chili mac.

Looking for cozy recipes for November? Check out our favorite one-pan fall dinners, under-an-hour comfort foods, and easy comfort food recipes.

Lasagna and penne alla vodka are two Italian-American staples that go hand in hand. Because our one-pot lazy lasagna skillet is a weeknight favorite, it only felt right to consolidate these two classics in one pan.

This streamlined version stays as true as possible to the authentic flavors, using readily available grocery store ingredients, but cuts down on the time by finishing things in the oven.

This sheet-pan chicken tagine is the ultimate glow-up, transforming the complex, slow-simmered flavors of the classic North African dish into a streamlined meal perfect for busy evenings or an effortless dinner party.

This pumpkin pot pie is basically a pumpkin coconut curry baked beneath a flaky, golden crust that turns out equal parts comforting and festive. The carved Jack-o'-lantern top transforms a simple pot pie into a showstopping centerpiece that's almost too cute to cut into.

Carbonara always feels like a luxurious dish, but it's made with the simplest ingredients: eggs, spaghetti, Pecorino Romano, and pork. Add a bottles of Shaoxing and soy sauce, and you've got yourself an unforgettable meal.

In the world of all of our Marry Me Chicken variations, this just may be our new favorite version. One spoonful instantly made me think of my childhood. This easy comfort food recipe is perfect on a cold night, and simple enough to whip up when you don't feel like making anything (like on a weeknight after a weekend full of potlucks and Friendsgivings).

Slow-cooked turkey legs are this year’s ultimate Thanksgiving hack (we're not stopping you the rest of the month either!). No basting, no inevitable dry meat—no fuss at all. All you have to do is make an easy festive herb butter, wrap everything in foil, and let it roast unsupervised.

This recipe combines the rich, smoky flavors of traditional barbacoa with a cheesy topping and buttery biscuits for an irresistible meal. At the heart of this dish is succulent beef chuck roast, slow-cooked in a blend of fire-roasted tomatoes, chipotle chiles, and a medley of spices.

And it’s not just like the stalwarts like Gap, Banana Republic, Abercrombie and J.Crew in the mix, although they are heavily in the mix. Abercrombie doesn’t have any specific promotions that are live at the moment, but the sale section was recently stuffed with some ideal fall building blocks—most notably some baggy cords—that will make a refresh as easy and affordable as you’d ever hoped it could be.

Nearly all of J.Crew’s spring-summer collection is on sale at the moment, over 300 pieces up to 40% off through May 26—including a whole bunch of heat-beating shirting, lightweight pants, archive classics and basically anything else you’d want to be on sale.

The first name in denim has a pretty nifty “buy two, get 30% off” promotion going on site-wide, so if you’re searching for some jeans, you might just want to buy a couple pairs. (Or maybe a trucker. Or sherpa-lined trucker. You’re in charge.)

Diving into Lost & Found’s sale section is one of the more enjoyable shopping experiences one can have online right now: the selection is great, the brand list is a top-five worldwide and there’s plenty of inventory, which puts it in stark contrast with some of the less rewarding sale sections.

One of the most quietly great, easy-to-wear brands in the game recently reloaded the sale section, and basically no category was left unturned. Of particular note, are the killer sweatshirts currently available with a healthy discount applied.

Mr Porter’s sale section is the kind you can lose an hour in without realizing it, even months after a seasonal sale has ended. Case in point: there’s roughly 500 pairs of shoes and 900 jackets on sale at this very moment, and while sizes might be hit and miss, the deals aren’t.

REI’s Deals section always lives up to the billing, but right now it’s about as good as it’s ever been. Hundreds of pieces from heavyweights like Arc’teryx, Patagonia, The North Face and more are discounted up to 50%, including plenty of winter-specific gear for anyone lacking in that department.

Todd Snyder presumably won’t be partaking in the Black Friday festivities this year—they announced a new sale structure a while back—but that doesn’t mean the already-on-sale fare doesn’t hold up to the promotions sure to fire up across the board.

This year in the US, Black Friday is on Friday, November 27, a day after Thanksgiving. While that’s the official date, many retailers roll out deals throughout November. You can expect the biggest discounts to happen between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday, but be on the look out for retailers to launch sales early.

Cyber Monday lands on November 30 this year, the Monday after Thanksgiving. Most brands keep the deals rolling through the week—but that doesn't mean a deal will last all day, so act fast.

Are clothing deals better on Black Friday or Cyber Monday?

Black Friday and Cyber Monday both deliver a plethora of clothing deals, but they play a little differently. Big-name retailers and legacy brands usually kick things off on Black Friday, while smaller menswear boutiques tend to hold their fire until Cyber Monday. Expect solid discounts starting around 20% off—and keep your eyes peeled for the coveted sale-on-sale action that’s become the norm in recent years.

#6665. No-Knead Pumpkin Focaccia

For those who fall into the pumpkin-should-be-savory camp, let us offer up a new recipe primed to become a seasonal staple: Pumpkin Focaccia. The iconic bread we know and love is ripe for the pumpkin treatment, lending it a golden hue and earthy sweetness. This version doesn’t require any kneading, making it straightforward enough to pull off in a single afternoon. You’ll perform a series of folds as it rises, simply pulling and stretching the dough to help it develop gluten. A showering of fresh rosemary and flaky salt on top is optional, but it takes crisp, plush focaccia from good to great. Serve it with a bowl of olive oil for dipping or a schmear of cream cheese to lean into the seasonal profile.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Mix one ¼-oz. envelope active dry yeast (about 2¼ tsp.), 5 cups (625 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. light brown sugar, and 1½ cups warm water in a large bowl until a dry, shaggy dough forms. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot 15 minutes.

Place a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough and moisten hands in water, shaking off excess. Stretch 1 side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat process 3 more times, turning bowl after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Remoisten your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat entire process 2 more times (folding and resting), about 1 hour more. By the last full fold, the dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Pour ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil into a 13x9" metal baking pan. Lightly oil your hands and punch down dough, then transfer to prepared pan. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Turn dough salted side down to coat both sides in oil. Press into an even layer with your fingers. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 450°. Unwrap focaccia and scatter rosemary leaves and more sea salt over if desired; drizzle with oil. Oil your hands and press fingers into focaccia several times to create dimples across surface, making sure to press fingers all the way down to the bottom of the pan. Bake focaccia, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until deep golden brown, 23–28 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let focaccia cool slightly in pan. Using a metal spatula, turn out focaccia onto rack and let cool completely.

Do Ahead: Focaccia can be made 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

#6664. Cranberry Meringue Pie

A big, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd. The vibrant filling is made even more sour with a generous amount of lime juice. Think lemon meringue pie but holiday-ified. Use our Perfect Pie Crust as the base to create a sturdy-flaky foundation, and be sure to start the pie the day before you plan to serve it, as the curd requires several hours of chilling to set into a sliceable texture. Cut into it too soon and it will run onto your plate, creating a messy—albeit delicious—slice.

We never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper. Our favorite is from Gestura. Use the scraper to cut butter, fold dough and nudge it into shape, transfer it from counter to plastic wrap, trim edges, cut strips, and, sure, scrape flour off your counter.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

3 hours (plus 30 minutes for freezing and 5 hours for chilling)

Whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too quickly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool.

Transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

Spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

#6663. A Night of Firsts: The History-Making Victories Across the 2026 Midterm Elections

It took 94 years for Kansas to elect another Democratic U.S. senator. It took the entire history of the United States for a Black woman to be elected governor. Both happened on Tuesday night—two significant milestones amid a night of major triumphs, firsts, and history-making moments.

The 2026 midterm elections delivered a political earthquake, with a series of candidates and statewide contests drawing national attention. Democrats reclaimed control of both chambers of Congress, flipping seven Senate seats—including in Republican strongholds where the party had not won in decades. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor in American history. In New Mexico, Deb Haaland became the first Native American woman elected to lead a state, while Minnesota’s Peggy Flanagan became the first Native American woman elected to the U.S. Senate. Michigan elected the country’s first Muslim senator, Abdul El-Sayed, and New Hampshire its first openly gay male senator, Chris Pappas. And longstanding political barriers fell elsewhere—from Texas electing its first Latina governor to Florida electing its first Black governor, Republican Byron Donalds.

And it was true that the gubernatorial races sent shockwaves from state to state. In California, Xavier Becerra, the former U.S. secretary of health and human services, became the first Latino ever elected governor of the state. And both Nevada and Wisconsin elected their first Black governors: Attorney General Aaron Ford and Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, respectively. Minnesota elected its first woman governor in Amy Klobuchar, who will leave behind her seat in the U.S. Senate after two decades. And in Ohio, former state health director Amy Acton defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy to become the first woman elected governor in the state’s history.

The Democratic gains were impressive across states where Republicans have dominated for years. In Iowa, state auditor Rob Sand became the first Democrat elected governor since 2006. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton defeated incumbent Roger Marshall to become the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from the state since 1932. South Carolina delivered another seismic upset as pediatrician Annie Andrews became the first Democrat to win a Senate election there since 1998—and the first woman ever elected to represent the state in the upper chamber. Former North Carolina governor Roy Cooper ended an 18-year Democratic Senate drought, and in Texas, state representative James Talarico became the first Democrat elected to the Senate since 1988, defeating Republican Ken Paxton.

There were significant victories further down the ballot, too. In Alabama, Democrat Allison Montgomery defeated Republican incumbent Phillip Rigsby to become the state’s first openly transgender lawmaker. The software engineer and LGBTQ+ rights advocate campaigned on issues including public education, healthcare, and affordability, despite facing dogged attacks on her gender identity from her opponent. In Indiana, 30-year-old Beau Bayh, the son of former governor and senator Evan Bayh and grandson of former senator Birch Bayh, became the first Democrat to win statewide office since 2012, defeating Republican Max Engling in the race for secretary of state.

Across the country, people voted in the midterm elections to significantly expand who holds power in America, all over a single night in which decades of political precedent were overturned.

#6661. Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman Is the Scariest Thing You’ll See All Year

In 2009, Andrew Garfield found a thread. He was preparing to play Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg in a little-hyped film called The Social Network, and he had located the thing in Zuckerberg’s story that he could pull on—the through line that turns personal experience into empathic performance and on into universal storytelling. Then he lost the part to Jesse Eisenberg. Director David Fincher had seen what, today, is obvious: Humanity flows fast and deep through Andrew Garfield. Fincher cast him instead as Eduardo Saverin, the betrayed cofounder and emotional counterweight to Zuckerberg’s opacity, who cries, sneers, throws a feint, and smashes a laptop (that’s one scene).

The movie made him a celebrity, and he brought an unusual depth of emotion to this job too. While serving as Spider-Man, he begged the public, via a handwritten sign held up for paparazzi, to care about a more important cause than what’s up with famous people. While promoting 2021’s Tick, Tick…Boom! on The Late Show With Stephen Colbert, he talked about the death of his mother; the clip still gets shared by grieving people.

Boxers by Hermès. Sneakers by Bottega Veneta. Socks by Jacques. Watch by Rolex.

Now, 15 years after The Social Network, Garfield has picked back up the tech-CEO thread to play Sam Altman in Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s film that covers the founding of OpenAI up to the coup that led to Altman’s firing—and his re-entrenchment. (OpenAI has an agreement with Condé Nast, the owner of GQ, which allows OpenAI to display its content in search results for a limited term.) The movie seems destined to occupy the same orienting role as The Social Network, helping us understand the technology and the men who are shaping our futures, almost in real time. But whereas that film was a legal drama about status (Harvard guy vs. hotter, richer-born Harvard guys), Artificial plays as a horror movie where the monster, AI, is real. (And it just learned how to do theoretical physics.)

Garfield brings Altman to life as a mad guidance counselor: rubbing the shoulders of engineers, taking security meetings cross-legged, and sucking green juice in the faces of his adversaries. Here, finally, is an ascendant tech overlord that makes unsettling use of Garfield’s famous sensitivity. When Garfield-as-Altman cries, you’re not sure whether they’re the tears of a true superintelligence believer or a duplicitous power-seeker. Or which one would be scarier.

When we meet in early October, Garfield is transformed by a beard and shoulder-length hair. He grew it all out to play the magician Roy Horn, of Siegfried and Roy, in next year’s show Wild Things, though they ended up putting a wig on him anyway. He was filming that limited series in Berlin immediately after wrapping The Uprising, a Paul Greengrass movie about the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, which shot before Artificial was even technically wrapped. “I did these three things back to back last year, and I did have a bit of burnout, to be honest. I was kind of sleepless in Berlin for a while, and not in a romantic way,” he says. “It was rough, dude. I should have just gone to Berghain and just rode it out.” Now, though, Garfield is visibly buzzing, both from watching Artificial with an audience at the New York Film Festival the night before—and from the chatter coming out of Silicon Valley.

This interview has been condensed and edited.

Andrew Garfield: I’ve listened to his podcast.

The walk was a key for me, and the clothes and the physicality. He’s a very slight, slim guy, Sam, and seems to be very image-conscious. Which is interesting to me, which is something that I felt compelled by. There’s a great video of Sam, in what looks like a diner, when he’s talking about Loopt [the company he cofounded before running Y Combinator and cofounding OpenAI], when he’s in his early 20s, and he was much freer with his physicality back then.

Sam did an interview with Vanity Fair [for the magazine’s New Establishment issue]. I think it came out yesterday, the day of our premiere, where he was very sweet about the walk as well. It’s a very generous thing for the boys to acknowledge that the walk was close, a good approximation of Sam and his vibe. I think that’s a very classy thing, to acknowledge the thing that seems to be working. But who knows what’s happening in their hearts and minds right now or within the family? I can project myself into that experience and imagine what it must feel like for an actor to be so presumptuous to play a character called Sam Altman in a major film. I can imagine that must be really strange, and I feel for…. I don’t know. In terms of taking it on, what outweighed that sense of responsibility for me was this sense of it is the defining inevitable invention of our times. It felt like a great responsibility to interrogate not just the machine, if you can even call it that, the kind of the consciousness or the technology itself, but to interrogate the people who are building it and who are putting their hearts and souls and life’s work into it, and where they may or may not be leading us.

That was deeply researched. This is what I gleaned. There’s a lot of people that know Sam. There’s a lot of people that are happy to talk about Sam. Some very, very protective; others, slightly more inside information. And I’m not going to name who these people are. But it was a kind of adding to the cauldron and through my lens of the interpretation of who this person is, combined with what was on the page and the specific cinematic story we’re telling and how we’re telling it, and Luca’s tastes and sensibilities. And, yeah, a lot of people said he would never sit conventionally. He was always sitting like a little boy.

Intimacy, but also ownership of a space—a kind of subtle, very soft dominance of a space. But also, as you say, a kind of, “Hey, we’re all just hanging out doing the coolest job ever. So why can’t we just sit like we’re in a dorm room?” It’s very psychologically interesting to me and smart. And who knows if it’s all calculated? Who knows if it’s not? I don’t know. What was interesting, in tracking his physicality in all the videos I saw is, at the beginning, he’s very free in how he twitches and moves. He’s just freer in his ability to be his true self maybe. And then as he starts to become more and more powerful, and ultimately becoming the face of the new world, this behemoth company that’s going to define where we are going—even if he doesn’t know where we are going, and none of them do—he becomes a slightly more homogenized version of a tech CEO. That was a really, really interesting kind of journey. And you can see, now, in [Altman’s recent interview with Vanity Fair], he’s very image-conscious, and I am too. I think we all are.

I mean, yes. One has to. This is the job. And this is why I wanted to do it: Because with The Social Network, I was getting ready to play Mark Zuckerberg, and then David Fincher calls me in and says, “We found someone that is just going to do it better. It’s Jesse, but we think you could also play this part. And you’re a very emotional actor, Andrew, so why would we waste all of that on someone who doesn’t seem to feel many emotions?” So Eduardo became my kind of guy, and I was very happy with that. But it left a little dangling thread, and I was like, “I need to understand.” Because I started to explore what it takes to win, to win on that level.

I think I’m a competitive person. I’m an athlete. I was raised by a swimming-coach father and, at that time, a proud capitalist. My dad has evolved his view of the world over the course of the last decades, which I find very moving and touching, as I have evolved my view of winning and losing and the beauty of losing and how humility is the only thing that actually grows us. I’m sorry, but to keep bringing it back to the film, I think what we’re dealing with is we’re in a very immature culture. Humility is a surefire way to get us back to our collective humanity, I feel. But it’s hard. It’s hard. I love winning. It’s so much easier when things are going great, but I think it’s probably better for your soul when things aren’t going so great.

It’s hard to find our own center within that lack-of-center in the world. A lot of people my age who I speak to are feeling a similar sense of a kind of falling apart, which feels right, because as a thing falls apart, the seeds of the future put back together start to get planted. Something else being born. I don’t mean to be glib, I don’t mean to be evasive, because I do like talking. I remember being a young person and wanting people I saw on magazine covers to say something real. So I feel a responsibility to that young person that is out there as well.

I was like, “I don’t want to be so sensitive. I don’t want to hug my bully after he beats the shit out of me.” I could just feel his pain. It would be a lot easier to not have to see and feel all of these things that I may just be making up, but I’m pretty sure I’m not. It was a radar that I’ve had since I was a kid, I guess. I think my family would say the same thing, and I think they would also agree that it was a bit of a pain in the ass.

I need a place to go and express all of the most difficult shit about me to other people in private where they’re expressing their most difficult shit about them. They walk into any room and they’re like, “Everyone’s so nice.” And it’s like, no. I don’t know this person, but you could say, “No, you’re just Tom Cruise, and everyone wants to hang out with Tom Cruise.” I mean, I do know Tom, and I haven’t seen him in a long time. I only bring him up because he’s one of the most famous people in the world and I happen to know him a little bit and really have enjoyed and have a lot of admiration for him. But for me, it was a big danger that I would start to think that was a reflection of who I am. Do you know what I mean? And so I think in order to hold on to my ability to be messy, my ability to lose, my ability to be “weak,” my ability to be all of the things that our culture says a man should not be or even a person should not be, I sought out places and people and spaces and groups that would allow for me just to stay in touch with all of the messiest parts of myself, all the stuff that I’m not going to talk about here because it’s not safe to talk about them here.

Pleasantly. It was completely unintentional. Well, it’s immature, and it’s deluded, and it’s a little adorable. It’s like, Oh, that’s so cute. You think you can outsmart the great mystery? Oh my God, it’s adorable. And I say that with some irony, I suppose, because we are being led by a bunch of younger guys right now who don’t know where this technology is taking us.

There was an overwhelming amount of reporting done about Sam having a specific relationship with the truth. And it was obviously a really vital ingredient in our story. Yes, I do. I think at that time, before The Social Network came out, people were scoffing at the idea of a Facebook movie. No one was really onto the tech industry and the people that were governing it in the same way, because they didn’t consciously pose as much of a threat to our existence. Now we’re all a bit more hip to it. By the public becoming more hip to it, but also powerful people becoming more hip to it, realizing that that’s where the power lies, means that a company like OpenAI will have much more authority and power. For regular people like you and I, it’s higher stakes because we all feel like we have our eyes slightly more open now to the real-world personal consequences of these technologies. So we’re healthily more invested in shining light where that power lies and where we’re giving our autonomy, but also simultaneously there’s a much larger vested interest in protecting those people and their technology.

I feel afraid now. But it’s outweighed by a faith in humanity, but also a faith in the mystery of life. I’m not sure. I’m not in their sphere, but I’m really, really, really curious to see how it all plays out.

But then there’s always people that come out and defend them. It’s so strange. Whether they’re bots or otherwise, I’m not sure, but there’s just an army of people that are like, “Leave those rich guys alone.” I’m like, “What?”

It’s the most obvious cliché stuff. I went to an Ezra Collective gig at the Roundhouse in London. It’s a British kind of conglomerate of amazing musicians in the realm of Afrobeat, jazz-inspired. Congratulations are in order for Formula 1 driver Charles Leclerc and his wife Alexandra Leclerc, who just became parents!

On November 4, the couple took to Instagram to announce the birth to their first child: a baby girl named Bianca. They shared the first photo of Bianca, showing the baby’s little legs and feet in light pink knitwear and socks with tiny bows. According to the post, she was born on November 3.

Alexandra and Charles were first linked in 2023, and married in a small civil ceremony at Mairie de Monaco, (Monaco City Hall) in February 2026. #6659. Pumpkin Cheesecake Muffins

Loaded with pumpkin seeds, canned pumpkin purée, and pumpkin pie spice, these big streusel-topped muffins are every fall lover’s dream come true. And to make things even better, the inside of each muffin is stuffed with a soft, lightly sweetened cream cheese mixture. Make the cheesecake filling and the streusel ahead of time to pace things out if it’s helpful. Don’t, even for a minute, consider using anything other than Libby’s 100% pure pumpkin purée (not pie mix). Nothing is better. We promise.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Whisk ⅓ cup coarsely chopped raw pumpkin seeds, ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour, 2 Tbsp. light brown sugar, ½ tsp. pumpkin pie spice, and a pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl to combine. Using your fingers, rub in 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, until moist pea-size lumps form. Chill until ready to use.

Do Ahead: Streusel can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and keep chilled.

Vigorously whisk 6 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar, 2 tsp. all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. vanilla extract, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl until combined and smooth.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and chill.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Line cups of a standard 12-cup muffin pan with paper liners. Whisk 2 large eggs, 1½ cups (packed; 300 g) light brown sugar, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, ¼ cup whole milk, 1 Tbsp. pumpkin pie spice, 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth, about 1 minute. Whisk 1¾ cups (219 g) all-purpose flour and 1½ tsp. baking powder in a small bowl to combine. Add to pumpkin mixture and fold in with a rubber spatula until just incorporated and no large dry streaks of flour remain (don’t overmix; batter will be lumpy).

Bake muffins until streusel is crisp and muffins spring back when gently pressed, 24–27 minutes. Let muffins cool in pan 5 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack and let cool until just warm or completely.

Do Ahead: Muffins can be made 2 days ahead. Store airtight at room temperature.

#6657. WNBA Finals MVP Gabby Williams on Game 7, Trans Athletes, and Her Cat, Halle Berry

“Print this,” said Joe Lacob, the billionaire owner of the Golden State Valkyries, at the start of the team’s playoff run. “Gabby Williams is the best player in the world."

It was one of the coldest quotes in recent sports memory. But at the time, Williams, the 30-year-old French-American wing, hadn’t yet won a WNBA Championship, much less been named Finals MVP. And, truth be told, no one expected this from the Valkyries, an expansion franchise in only its second year of existence, and one without a single All-WNBA selection on its roster.

No matter. After defeating the Atlanta Dream in a winner-takes-all Game 7 (the first in WNBA history) this past weekend, the Valkyries brought their first ever WNBA Trophy back to the Bay. And it was largely because of Williams, who lived up to Lacob’s promise by executing the most memorable second-half takeover in WNBA Finals history.

Here’s how it went down: With three minutes left in the third, the Valks trailing by six, Williams called for the ball, went between-the-legs, and took a step back jumper from beyond the perimeter. She followed that up moments later with a catch-and-shoot three in Angel Reese’s grill. The following possession, Williams freed herself up from a double team, then sprinted out past the three-point line for a money ball.

Williams’ back-to-back-to-back triples broke Atlanta and gave life to “Ballhalla,” San Francisco’s fortress of 18,064 violet-clad, women’s basketball fanatics. After trailing for most of the game, Golden State snatched the lead and didn’t look back. Williams finished with 28 points in the second half (a WNBA post-season record) on her way to a game-high 30. When it came time to name the Finals MVP, there was little question about which player on an otherwise balanced roster had been most crucial to the Valkyries’ fairytale fun.

Watching Williams, you might not have guessed that, when she’s not hooping, she simply wants to cuddle with her cat and binge-watch anime. Just before the Valks’ championship parade, GQ got to know this smooth assassin a bit more intimately.

No matter what, when I was overseas, as soon as I came home, I would tell HB how my game went. It's the first thing I do. I walk in the door, “Oh, HB, we lost today. I played so bad.” Or “Oh, HB, we won. And this happened.” First thing I do [after winning the WNBA Finals], “HB, we freaking won. Can you believe it?” And she was like, “Can you feed me?”

I love animals, and I do have two family dogs who I absolutely love. But a cat is just like, they have boundaries. Dogs are kind of dumb and just they'll love whoever walks in the door. And she's definitely a Velcro cat. She sleeps right here [next to my face] and there's just no better feeling.

The coaches knew that Atlanta had been putting a lot of tension on me defensively all series and it was causing me to… It was really tough to find my rhythm. So Nat [head coach Natalie Nakase] was just like, “Let the game come to you. Stay patient. The game will open up.” She's like, “Just wait till the game opens up.” At Halftime, V [Veronica Burton] looked at me, she was like, “What do you need?” And I was like, “I'm good. I'm going to get going. I got it.” She's like, “Okay, I got you.” So V was a really big one in helping me out of that locker room because she just looked at me just like, “I trust you.” And that was huge just to see that in her eyes. And then [assistant coach] Sugar Rodgers, who I've leaned on all season, she was like, “Go off.”

She's like, “I'm waiting for you to go off.” And I was like, “I got you.” KP [assistant coach Kasib Powell] and [assistant coach] Landon [Tatum], both of them were like, “We got the first play for you. Get going, open it up, and the rest is yours." Having that trust after seeing how that first half went and everyone just going like, even with 20 minutes left in the last game of our season, that's not as much of a testament to me, but a testament to the trust that we have as a team.

When I hit that shot, I wasn't thinking about it in the game, but as soon as I hit it and I heard the crowd pop, I was like, “Yeah, they've been waiting for this.” I could tell that the fans were like, “Finally, Gabby. Dang.” But in the most positive way ever. So I saw one go through, and I didn't realize until I came home hours after the game, and then I finally opened social media after the party and stuff, and I was like, “Oh, those three’s were three possessions in a row.” I didn't realize that in the moment.

I've been in deficits before where you come back and all you can think about is stop, score, stop, score. You're not thinking about what happened in the last possession. So I swear, I didn't realize that it was literally three possessions in a row until I came home and watched something I was tagged in. And I was like, “That's kind of crazy.”

#6656. Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie

The one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so plan ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling)

Whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

Unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6655. Farmers Market Salad With Miso Maple Dressing

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

The farmers market is my biggest hack for solo cooking. Instead of committing to a three-pound bag of carrots, you can buy just one, and choose your produce based on beauty or mere curiosity. That’s how I came up with this fall salad, comprising a single head of Little Gem lettuce and some crunchy produce, including that carrot we mentioned, cucumber, watermelon radish, and an Asian pear. Slicing those elements thinly with a mandoline and throwing them in an ice bath for a brief soak helps keep everything cold and crisp.

The dressing is equally important. I start with Kewpie mayo for its richness and savory depth—it’s made with only egg yolks and contains MSG, giving it a fuller flavor than standard mayonnaise. White miso brings even more umami, while rice vinegar keeps things bright. The result is a creamy finger-licking dressing that clings to every bite. Serve with a fried egg (or your protein of choice) and a piece of fresh bread to scoop up the leftovers. Make a double batch of dressing for dipping crudités or marinating salmon, chicken, or roasted vegetables.

Read More: The Farmers Market Is Built for Solo Cooking

Combine 1 small head of Little Gem or other crunchy lettuce, leaves separated, cut into 2"–3" pieces, 1 rainbow carrot, peeled, very thinly sliced lengthwise into ribbons with a mandoline or vegetable peeler, 1 Persian cucumber, thinly sliced, preferably with a mandoline, ½ small watermelon radish, peeled, halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, and ¼ medium Asian pear, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, in a large bowl of ice water. Let soak 10–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 2 Tbsp. seasoned rice vinegar, 2 Tbsp. white miso, 2 tsp. Kewpie mayonnaise, 2 tsp. pure maple syrup, and 1 tsp. toasted sesame oil in a small bowl until smooth and emulsified (or combine in a small glass jar, cover, and shake). Taste dressing and season with kosher salt.

Drain vegetables and run through a salad spinner or pat dry with a kitchen towel to remove excess water. Wipe out large bowl, return vegetables to bowl, and drizzle 2 Tbsp. dressing over. Toss, adding more dressing as needed, until evenly coated (reserve any remaining dressing for another use).

Transfer salad to a shallow bowl or rimmed plate. Top with a fried egg and serve with country-style bread if desired.

Do Ahead: Dressing can be made up to 3 days ahead. Cover and chill.
