#6654. Book Breakfasts, Babysitters, and the Russian Tea Room: A Day With Author Tarajia Morrell

Forget 9-to-5. Mothering knows no schedule—often it feels more like 5-to-9 and everything in between. In this series, we look at the hectic, messy, sometimes beautiful, often frustrating enterprise of being a mother—and maintaining a life of your own. Consider it a “day in the life” for the forgotten hours.

Today, we’re following Tarajia Morrell, the James Beard Award–winning food writer, author, and communications consultant. Her new memoir, Desire Feeds the Feast, is out now. The book is a rich and lyrical telling of her childhood as the daughter of a dynasty of Manhattan wine sellers; her days on the New York City club scene of the late ’90s; her culinary studies, acting auditions, and restaurant jobs; and more.

A single mother, Morrell lives in her childhood home—a rent-stabilized Manhattan apartment that she fought for and won—with her five-year-old daughter, Viva. On a recent Thursday, she brought Vogue along for a busy day, which included everything from the school bus stop and a book breakfast to a podcast taping, a party, and the realities of mealtime. (“Indeed, I am a food writer whose child is a picky eater,” she writes.)

My alarm goes off. Immediately, I recall that today is not a normal day at my desk at home, writing copy for the hotels for which I’m the communications director. Today is a day in which I must also focus on my book, and it’s going to be a doozy.

I go make myself some jet fuel. While the coffee pot is on the stove, I turn on my morning music: Alice Coltrane Radio on Spotify, which both soothes and invigorates me at once with its harp and organ. It’s still almost completely dark out, but, from the living room, I can see the first blush of light above a little slice of the 59th Street Bridge. This sight (and the coffee) has its usual effect: I have a jolt of how lucky I am to be exactly where I am—in this home with this child.

It’s been a challenge to pry Viva from sleep for her new kindergarten wake-up time, so I am delightfully surprised when I open the door to her tiny bedroom (the tiny bedroom of my childhood!) and she’s sitting in front of her dollhouse at play. Blaring Alice Coltrane and Éthiopiques is clearly an excellent, calming way to start her day too.

Viva colors while she eats her breakfast of a cinnamon-raisin English muffin with Nutella (I know, I know), berries, and juice. Indeed, I am a food writer whose child is a picky eater. A predawn morning is not the hour to prove points.

I help Viva dress for school even though I am supposed to let her do it entirely independently. My excuse is that time is of the essence, but that’s true in more ways than one. I stare at her long, lithe limbs and wonder where my chubby baby has gone. Since having her, time has changed. It used to be something that haunted me with its slow creep; now I am always chasing more of it.

Our school bus is meant to arrive at 7:22 but is always outrageously early or late. I receive a text from the dad of an older girl who also gets picked up at our stop, saying “The bus is running early,” so I grab a coat and Viva’s things and we dash. As we make our way, I feel enormously grateful for this relative stranger whose tiny updates help my life be less stressful. As a parent in general, but particularly as a solo parent, supportive gestures that help the wheels stay on (and help me avoid a school run) are more appreciated that I can express.

We do a weird little dance while we wait, with Viva basically inside my coat for warmth and cuddles. The song I hum is vaguely reminiscent of the Beverly Hills Cop theme song. I don’t care what I look like in these stolen silly moments of just being her mother.

Back home and I hop in the shower. My literary agent, Andy McNicol, is picking me up to go to a breakfast hosted at Claudette by owner Carlos Suarez on lower Fifth to celebrate my memoir, Desire Feeds the Feast.

Andy is right on time and we head downtown. Twenty minutes into the ride, I ask the driver why we skipped our exit off the FDR, and it turns out that it’s because he has the wrong address. I tease Andy about typing without wearing her glasses. One of the many indignities of aging is that none of us seem to be able to see without our glasses.

We arrive at Claudette and I instantly feel more calm. Writing the book has been a very solitary experience—done after Viva falls asleep—and finally getting to squeeze my pals and feel less alone in it is a balm to my nerves.

So many people I love are here from many chapters of my life, and an adorable number of them are wearing red and black—a clear nod to my book cover—as am I. My friend Batsheva Hay clocks my dress and asks if it’s vintage Geoffrey Beene. We both laugh: She’d had her eye on the same one on The RealReal. I am the geek who enjoys matching my book cover. Plus there’s a great vintage Geoffrey Beene scene in the book (i.e., in my life), so it feels pleasantly full circle.

The breakfast ends and I prepare to depart for the rest of my day. I tucked jeans into my bag, but, unfortunately, I forgot to put in a shirt. Classic me to find myself in this predicament on a day that I am reporting to, ahem, Vogue. I put on my leather jacket without a shirt underneath and go hunting for a T-shirt before my next rendezvous. Save Khaki United on Greenwich Avenue seems like the best and closest option, and sure enough, I find a perfect simple long-sleeve T-shirt there.

I meet creative director Anna Polonsky at the new Santo Taco on Carmine, where she’s overseeing a photo shoot with Gentl and Hyers of the food and space. Anna and I have done branding projects together for both Troutbeck and Belden House & Mews, the sister hotels with which I work. We catch up over agua frescas and divine tacos and discuss branding for Firehouse—the soon-to-open membership and events space for Belden. We soon discover we will also both be at the same event later that night; love it when that happens.

I fly by The Strand, the legendary bookstore where I am launching my book on November 4 (!), and its events director greets me for a quick tour of the room I’ll be in. I am completely verklempt to see my book on little posters, including on the elevator. I’m pinching myself…even more so when I am taken to the greenroom and see the walls covered in photos of my literary idols who have read there.

I walk up Broadway to the Malin to meet Angela Ledgerwood of the podcast Lit Up to record an episode on my book. We also did one for Savor: A Chef’s Hunger for More, which I coauthored with Fatima Ali, and since our last recording session, Angela married a friend of mine from high school. They’ve become winemakers, launching Old Sound Vineyard on the North Fork. If insomnia and needing glasses are drawbacks of getting older, one of the enormous pleasures is this sort of happenstance: people you love finding love with people you love.

I take the R train downtown to meet Charlie Champalimaud, an owner of Troutbeck and Belden, at Thompson Street Studio, where artist Kiva Motnyk has her more commercial practice. Charlie has commissioned a work by Kiva for Belden, so we go to see sketches for it and discuss timing for delivery. I learn that Kiva grew up in the building we are in, which feels like another good omen, since my book is about unexpectedly finding myself in the New York City apartment in which I began.

I am properly zonked. I consider a taxi but despise being stuck in traffic and the absurd prices, so I get on the R at Prince Street and start to tackle my neglected emails. I am so distracted and fried that I forget to switch to the Q and accidentally go to Queens instead of 86th Street. Amateur hour. I take the train back to Manhattan and hail a cab to make up for lost time.

I pick Viva up and we head home. I ask her what she had for lunch at school, and she tells me “applesauce, french fries, and broccoli.” Super.

Home. Quick dinner of “crispy chicken,” which is hammered panko and egg-battered chicken breasts that I made the night before and is no longer crispy, blanched broccoli (Viva’s requested veg for the night, despite its presence at lunch), and avocado with sea salt.

The lovely sitter arrives and immediately engages Viva in an art project. Nothing is normal this month of book launch and tour, and it would be impossible without my mother and support system of other mom friends helping enormously. I am so tired that when I sit down for a moment of sunshine on the terrace, I consider bailing on my plans for the evening, but the sitter is already here.

I arrive at Le Monde Beryl’s new shop on 67th Street for a cocktail party cohosted by The Perfect. One of my oldest friends, Lily Hanbury, started LMB 10 years ago with Katya Shifrin, and they’ve just opened this stunning store designed by Silka Rittson-Thomas. I live in Le Monde Beryl shoes because I can walk everywhere fast in them (Viva calls fast walking “city walking,” which I love). I am wearing a long silk dress by DeMeric, really chosen for my next and final stop, so am a bit dressed up for the cocktail at LMB, but old buddies and immediate laughter (with me? at me?) make it irrelevant.

I arrive on that strange crest of 57th Street to the Russian Tea Room, which is celebrating 100 years. I’m in a room with my food world family…as well as the trademark bawdy ice sculptures, gilt details, and red patina. I try to recall the last time I was here. I think it was 1999, at a dinner with Paris Hilton before a wild evening at a nightclub.

My exhaustion hits me hard. We restaurant folk commence our usual conversation of where we can go to get food immediately, and I suggest Dim Sum Palace, around the corner on 56th. It is not a palace, but it is a great place to go when you’re starving with six friends and no reservation at 8:30 on a gorgeous autumnal Thursday.

Home. When you parent alone, a babysitter who puts things in the dishwasher is like winning the lottery. I climb into the loft bed that was once mine and kiss my child, pulling the covers she’s kicked off back over her. As I fall asleep in my own bed, I am thinking of how well our home fits us—a mother and child, just us. It’s still pretty unfathomable that I lived in this fabulous but not so large apartment with two parents until I was 15. My last thought is to marvel at the strangeness of it all, the gift of it, being here with her. All this searching, hunger, and marveling is what drove me to write the book. Good night.

#6652. What You Need to Know About Volufiline, Everyone’s Latest Skin Care Obsession

Social media is full of products that promise to transform your face. The latest one making the rounds? Volufiline, an ingredient being likened to natural filler. Guys are swiping and dabbing it onto their undereyes, smile lines, and lips in the hopes of restoring volume and looking younger with no needles, lasers, or scalpels in sight. Fans credit the topical for improvements in undereye hollows and skin quality and making them get carded again. One X user even claims that it looks like “you’ve genuinely gotten a facelift” after two weeks of use.

The pitch is that Volufiline is basically filler in a bottle. But does it actually check out?

Volufiline is a trademarked cosmetic ingredient made with Anemarrhena asphodeloides root extract (a source of the compound sarsasapogenin) and hydrogenated polyisobutene (an emollient that softens and smooths skin). “The theory is that sarsasapogenin encourages fat cells to develop and store more lipids, making them fuller,” says Kseniya Kobets, MD, director of cosmetic dermatology at Montefiore Einstein Advanced Care. Essentially, the hope is to counteract volume loss that naturally occurs as we grow older.

We’ve spent the last year sampling the latest releases in men’s skin care, hair care, and more. Our favorites will help you level up.

In a small study by Sederma, the French company that manufactures Volufiline, 28 women applied a cream containing Volufiline to one breast for 56 days. While the treated breast’s average volume increased by 2.2%, the result wasn’t statistically significant. Kobets also points out that the comparison was with an untreated breast—rather than the same cream without Volufiline—so it’s unclear if Volufiline or other ingredients in the cream drove the increase in volume. Plus, we can’t exactly extrapolate the results seen in a female breast to a man’s face.

Despite the lack of robust clinical evidence supporting its anti-aging claims, Volufiline is the latest topical du jour that people are crediting with their plumper, more supple skin—namely in areas prone to volume loss like the undereyes, smile lines, cheeks, and lips. Some before-and-afters on social media are visually compelling. But the bigger question is whether Volufiline meaningfully increases facial volume or if the improvements are simply due to a temporary plumping effect—or even the other ingredients paired alongside it.

“Some improvement likely comes from the moisturizing formula: hydration softens fine lines, emollients smooth the surface, and that finish changes how light reflects off skin,” Kobets says. (Changes in lighting and specific camera angles can also make the after photos look more striking.) While Volufiline might help your skin look better, the jury’s still out on whether it meaningfully restores lost volume. “Making skin look hydrated and plump isn’t the same as rebuilding the fat underneath it,” Kobets says.

As for those filler in a bottle claims? Alexandra Bowles, DO, a board-certified dermatologist at MONA Dermatology, sets the record straight. “Volufiline is designed to support volume in the skin, and some people may notice slightly plumper, fuller-looking skin over time,” she says. Meanwhile, injectable filler adds immediate volume and structure and can reshape areas like the tear trough, lips, and jawline. “A cream or serum works at the surface and builds gradually, so it can’t create that kind of change,” she says. Read: While it may complement your skin care routine, it won’t replace or replicate results from filler.

Both derms are open to patients experimenting with Volufiline, but with a few caveats. “I think Volufiline is worth trying if you have realistic expectations, but it’s definitely overhyped as an alternative to filler,” Bowles says. If you really want to (pardon the pun) move the needle on undereye hollows, loss of lip volume, or a less-defined jawline, she says carefully placed filler or other in-office treatments may be more effective.

Kobets doesn’t rule out trying Volufiline, either, so long as you’re not expecting to restore facial fat. That said, she advises being cautious if you have a chronic skin condition like eczema or rosacea, or if you’re acne-prone. Try a patch test first and stop if your skin stings or burns.

Bowles suggests prioritizing reputable brands with clear ingredient lists and modest claims around a gradual improvement in the look and feel of skin. Be wary of products that promise instant results, have vague ingredient lists, or come from unverified sellers. “Don’t experiment with raw ingredients or assume a higher percentage works better,” Kobets adds.

The TL;DR: Volufiline is intriguing, but the hype is outpacing the evidence. More rigorous research is needed to address its volume-enhancing claims for facial skin, so take them with a grain of salt. Consistently using a well-formulated product might help your skin look more supple and hydrated; just don’t expect any miracles or a true dupe for injectables. “Good skin care improves skin quality, but it can’t do every job we’re asking of it,” Kobets says.

#6651. Salted Coffee Custard Pie

If you can’t be fussed with making coffee and dessert after a big holiday dinner, consider this twofer instead. The silky, sliceable, cool custard is rich and intense with two kinds of coffee, while the oatmeal crust is a tweedy-textured study in contrast. It’s prebaked to mitigate sogginess but doesn’t require pie weights. Mascarpone keeps the whipped cream firm and fluffy for a full 24 hours.

Don’t be tempted to skip the cold-brew concentrate. You don’t want regular cold brew, and definitely not brewed and cooled coffee from your coffee machine at home, no matter how fancy. The concentrate (highly recommend Grady’s Cold Brew Coffee Concentrate) is consistent every single time with exactly the right strength to stand up to the dairy and eggs in the filling.

Cook’s notes: This pie requires a 9"-diameter deep-dish pie dish.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

Place a rack in middle of oven and preheat to 350°. Butter pie dish with unsalted butter. Pulse 2 cups (180 g) old-fashioned oats, ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour, ¼ cup (packed; 50 g) dark brown sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a food processor until oats are coarsely ground. Drizzle in 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled; pulse just until mixture comes together. Transfer to prepared dish (such as East Fork Ceramic Pie Plate); wipe out and reserve food processor. Press crust firmly and evenly across bottom and up sides of dish with a flat-bottomed measuring cup. Bake until golden and surface looks dry, 25–30 minutes. Transfer crust to a wire rack; reduce oven temperature to 325°.

Pulse 1 cup (packed; 200 g) dark brown sugar, 2 Tbsp. all-purpose flour, 2 Tbsp. instant espresso powder, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in food processor until no lumps remain, about 1 minute. Add 3 large eggs, ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, and 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and pulse until smooth. Add 1 cup cold-brew coffee concentrate and 2 cups heavy cream and pulse until well combined.

Pour custard into crust (it’s okay if crust is still warm). Bake pie until edges of filling are set and slightly puffed but center still wobbles a little when gently shaken, 40–50 minutes (filling will continue to set after baking). Transfer to a wire rack; let cool at least 3 hours, or, preferably, chill 12 hours.

Using an electric mixer, beat ½ cup mascarpone, 4 Tbsp. granulated sugar, remaining 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ⅔ cup heavy cream, and 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract in a medium bowl until soft peaks form. Spoon whipped cream mixture over pie; swirl lightly to create divots and peaks.

Just before serving, dust with instant espresso powder if desired; sprinkle generously with flaky sea salt.

Do ahead: Pie (without espresso powder and sea salt garnishes) can be made 1 day ahead. Cover loosely and keep chilled.

#6649. Spiced Beef Baked Potatoes

Baked potatoes may not seem like a dish that requires much technique, but there’s a difference between a good baked potato and a great one. Wrapping them in foil can lead to a tender interior but render the skin too soft. For the most crisp skin, bake them right on the oven grate at quite a high temperature. (To make it taste almost like a potato chip, rub those scrubbed russets with vegetable oil and season with plenty of salt.) Shockingly, this doesn’t prevent a fluffy interior—that comes down to the internal temperature reaching at least 212°. Sure, it may seem strange to take your potato’s temperature, but it’s a fail-safe route to the most enjoyable potato.

Some, including the Idaho Potato Commission, swear that the way a baked potato is opened affects the texture, eschewing a knife for a fork to gently poke a plus sign into the surface. Others, like beloved food writer Nigel Slater, prefer to strike the potato as though it were part of a martial arts competition. “Bring your hand down fast and sharp as if you were doing a karate chop but only hard enough to crack open the potato skin,” he writes in a piece for The Guardian. (Whether or not to attempt this feat is literally in the hands of the potato-baker.) We found a single fork-pricked line down the length of the spud is the most effective.

Once opened, a baked potato can be filled with anything from tuna salad to cheesy baked beans. Here, it’s a picadillo-inspired mixture with ground beef (packed with protein, iron, and creatine—though ground turkey or chicken work nicely too) adorned with golden raisins and stuffed olives. A spicy tomato sauce will slowly soak into the potato, further seasoning it with every passing minute. Make sure to use a chili powder that’s a mix of spices like chiles, cumin, oregano, garlic (not just dried ground chiles).

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week. Read more: White Potatoes Are Not Empty Calories. They’re Actually Great for You.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Prick 4 large russet potatoes (about 10 oz. each), scrubbed, patted dry, all over with a fork, then rub all over with 1 Tbsp. vegetable oil and sprinkle with 1¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Bake directly on oven rack until skins are crisp and flesh is very soft (an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should register 212°–220°), 55–75 minutes. (If thermometer registers 210° before beef mixture is finished, turn off oven and leave potatoes inside until ready to use.)

Meanwhile, pick enough leaves from ½ bunch cilantro (about 2 oz.) to measure ½ cup; set aside for serving. Finely chop remaining leaves and all of stems (you should have about ¾ cup); set aside separately.

Heat remaining 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium. Add 1 medium red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is softened, 8–10 minutes. Add ¼ cup double-concentrated tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until deepened in color and slightly tacky, about 2 minutes.

Increase heat to medium-high. Add 1 lb. ground beef, 2 Tbsp. chili powder, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Cook, stirring and smashing often with a heatproof rubber spatula to break up meat, until cooked through, about 4 minutes.

Reduce heat to low. Add ½ cup golden raisins, ¼ cup sliced pimiento-stuffed green olives, reserved chopped cilantro, and 1 cup water. Cook, stirring occasionally, until sauce thickens slightly and flavors come together, 8–12 minutes. Taste beef mixture and season with more salt if needed. Remove from heat and cover. Let sit until ready to use.

Transfer potatoes to a platter or plates and let cool 5 minutes. Using a fork, prick a 3"–4"-long line in the center down length of each potato, leaving 1" unpricked on each end. Using your hands, firmly press ends down toward platter to split potatoes open. Smash flesh as desired, then season inside of potatoes with salt. Divide beef mixture among potatoes and top with reserved cilantro leaves.

#6648. Everything You Need to Know About Fiber and Crohn's Disease, According to Dietitians

Just thinking about fiber can make many people with Crohn’s feel nervous. After all certain fiber-rich foods can be tough to tolerate, but the ones that cause trouble aren’t always obvious. Even a seemingly harmless omelet or a fruit smoothie can trigger symptoms in some people. So if you’ve been avoiding the nutrient, that’s understandable—and not uncommon. Research suggests people with Crohn’s tend to eat relatively little fiber, even during remission. One 2015 study found the average daily intake for individuals with the condition was just 16 grams. For context, experts recommend that men aim for 38 grams a day.

But here’s the thing: Having an inflammatory bowel disease doesn’t necessarily mean you should stick to a low-fiber diet. Some studies have found that eating foods rich in the nutrient may actually lower your risk of future flares, improve gut health, and reduce inflammation not only in your gastrointestinal tract but throughout your body.

We get it, though—navigating the sometimes confusing and land-mine-filled world of fiber can feel overwhelming, especially post-flare, and the stakes are high. No one wants to feel crummy or worry about being stuck near a toilet all day. That’s why we asked a group of registered dietitians to answer some of the most pressing questions about Crohn’s and fiber. Here’s what they said about getting enough without upsetting your stomach, which types may be harder to tolerate, and more.

Let’s take a step back and review some nutrition science 101.

In the simplest terms, fiber is a plant-based carbohydrate our bodies cannot fully breakdown or absorb. It resists digestion in the stomach and small intestine and depending on the type, is either partially or fully fermented by gut bacteria in the colon. This makes it different from other nutrients like fats and proteins, which the body breaks down and absorbs.

There are two main types of fiber, each with its own functions and benefits. Here’s a quick overview of each:

What it is: A type of fiber that passes through the GI tract largely intact, adds bulk to stools, helps keep you regular, and aids in regulating blood sugar. Foods rich in insoluble fiber are typically the ones we think of as hard to digest.

Where to find it: Pear and apple skins, raspberries, wheat bran, leafy greens like kale and collard greens, nuts, seeds, and legumes, among other foods.

What it is: A type of fiber that dissolves in water and forms a gel in the gut, slowing carbohydrate absorption. It helps control cholesterol, increases satiety, and makes stools easier to pass.

Where to find it: Beans, oats, barley, carrots, and the flesh of pears, among other foods.

The short answer: yes. But proceed with caution. During an active flare your fiber intake should depend on what you can tolerate, with amounts gradually increasing as symptoms improve.

“The goal is not to eat as much fiber as possible,” says Anya Argosh, MS, RD, a registered dietitian and the founder of Birchwell Clinic. “It’s to build as much dietary variety as your gut can comfortably and safely handle.”

A lower-fiber diet is often recommended during flares to give the GI tract a “rest.” However, Dahlia Marin, RDN, LD, CGN, a registered dietitian specializing in GI issues and co-founder of Married to Health, says limited evidence supports this approach for people without strictures (abnormal narrowings in the GI tract). “Historically, people with active Crohn’s were often told to follow a low-fiber diet, particularly when experiencing diarrhea, abdominal pain, or increased bowel movements. However, current research does not strongly support eliminating all fiber during a flare,” Marin says.

Instead, Marin recommends tailoring food choices to your symptoms and tolerance.

For example, if certain textures are hard for your body to handle, changing how you prepare foods may help.

Consider “choosing well-cooked, peeled, blended, or puréed fruits and vegetables rather than large amounts of raw, fibrous foods,” she says. That might mean roasting carrots or pears instead of eating them raw in a salad or opting for puréed vegetable soup or smoothie.

During a flare foods high in insoluble fiber—such as fruit and vegetable skins, fibrous leafy greens, nuts, seeds, popcorn, and corn on the cob—may also need to be temporarily limited until symptoms improve.

If you have a stricture, eating softer foods or modifying textures, limiting sources of insoluble fiber, and chewing thoroughly are especially important to help reduce the risk of an obstruction. However, fiber tolerance varies from person-to-person and if you have a stricture, you should work with your healthcare provider to come up with an individualized plan.

Kelly L. Burgess, MBA, RD, LDN, the founder of To Better Health LLC and the creator of the HealthyBites HealthyLife app, says she sometimes suggests a low-FODMAP diet during an active flare. This short-term approach may help people whose symptoms are triggered by FODMAPs, fermentable carbohydrates that can be hard on the gut. High-FODMAP foods include certain beans and legumes, as well as vegetables such as cabbage, cauliflower, garlic, and onions, which can cause symptoms like gas and bloating in some people.

A low-FODMAP diet is typically used on a temporary basis in people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) to identify symptom triggers and may help relieve symptoms in people with Crohn’s who have IBS-like symptoms.

Whether you’re coming off a flare or in remission, it’s best to take a “low and slow” approach to adding more fiber to your diet, Argosh says. Introducing too much too quickly can worsen symptoms, leaving you bloated and uncomfortable. “Pace your fiber—don’t force it,” Burgess says. “Begin with small amounts and increase them gradually as tolerated.” In practice, this might mean starting with small portions of well-tolerated fiber-rich foods spread throughout the day, then gradually expanding the types and amounts of fiber you eat at meals and snacks.

Some experts suggest a multi-step approach, starting with easy-to-tolerate, soft fruits, veggies, and grains—think potatoes, white rice, and bananas—and gradually progressing to harder-to-digest salad, seeds, corn, celery and dried fruit.

It’s worth noting that hydration should also increase as fiber intake rises to soften stools and prevent constipation.

When it comes to getting fiber, the dietitians agree that food is generally the best place to start. Fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and other plant foods offer more than just fiber—they also provide other vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants that support overall health and may help with inflammation.

That said fiber supplements can sometimes come in handy, especially when you’re traveling or don’t have access to the foods you typically eat. Finding one that works for you may take some patience, though.

Marin says different supplements can affect your gut in very different ways. “For example, psyllium is a soluble, gel-forming fiber that holds water but is not heavily fermented, while fibers such as inulin and fructooligosaccharides are much more fermentable and can have a greater effect on the gut microbiome.” In practical terms these variations mean one supplement might sit just fine with you and another could leave you feeling gassy or bloated. Which brings us to…

If you’re having trouble eating enough, losing weight without trying, finding yourself cutting out more and more foods, or feeling unsure how to add fiber into your diet after a flare, consider seeing a registered dietitian who specializes in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). These professionals can help you get the nutrients you need while figuring out which foods and textures work best for you so you don’t unnecessarily restrict your diet. They can also check for nutrient deficiencies and help tailor your diet if you have a stricture, have had surgery for Crohn’s, or are dealing with other Crohn's complications.

A registered dietitian can also help you identify your trigger foods. Triggers generally vary from person to person, which can make them tricky to pin down. Some people tolerate oats and nuts, while others can’t eat either. The same goes for raw fruit and veggies, whole grains, and other fiber-containing foods. It comes down to trial and error: figuring out what works for you—and what doesn’t.

Your gastroenterologist should be involved if you have new or worsening symptoms, particularly if you’re experiencing persistent abdominal pain, frequent diarrhea, blood in your stool, unexplained weight loss, worsening fatigue, and/or vomiting. Get urgent medical attention if you have severe abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, abdominal swelling, or can’t pass stool or gas. These can be signs of an intestinal obstruction, which is especially important to watch for in people with Crohn’s-related strictures.

#6647. Kim Kardashian Brings a Piece of ’90s Vintage Into 2026

Kim Kardashian is becoming a bona fide vintage hound. Since the reality star hired stylist Law Roach earlier this year, the pair have scoured archives from Tom Ford’s Yves Saint Laurent to Cristóbal’s Balenciaga. Kardashian’s longtime friend Olivier Rousteing even tossed her the keys to the Paco Rabanne archives for her birthday, lending her two chainmail minis from fall 1995 haute couture for her birthday dinner.

Today, amid her All’s Fair season 2 press bonanza, Kim Kardashian added yet another piece to her impressive vintage collection: a burgundy open-knit minidress with needlepoint rose motifs on the skirt—look 15 from Dolce & Gabbana’s fall 1997 collection.

Kardashian abided by some of the original 1997 styling, wearing the see-through dress over a black balconette bra and white skirt, but she made the look distinctly her own. Kardashian took the grungy (or, at least, grungy for Dolce) look in a sexier direction, opting to ditch the scalloped slip skirt for a tighter white underskirt, and eschewing the kooky black stockings with floral embroidery and glittery heels for a pair of PVC Gianvito Rossi mules.

Kardashian is wont to make things her own—after all, she is adding a new chapter to the garment’s history. But as she delves deeper into fashion history, it would be nice to see her go full throttle fashion girl and wear the full look—kooky tights and all.

#6645. Toasted Meringue Hazelnut Blondies

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Lightly coat a 9x9" pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Line pan with parchment paper, leaving overhang on two sides. Toast 2 cups blanched hazelnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown and fragrant, 15–18 minutes. Let sit until cool enough to handle, then coarsely chop; set aside.

Cook 1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring often, until butter foams, then browns (do not burn), 7–9 minutes. Remove from heat.

Whisk 2 large eggs, room temperature, 1 large egg yolk, room temperature, 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, ¼ cup (packed; 50 g) light brown sugar, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¾ tsp. instant espresso powder (if using) in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium-high speed until mixture is pale and doubled in volume, 6–9 minutes (mixture will form an unbroken ribbon when whisk is lifted from bowl).

Reduce speed to low and with motor running, gradually pour in brown butter in a thin, continuous stream; beat until incorporated, about 2 minutes. Remove bowl from mixer and gently fold in 1½ cups (187 g) all-purpose flour with a rubber spatula, scraping down sides and bottom of bowl, until no large, dry streaks of flour remain. Scrape batter into prepared pan; smooth surface. Top with reserved hazelnuts and press in gently to adhere (surface will be smothered with nuts).

Bake blondie until edges are golden brown and center is just set, 35–45 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let blondie cool in pan. Using parchment paper to help, lift blondie out of pan and transfer to rack.

Meanwhile, combine 3 large egg whites and 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar in the clean bowl of stand mixer and set over a saucepan of just simmering water (make sure bottom of bowl does not touch water). Heat, whisking constantly, until sugar is dissolved and an instant-read thermometer registers 170°.

Fit bowl onto mixer fitted with clean whisk attachment. Beat egg white mixture until thick and glossy and mixture is barely lukewarm, 8–10 minutes. Add 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt; fold in with a rubber spatula just to combine. Taste meringue and season with more kosher salt if needed

Peel away parchment paper from blondie and transfer to a heatproof platter. Using an offset spatula, spread meringue evenly over blondie, covering from edge to edge. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue until deep golden brown. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Using a long knife and wiping off with a damp kitchen towel between cuts, slice blondie into 9 squares.

Do Ahead: Blondie can be baked 24 hours ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6644. Silver Fox at 16. How Men Are Embracing Gray Hair at Every Age

At 16, James Chudley’s first gray hair was spotted by the girl sitting next to him in Biology. He thought it was a joke. She took a photo to prove it. There it was: one silver thread, just above his ear. “For the rest of the year,” he says, “every Biology lesson, it was: ‘Oh, there’s another one!’”

Chudley, now a personal trainer-in-training from Surrey, England wasn’t too bothered. “I thought I’d just pluck it out,” he says. By 19, though, there were too many to pluck. An anti-gray shampoo turned his bath blue; dye was another option, but he had reservations: “I didn’t want to end up looking like Dracula.”

Away from school, Chudley gradually got comfortable with his grays. Even so, he mentioned them before anyone else could, “almost as a defense mechanism.” Usually the response was playful roasting, sometimes even a compliment. But then someone would catch him off guard. Chudley, now 22, was recently working as a delivery driver when a customer looked him up and down. “Bit young to be going gray, isn’t it?” she said. Almost as an afterthought, she added, “Is it stressing you out?”

Gray hair is an inevitability for most men. Live long enough, and the color starts to drain. For many people, that begins in their early 30s and becomes more visible with age. By 50, suggests a study by the British Association of Dermatologists, up to 23% of us will have half a head of gray hair. The science is straightforward. Hair follicles contain melanocytes, the cells responsible for producing pigment. As we age, the stem cells that replenish them become less active, and the color fades. It’s like a printer cartridge running out of ink: the paper keeps coming, but eventually, there’s nothing on there.

Going gray in your teens and early 20s, however, is another matter. It’s relatively uncommon, although anecdotes are easy to find. Spend five minutes on TikTok and you’ll see plenty asking why they’re suddenly gray. Reddit has versions too, with users swapping stories and theories about why they—and seemingly everyone around them—are losing their color so young. “I don’t know if you’ve noticed, but people’s hair seems to be turning white really fast lately,” says one post. “How did we end up in the worst century where literally anything can go wrong?”

It’s hard to say if we’re actually going gray earlier, or if it’s just that more people are talking about it. The theories, meanwhile, keep on coming—from mineral deficiencies to heavy-metal exposure. There’s also an optimistic explanation: More people are open to embracing it.

Young men are spending more money than ever on looking good—even on their grays. Rather than shopping for cheap cover-ups, they are forensically researching science-backed cosmetics. Part of this also means a rejection of chemical-heavy products and a more skeptical attitude towards unnecessary cosmetics. Hair dye, after all, is not entirely harmless.

Online communities like “Gray and Proud” and “Silver Revolution” have tens of thousands of members. Paul Mescal and Jeremy Allen White have also done their part for gray-hair representation among young(ish) people: The Times dubbed them “silver fox cubs.”

Maybe things really are shifting. But if the demand for anti-gray products is any indication, the revolution is still a way off. Anti-gray serums are becoming big business. The global market is expected to jump from around $1.3 billion to $2 billion by 2031, according to Deep Market Insights. Cosmetics Business magazine calls it the “next men’s grooming trend,” with growing interest in peptide-based products. On the internet, you see both sides. On Reddit, a 26-year-old guy shares a photo of his gray head of hair, saying that he’s already got more than his dad. The top comment reads: “Do your due diligence, of course—bloodwork, diet etc.” Someone else follows up with: “[Guys] with gray hair are [hot].”

One person making the case for Gen Z’s grey-haired men is model and musician Charlie Jeer. The 24-year-old first found fame on the Netflix dating show Too Hot to Handle. He has the chiseled jawline and cheekbones of a conventional heartthrob, but there’s another feature viewers can’t seem to get past: his hair. “I feel like it gets brought up in conversation every single day in my life,” he says.

Jeer first noticed the grays as a teenager, and mostly shrugged off the comments. Online, it’s a different story. “Why are you going gray?”; “Can’t tell if bro is 15 or 60; ” “Err this old man.” “It’s relentless,” he says.

Now, Jeer sees the grays as an opportunity to stand out. They’ve helped build his profile as a model, too, partly because of the “age ambiguity” they give him. He’s picked up credits with brands like Davidoff and Adidas. “There’s a massive commercial potential for me to make a black hair dye and just start marketing that,” he says. “I never did because I was like, ‘No, I’m proud of my hair the way it is.’”

On TikTok, Jeer takes on his critics with captions like: “Joke’s on them when I’m a silver fox by 30.” He really likes it when he hears from other young guys going gray. “I’ve had a little gray-haired community of people come forward and present themselves,” he says. “It’s nice to hear someone else say that they’ve had people come at them for being gray-haired and that they’re going to continue to wear it with confidence.”

Jeer might be on the young end of the gray-hair population, but as a guy, he’s riding a well-worn track. Men have always been afforded the privilege of associating their grays with looking more distinguished. You don’t have to be George Clooney (or a Too Hot to Handle contestant) to benefit from that. Women, meanwhile, aren’t part of that deal: gray hair is more often simply read as old, an obviously unfair double standard.

It still come with baggage for men, though: age, lost virility, fading relevance. “The first gray” is practically a trope in its own right—a visual shorthand in films, books and TV for a character beginning to age, often followed by the inevitable midlife crisis. There are dozens of those scenes, in everything from The Simpsons to Vanilla Sky.

Matt Newman is a New York–based hairstylist who hates his gray hair. “There are so many examples of men with premature grays that people love and adore,” he says. “But in your 20s, that might not be an aesthetic you’re ready to dive into.”

Perhaps that’s why Jackass star Johnny Knoxville waited until 49 to finally embrace his natural hair color. He started going gray in his 20s and dyed it for most of his life. Then, during lockdown, he asked his wife to give him a buzz cut to reveal the silver underneath, on Instagram. “I should start a challenge but I don’t want to call anyone out,” he wrote on Instagram. Going gray, declared one Mr. Porter headline, was now a “punk power move”.

That’s not quite how Saavan Varambhia, 25, a data analyst from Buckinghamshire, would have described it. Not at first, anyway. Like Chudley, he was at school when a group of female friends spotted his grays and tried to pluck them out. “I was like, ‘Hmm, I don’t know how I feel about this,’” he says. A few years later, he had enough gray hairs on his head to “stop people in their tracks.”

For Varambhia, the contrast was hard to miss. He’s South Asian, with naturally deep-black hair, so the grays stood out. The Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology reports that people of Asian descent also tend to go gray later, often in their late 30s. According to Professor Desmond Tobin, a professor of dermatological science at University College Dublin, many Eastern cultures have traditionally been less accepting of grays than the West, with men and women both more likely to dye them.

“At first, I felt like I didn’t want to seem a lot older than my peers,” Varambhia says. Over time, though, he came to see the silver as something that set him apart. “I’ve always been one to stand out, and it was another attributing factor to that.”

When there are too many gray hairs to pluck, do you reach for the Just for Men, or join the silver fox cub club?

Turning gray at any age can make you wonder why it’s happening. According to Tobin, the answer is usually in your DNA. “The first thing to do is just to look at your [previous] generation of relatives,” he says. “They’re going to give you a road map for where you’re going to be. And if you have early grayers—teens, early 20s—then that’s really mapped out quite starkly in the family.”

Other things can speed up the process, too. Stress is a big one. Tobin says it can damage the cells responsible for producing hair pigment, acting like a “sledgehammer” if the process has already begun. Just look at Barack Obama’s hair before and after his time in the White House. Nutrition can play a role, too, and a blood test can pick up any deficiencies. But Tobin says the nutritional deficiencies linked to premature graying tend to show up in countries where malnutrition is more widespread.

Crucially, though, Tobin says he hasn’t seen hard evidence that young people are going gray earlier across the board. Modern life might come with its share of chronic stressors, he points out, but humans have been enduring trying times since long before social media, climate change, and cost of living crises entered the picture.

Tobin is skeptical of the “overstated claims” made by supplements and serums that promise to “tickle your stem cells.” If you want to slow the process, he says, your best bet is the boring stuff: less stress, plenty of sleep and an antioxidant-rich diet. That might hold things off for a while. But for anyone genetically predisposed to graying, it might not make that much of a difference.

“Would maximum antioxidant intake really stop somebody from graying who’s genetically headed that way? It’s not likely to be a very significant contributor,” Tobin says. “It might, in a multi-prong way, add up to something, but if you’re graying significantly in your teens, that is probably the die that’s being cast for you.”

The good news? Going gray early doesn’t mean the rest of you is aging at the same rate. In fact, there may be a silver lining. People who go gray prematurely are more likely to keep their hair; “nearly all people who bald [do so] with their natural hair color,” says Tobin.

But for anyone who doesn’t want to live with their grays, the hunt for a treatment is on. Research into gray hair has surged alongside the wider boom in longevity science. Tobin says the past five years have felt like a return to the 1980s, when the topical hair-regrowth drug Rogaine first shook up the haircare world. He has consulted for startups developing anti-gray treatments aimed at reducing oxidative stress or extending the life of melanocyte stem cells. The science is promising, but so far, nothing has produced evidence strong enough to satisfy regulators.

Researchers are beginning to understand that graying may not be irreversible, as once thought. Melissa Harris at the University of Alabama has studied the melanocyte stem cells behind hair pigmentation, and immunotherapy as a way to reverse graying. Other research has shown that some hairs can spontaneously regain their pigment, with changes appearing to track periods of stress. It hints that some aspects of aging may be less linear than we assume.

Dr. Greg Williams, a hair restoration surgeon at the Farjo Hair Institute, has watched the field develop. He hosts conference sessions on gray hair and, a couple of years ago, set up a WhatsApp group where specialists around the world could swap ideas and compare notes. “Gray hair is very poorly understood,” he says. “There’s not a lot of research in humans around it.” Maybe that’s surprising, given how universal it seems to be. But commercial fallout is huge. The global hair-and scalp-care industry is worth nearly $9.4 billion, and Williams thinks anyone who figures it out “would be a Nobel Prize winner”.

As for Varambhia, the science seems to fit his experience. Genetics are clearly part of the picture: his dad’s hair has been white for years, and he still has a full head of it. Varambhia also suspects stress sped things up. His grays arrived rapidly as he settled into corporate nine-to-five life. Since hitting the gym regularly, he thinks the process may have slowed.

Knowing other people going through the same thing has helped. “I know eventually I’ll go fully gray. I hope it’s a bit later on than sooner,” he says. But when the time comes? “I’ll embrace it.”

A version of this story originally appeared in the November 2026 issue of British GQ with the title “Gray Ahead of Schedule”

#6643. November’s Bake Club Is a Triple Feature of Holiday Pies

We’re Jesse and Shilpa, senior editors and the resident bakers of the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen. We love to bake—some might even call us obsessive—and we love to talk about all the hows and whys and what-didn’t-works that come with it.

Think of the Bon Appétit Bake Club as a book club, but for baking. Each month we share a brand-new meticulously tested recipe. Bake along with us, share your wins (or your fails—we’ve all been there), post pictures, ask us your pressing questions. We’re creating a community of confident, curious bakers who find just as much joy in the process of baking as the final results.

First, and most important, save each month’s recipe and bake it! You’ll find all of them below.

Join the Bon Appétit Bake Club chat on Substack and we’ll take you behind the scenes of our recipe development process.

Post and share photos of your beautiful bakes on Instagram using the hashtag #BABakeClub.

Share feedback and ask us questions in the Recipe Notes section of the recipe page in the Epicurious app. We read every comment and look forward to talking with you about butter, sugar, and more.

Send your baking questions to [email protected] for a chance to be featured on our podcast. Each recipe’s episode goes live at the start of the following month on the Bon Appétit podcast feed.

To celebrate pie, the iconic food of this American holiday (move over, turkey), we’re bringing back our trusty flaky-as-a-croissant crust that debuted in 2022. It has since become the only pie dough we use in the Test Kitchen—and in a room full of pro cooks, that’s a ringing endorsement. This year it’s the base of two recipes: a single-crust Cranberry Meringue Pie that will teach you all about blind baking and impress your loved ones with its towering slices, and a lattice-topped Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie whose double crust shows off all those buttery layers encasing lightly boozy caramel-draped fruit. Want homemade pie without making your own dough? We didn’t forget about you! Our Salted Coffee Custard Pie has a press-in oatmeal crust and a silky custard filling gilded with an airy layer of mascarpone-whipped cream.

Imagine a Parker House roll having a tryst with Asian-style milk bread and a classic French croissant—that’s the essence of salt bread, a.k.a. shio pan in Japan and sogeum-ppang in Korea. Each soft bun holds a rich secret: a nub of salted butter bundled within the shaped dough. The little pat of fat melts in the oven, pooling on the baking sheet to effectively fry the bottom crust, yielding a crisp, savory shell akin to something you’d find in a patisserie. I like to tear it in half to revel in the buttery, hollow center, then unravel each flaky layer, just like a croissant. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food editor

Is it even fall if you haven’t been apple picking? And have you even been apple picking if you didn’t end the day racing to the farm stand selling still-warm cinnamon-sugar doughnuts? Our latest recipe is designed to recreate that experience—apple-studded dough, a hint of grease, a jolt of sugar and spice—without waiting for yeast to rise.

For those unfamiliar with karpatka, a.k.a. Carpathian Mountain Cake, let us enlighten you. Traditionally, two disks of tender, airy pâte à choux house a layer of pastry cream lightened with whipped cream or crème mousseline. This version ditches the classic filling for a no-bake cheesecake (!) ribboned with homemade plum jam. It’s make-ahead-friendly and endlessly fun; just the thing to keep the summer vibes going a little longer.

This sunflower yellow cake with an alluring bounce is Bake Club’s midsummer stunner. Fresh (or frozen! I don’t mind) corn blended with a can of sweetened condensed milk and our defining ingredient, sweet rice flour, makes up the bulk of the batter. The end result is a textural masterpiece with gentle resistance and slight elasticity that tastes like buttered corn, toasty coconut, and nutty caramel all at once.

If a tomato sandwich, pizza, and flaky pastry started a band, these tomato galettes would be their first hit single. Start by making a black-pepper-spiked pie dough, which needs no specialty equipment to bake up crisp and layered. Each little round is filled with a dollop of garlicky Parmesan and herb mayo, which acts as a barrier between each little galette’s juicy tomato slice and delicate pleated crust. —Rebecca Firkser, Test Kitchen editor

Lemons are a powerful ingredient. So why miss out on their full potential by only using their juice and zest? That was the thesis behind these bars. By blitzing up two whole lemons into the curd, then straining out the pulpy bits, we keep lemon’s most exciting qualities: the bitterness of the pith, the essential oils of the skin, and of course, the acidity of the juice. Think Lemonhead candy. It’s everything I love about classic lemon bars with the volume turned up to a reckless decibel level.

Last year, for deputy food editor Hana Asbrink’s birthday, I made a strawberry roll cake filled with whipped cream and tiny jewel-red strawberries. It was an immediate hit and we decided right then that it belonged in Bon Appétit Bake Club. With fluffy cake, vanilla-bean-flecked cream, and juicy berries, it’s a dream dessert, tailored for this joyful season filled with new blooms and tender asparagus. Roll cakes traditionally require a complex series of steps when it comes to shaping, but this version utilizes an oil-based chiffon sponge, making it particularly easy to roll with no cracks and no heartbreak.

After last month’s cheesy biscuits, we’re going back to our dessert-loving roots and baking chocolate cake. But not just any old chocolate cake—this is a malty, brawny loaf imbued with Guinness stout. The crumb is tender beyond belief because of how you mix the batter. You’ll combine the dry ingredients, then rub in the butter by hand, until it practically disappears. This mimics a technique called reverse creaming and prevents excess gluten from forming. And there’s no special equipment, like a stand mixer, required.

A biscuit warm from the oven, split open so the steam rises to meet you, rivals the pleasure of an exalted loaf of homemade bread, all for a mere fraction of the effort (and wait time). This month’s recipe is packed with cheese and zhuzhed up with Old Bay seasoning. These biscuits are tall and layered like a lasagna, thanks to a quick and dirty lamination technique not unlike croissants. You don’t need any special equipment for these, but I highly recommend availing yourself of a nice bench scraper. It makes shaping the dough so much easier. Chris recently handed me a set from Gestura and I’ve been loving it because it’s small but sturdy, with thoughtfully curved edges and a minimal handle.

With a few pantry staples and a little time, this recipe yields a dozen delightfully chewy bagels that rival the most beloved of NYC shops. The trick? A two-step process: The bagels are first boiled, then baked. This dual approach gives them their signature chew, tanned sheen, and pleasantly dense (not tough) interior. And for a little fun: You can top these bagels with just about anything you like. Some of our favorites are furikake, Parmesan, sesame seeds (classic), and flaky salt.

This bake is inspired by Black Forest cake, a Bavarian dessert defined by its layers: chocolate cake, cream, cherries, and kirsch, a cherry brandy. Over the years it spread far beyond its woodland origins, to countries like India, Fiji, the Philippines, and the Caribbean Islands. One bakery in Chennai, India, where I grew up, made tall triangular slices, a treat my parents brought home if we did well on our school tests. Pavlovas are prone to crack, weep, or turn soggy and chewy. The key is in the ratio of sugar to egg whites. Two parts sugar to one part egg whites (by weight, of course) gives you a sturdy, crisp, snow-white pavlova.

Designed to maximize the ratio of sticky, gooey insides, arguably the best part of the pastry, this giant cinnamon roll was received with joy almost every time I made it. A little instant vanilla pudding mixed with cinnamon sugar mimics the ooey-gooey texture of mall-famous cinnamon roll filling, thanks to the modified food starch it contains. It’s purposefully large enough to cut into slices like a cake, but if you’re like us, you won’t be able to resist tearing it apart with your bare hands. Nor should you.

For those unfamiliar with the old-school pageantry of this French pastry, let us enlighten you: A Paris-Brest is a giant wreath of pate à choux (a foundational pastry dough) that puffs and expands dramatically in the oven. This version swaps the traditional praline mousseline filling for a banana-peel-infused (yes!) diplomat cream (just a fancy term for pastry cream lightened with whipped cream) and layers it with candied nuts and slices of banana. Everything good about Southern banana pudding, just in a flashier, French package.

Turn on the AC, because this month we’re making a lovely, homey pie. It’s everything good about summer (fruit! leisure! long days!) tucked away in a crisp, flaky crust, lightly scented with cardamom, and topped with a brown sugar streusel. There are some powerful learning moments in this bake: How to make a crust that will never fail you. How to select the best fruit for a pie. Why it’s important to precook a high-moisture filling so your pie crust is crisp rather. And perhaps the hardest and most important lesson of all: How long to wait before you dig into your pie ( it’s longer than you think).

This is no squishy sandwich loaf, but rather a big, browned boule studded with fresh jalapeños and chunks of cheddar. It’s ultra-savory and just a touch spicy. For those who might be intimidated by homemade bread (we see you!), think of this recipe as an intro course. It’s made with instant yeast, so it comes together quickly, without having to fuss over finicky active dry yeast or sourdough starter. And you don’t have to knead it; a few quick folds is all it takes.

This month we’re making Hummingbird Cake, an imposing icon from the American South. It’s a storied dessert with an interesting history that involves a Caribbean island, possibly a bird, and a magazine that’s over five decades old. If you’re unfamiliar, think of it as a banana version of carrot cake, full of nuts, spices, fruit, and cream cheese frosting.

The tang of cultured dairy from sour cream makes these scones stand out, keeping them moist but not claggy. And with that addition, channeling coffee cake became the natural next step. With clusters of streusel on top and a cinnamon sugar swirl within, these are scones that anyone will love.

Millionaire’s shortbread is the ultimate show-off bake. Our version went through about 10 rounds of testing until every detail was just right. The base of these bars—a simple, ultra-tender shortbread—gets a special upgrade: toasting a bit of the flour beforehand. This lends a deep nuttiness, almost like coffee, without any extra ingredients. The caramel takes a hybrid approach, bolstering caramelized sugar with sweetened condensed milk, so you get a bittersweet flavor with a sliceable texture. The final layer combines chocolate with butter for a mirror-like shine and fudgy bite.

The key to this pistachio cake’s tender crumb and mowed-grass green hue? A blender. It does all the hard work for you, decimating the nuts into a coarse flour and evenly distributing the dry ingredients (no sifting needed). This cake is satisfyingly hefty and moist thanks to the pistachios’ natural fat content, a combination of melted butter and oil, plus a pearlescent lemon glaze.

It’s easy to see the appeal of Basque cheesecake—dramatic visuals aside, it’s astonishingly easy to make. You don’t need a crust, or a water bath, or the long, slow cook of a New York–style cheesecake. The trick lies in cooking it hot and fast, much like pizza or steak, resulting in a cheesecake of epic contrasts, deeply caramelized on the outside while remaining quiveringly soft inside. I’ve added buttery mascarpone and a not insignificant amount of instant espresso to the batter to mimic another custardy classic, the iconic tiramisu. Topped off with a rosette of cocoa-dusted cream, it is two desserts for the effort of one.

Our pizza recipe meets you where you are: It can come together in fewer than 4 hours and is adaptable to an overnight rest. You don’t need a stand mixer, a clunky baking stone, or a specialty oven. And you’ll still get a world-class pie. The decidedly untraditional two-step cooking method (stovetop plus broiler) is a game changer, guaranteeing a puffy crust with enviable char (or leoparding, as the pros call it). To make dough-handling easier, we highly recommend a flexible bowl scraper.

This one-bowl cake has olive oil in both the chocolate cake and the ganache-like frosting. It’s a low-effort, high-reward recipe. And if there are any leftovers, thanks to that olive oil, the crumb will stay moist for days. Using Dutch-process cocoa powder gives this cake an intense chocolaty flavor. Our go-to brand for pretty much anything baking-related is Guittard Cocoa Rouge. It has a bold, concentrated complexity without any of the dull chalkiness common in other brands.

This project bake screams autumn. The perfect follow-up to apple picking, it’s a fruit-studded beauty, drenched in a tangy cider caramel and using almost half a gallon of apple cider. Make sure to use a 12-cup or larger Bundt pan for this recipe. Using a smaller variety can result in the dough proofing out of the pan. Nordic Ware actually invented the Bundt pan, and we love their version for its sturdy construction and even heat distribution.

#6641. Deb Haaland and Peggy Flanagan Mark Their Historic Wins in Intentional Earrings

Last night, the 2026 midterm election results delivered plenty of historic firsts. It was a particularly powerful night for Native American representation: Democrat Deb Haaland became the first Native American woman to be elected as Governor of New Mexico, while Peggy Flanagan—the current lieutenant governor of Minnesota—became the first Native woman to win the U.S. Senate seat in her state. (And there could even be a third victory for the Indigenous community today: at the time of publishing this story, Alaska’s Mary Peltola is currently leading the race for a Senate seat, too.)

As the race results were officially called yesterday evening, both Haaland and Flanagan emerged to celebrate their historic appointments in their respective states. And better yet, they chose intentional accessories to do so: Both politicians wore statement earrings made by Indigenous artists, a thoughtful move to uplift and spotlight the unique beauty found within their own communities. It was a fitting fashion choice, given that many Native artists utilize earrings as a cultural identifier—a stylish way to keep their traditional materials and motifs alive.

Haaland wearing Pat Pruitt’s dragonfly earrings.

Haaland—who is a Laguna Pueblo congresswoman and the former interior secretary under Joe Biden’s administration—made an appearance in Albuquerque, New Mexico. She wore a pair of titanium dragonfly earrings by Pat Pruitt, a Laguna and Chiricahua Apache artist based in the state. Along with spotlighting one of the Native community’s most well-known artists, her choice to wear dragonfly earrings was also symbolic: They represented taking flight, change, and transformation.

The dragonfly earrings are one of Pruitt’s signature pieces, though he also specializes in sleek cuffs and necklaces, too. “The first version of the dragonfly earrings debuted in 2015, heavily influenced by the work of fashion designer Pilar Agoyo (Ohkay Owingeh/Cochiti/Kewa Pueblos) and my mentor, Greg Lewis (Laguna Pueblo),” says Pruitt of Haaland’s earrings. “The design brought together the traditional double-cross motif Greg taught me and the bold, black dragonfly imagery Pilar was incorporating into her work at the time. Titanium has since become my material of choice, allowing me to produce the earrings in a variety of colors.”

Flanagan wears dentalium shell earrings by Jessica Mendez.

Meanwhile, in Saint Paul, Minnesota, Flanagan—who is a member of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe—celebrated her win by speaking to the crowd at an election night watch party. The politician chose to wear a long, dangly pair of dentalium shell earrings by Yurok artist Jessica Mendez, paired with a burgundy suit. Similar to Haaland, Flanagan’s earrings were an intentional homage to celebrating Indigenous craft: Dentalium shells hold great meaning and importance within the Native community.

The long, tubular shells—derived from dentalium, a type of marine mollusk—resemble tusks due to their curved shape and milky color, and they are considered just as precious as diamonds (if not more), because they are becoming increasingly difficult to find. The use of dentalium in Indigenous culture, as a form of adornment, predates European colonization; Today, many contemporary Indigenous artists create jewelry using the shells, including Jamie Okuma’s signature tiered styles, or Tania Larsson’s striking necklaces.

Flanagan wears dentalium shell earrings by Jessica Mendez.

Tonight is not the only occasion that the politicians have used their platform to uplift Indigenous creatives. Throughout their campaigns, both Haaland and Flanagan have worn pieces by Native designers. Flanagan has worn printed Jamie Okuma suits and shapely Copper Canoe Woman earrings. (There is even an entire Instagram account dedicated to Flanagan’s fabulous earrings.) Haaland, meanwhile, has donned traditional ribbon skirts, including during her 2021 swearing-in ceremony as Secretary of the Interior.

Both Haaland and Flanagan’s choice to use fashion as a form of cultural pride last night, however, echoes how they plan to approach their historic appointments moving forward. With their respective platforms, both politicians pledged to fight for Indigenous rights and give a long-overdue voice to their community. “I believe that no matter where you come from, how much money you have, or what challenges you’ve faced, every New Mexican deserves the chance to thrive,” Haaland said during her speech. Flanagan echoed the sentiment. “You fought for me,” she said, “and I’m going to fight for you.”

#6640. Frico'ed Brussels Sprouts

A slick of oil and a sprinkling of salt are the only adornments brussels sprouts need to shine. But put a crispy Parmesan skirt on them and suddenly the humble veggie becomes the belle of the ball. This recipe does just that. By roasting the brussels sprouts snuggled into a blanket of grated Parmesan cheese, the cheese melts into a crispy, frico-like sheet that clings onto the sprouts, surrounding them in a lace-like halo. It’s a dramatic side dish, but one that makes a serious statement. If roasted correctly, and the stars align in your favor, you can peel off the entire sheet in one swift swoop, presenting it as the culinary masterpiece it is. Fans of fun, this is for you.

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: Your Brussels Sprouts Need a Crispy, Cheesy Skirt.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a baking sheet with a nonstick baking mat or a sheet of parchment paper generously coated with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Toss 1½ lb. brussels sprouts, trimmed, halved, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a medium bowl to combine. Scatter 4 oz. store-bought grated Parmesan (pre-grated works better here than grating from a block) in an even layer over baking sheet, leaving a ½" border around edges. Arrange brussels sprouts, cut side down, in a single layer on top, spacing evenly to fill baking sheet. Bake until brussels sprouts are tender and browned and cheese is deep golden, 20–28 minutes. (If the cheese in the very center is browned, it’s done.) Let cool at least 5 minutes, then break into pieces to serve. (Or place another parchment-lined baking sheet upside down on top; holding together, swiftly turn over, peel away mat, and present cheese side up.)
