#6638. Why Do We Keep Coming Back to Godzilla?

Like most people born in the western world after 1954, I knew of a monster named Godzilla before I’d heard of a country called Japan. It’s not a rare perspective. For as long as nearly any living person can remember, Godzilla has been hugely popular, far exceeding the global recognition afforded most leaders, athletes, and certainly his human co-stars, those men and women whose dramatic dealings are the universally agreed-upon bargain for apocalyptic havoc that millions upon millions have gladly paid to see for over 70 years.

What Godzilla hasn’t been is prestigious. The irradiated dinosaur of very few words—mainly deafening screams—is a beloved figure more in the key of Harry Potter, Batman, or James Bond than the loftier fare that typically gets recognized by major festivals or awards bodies. But exceptions to the rule do exist. The Criterion Collection issued Ishiro Honda's 1954 original on a deluxe Blu-ray in 2012 and marked their 1,000th release with a lavish set of Godzilla’s Shōwa era (1954-1975), which both documents film history and calls to mind John Huston’s Chinatown line about sticking around long enough to become respectable. Writing an introduction to Honda’s biography A Life in Film, from Godzilla to Kurosawa, Martin Scorsese deemed the series’ first director "an extraordinary artist and craftsman" and placed Honda’s 1954 film (alongside spin-offs Mothra and Rodan) among “pictures that haunted the imaginations of young moviegoers like myself and millions of others for years to come.” Kiyoshi Kurosawa—perhaps Japan’s greatest living filmmaker, and certainly its finest practitioner of austere horror—deemed Honda’s film an early lesson in national trauma. Thomas Pynchon, too, had ambitious plans to write a novel about the insurance adjuster who responds to Godzilla’s wreckage (the idea never fully materialized, though it did become a nice tangent in his 1990 novel Vineland). We can look at the films and countenance such appreciations from geniuses. In the meantime, good luck to anyone counting the exact number of action figures, coloring books, sticker packs, and lunchboxes boasting Godzilla and friends.

A critical shift started somewhere in the last decade. Toho ostensibly shelved Godzilla with 2004’s Final Wars, a grand finale that was the big-budget equivalent of a child smashing toys. (That is a compliment.) Godzilla LLC boasts enough films and ancillary products to be financially solvent until the sun burns out (or an indomitable monster rises from the sea), but that retirement was short-lived. Toho resurrected the franchise in aggressive form with 2016’s Shin Godzilla, both a complete series reboot and (across several stages, each grotesque and terrifying) character reinvention that dispensed with typical monster-movie hijinks. An unholy experiment that would make the series’ many mad scientists proud, Shin Godzilla fused the hilarious bureaucratic hallway-rushing of In the Loop or Veep with cosmic horror befitting its director, Hideaki Anno, whose contributions to Japanese culture are nearly Godzilla’s equal on the strength of Neon Genesis Evangelion alone. With time, it’s downright eerie to see Anno’s foreshadowing of the global unrest of Trump, Brexit, COVID, and our endless misinformation era. But rather than keep the great filmmaker on retainer for any number of sequels or spin-offs, Toho regrettably followed Shin Godzilla with an anime trilogy produced for Netflix, a rare class of films I’ve been too embarrassed to even log on Letterboxd.

Whether genius or dreck, none of these films quite anticipated 2023’s Godzilla Minus One. It’s one thing to become the highest-grossing Japanese-language release in U.S. history—any Godzilla movie that doesn't at least aim for such a distinction isn’t worth its salt. It’s harder to imagine anyone, even or especially the franchise’s most ardent fans, anticipated lavish public praise from a quintet of Best Director winners in Steven Spielberg (who claims to have seen the film at least three times), James Cameron (who offered to work on a sequel), Christopher Nolan, Guillermo Del Toro, and Bong Joon-ho. In a recorded conversation with Yamazaki, Tom Cruise and Christopher McQuarrie credited the film as an inspiration; the actor went so far as to call it “perfect.” Which is to say nothing of the fact that Godzilla Minus One earned the series its first Oscar, a VFX prize awarded to none other than writer-director Takashi Yamazaki—a nice encapsulation of the film’s balance between spirit and spectacle.

Because Godzilla Minus One resonated more than anyone could have anticipated, Godzilla Minus Zero, which arrives in theaters this weekend, shoulders the burden of expectation. The first shot across the bow was its world premiere at last month’s New York Film Festival, where Zero debuted alongside prestige fare like Luca Guadagnino’s Sam Altman biopic Artificial and Tony Gilroy’s star-studded Behemoth! There, NYFF’s artistic director Dennis Lim introduced the movie to a sold-out crowd at the Alice Tully Hall, praising Yamazaki for exemplifying "the endless possibilities of creative VFX and genre filmmaking." Minus Zero indeed thrives on spectacle: its opening sequence blazes a merciless path of carnage aided by an elegant long take, while subsequent scenes centered on one of Godzilla’s classic foes, the three-headed Ghidorah, inspire genuine terror more than cheap thrills. This is the first Japanese film shot for IMAX, a large-scale exhibition that’s often torqued for discomfort. Yamazaki’s centerpiece battle pitting the monster against a squadron of fighter planes is dogged by fatalistic doom: a mother and child screaming as their house crashes to the ground don’t get the last-minute salvation we’ve come to expect, and even the sentimental-seeming inclusion of a pilot named Honda is complicated by his eventual fate.

If not quite so grave as the visions of death that imprinted upon a young Kiyoshi Kurosawa, Yamazaki’s narrative—including a face-melting sequence that U.S. distributor GKIDS have asked not be spoiled—provides a stark contrast to the bloodless carnage of American blockbusters. It’s quite the cultural coup, too, that a film this brutal and generally skeptical of American imperialism has secured a simultaneous international release: every English-speaking actor (none recognizable, each portraying arrogant allied military) bears an amusingly off-market quality à la the nefarious white time-travelers of 1991’s altogether underrated Godzilla vs. King Ghidorah.

Nearly all Godzilla films are a total restart. Minus Zero is immediately notable as a direct sequel. The results suggest that Yamazaki overestimated his initial project. Godzilla is not much of a presence in Minus Zero, first appearing around the 50-minute mark and then again in a suitable, albeit brief climax. Far more time is spent with those we came to know and like during Minus One, each reprised by an entirely competent ensemble that fails to elevate interest higher than a certain co-star’s 50 meters. (The protagonists’ adopted daughter from Minus One returns here for the sole purpose of standing in place and crying.) Whatever its pretensions towards grandeur, this is still a film where a scientist explains his master plan by smashing together two monster figures. It takes little to delight in this moment, a literal and figurative collision of serious storytelling and childlike abandon. More of that spirit might’ve served the final picture.

My mild disappointment is nothing compared to the agony Godzilla has wreaked on the district of Ginza, which last week hosted the first public screenings of Minus Zero through the Tokyo International Film Festival. Godzilla’s annihilated the city’s landmarks enough times that when we think of all-out destruction on the sprawling megalopolis that is Tokyo, we’re probably picturing its uber-fashionable shopping sector laid to ruins. When he emerged from the sea in 1954, he wrecked the district’s historic Nichigeki Theater, which was again destroyed (in real life, of humans’ accord) and reopened as the Yurakucho Mullion building in 1984—the same year as The Return of Godzilla, where he inflicted yet more damage on the brand-new structure. Godzilla Minus One recreated the Nichigeki Theater in loving detail only to destroy it again in a sequence that deployed modern visual effects to cause maximum tactility and human misery. That Hiroshima-like site is revisited in Minus Zero, leading one character to declare that “Ginza is again the battleground.” Time’s healed those wounds, however. The night before Minus Zero’s Japanese premiere, a small crowd gathered outside the Yurakucho Mullion’s Seiko watch for an extravagant display: the clock lifted, and out came a small set of Godzilla puppets that strike chimes while Akira Ifukube’s iconic theme plays.

Ginza’s Wako Clock Tower has fared no better: it was torn to ribbons in the 1954 original, 1995’s Godzilla vs. Destoroyah, Shin Godzilla, and Minus One. After a time you must wonder what keeps bringing Godzilla back to the neighborhood. Is it animal instinct, or mere coincidence, or an atomic hatred for its glowing consumerism? The Wako Annex, a nearby pastry shop that Google not-inaccurately describes as “chic,” currently advertises a Christmas-themed cake recreation of the oft-doomed Clock Tower with Minus Zero’s monster looming over it; accompanying text informs us that “Godzilla strikes Ginza’s Wako once again.” The nearby Toho cinema is within Hibiya Godzilla Square, featuring a small but impressively detailed statue and a plaque reading, “The human race must coexist with Godzilla.” Immediately adjacent is a three-story shopping mall hosting a Toho store selling numerous Godzilla ephemera. (I bought the tea cup.)

Even Americans accustomed to the fetishization of disaster would be impressed by Japan’s ability to marry suffering and spectacle to great financial gain. Perhaps it’s the same haunted fascination of a young Martin Scorsese or Kiyoshi Kurosawa cast unto the world at large; Godzilla might be scary as he destroys Ginza, but he’s something to admire when shrunk down to human size and displayed inside the Yurakucho Mullion’s lobby. (The photo-snapping crowds that gather every time I walk past suggest that bit of marketing paid off.) Even as Minus Zero’s first reviews show a less rapturous response than Minus One, this series’ viability—and its newfound prestige—shows little indication of flagging. Ginza’s residents were beyond happy to see Godzilla, at least in ossified, action-figure form. But who's to say they wouldn't be just as excited if, one day, his path of destruction broke through the screen?

#6637. Why I Love Texas (Today More Than Ever)

I was born in Texas—but it’s been a while since I’ve found myself choosing it. From rolls of razor wire being installed along the banks of the Rio Grande to the destruction of Big Bend National Park and the stripping of a woman’s right to make decisions about her own body, the Friendship State has felt less and less friendly recently.

But last night, James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa accomplished what long felt to me like an impossible feat: In January, Texas will be blue. Not a sort-of shade of light blue, but bright, bold, Yves Klein blue. Texas will have Democrats as governor and senator, but also as lieutenant governor, railroad commissioner, attorney general, comptroller, and agricultural commissioner.

None of this seemed possible to me as a girl growing up in Dallas, the city I called home until 2017. My dad used to joke that I was born liberal—never more so than when, at age 12, I declined to shake then-president George W. Bush’s hand at our local country club. At 17, I skipped school to watch future president Barack Obama speak at a campaign rally and during my college years I volunteered at Planned Parenthood. None of this kept me from loving my Republican friends and family members, even when we disagreed. Being from a red state, navigating those differences was just a part of life.

But some time not so long ago, I couldn’t help but notice those Republican friends and family members begin to change. The GOP was undergoing a shift and not all Texans liked it. At first, the hints were subtle. Friends began to reach out to talk about how President Trump’s remarks (about immigrants, “beautiful” tariffs, the war in Iran, or just politics in general) didn’t resonate. After the fall of Roe, Texas women I knew began to support women’s health organizations for the first time in their lives.

All of these people were good people, they always had been. But the feeling of sharing common ground with them? That was new. When I went home to celebrate my nieces’ birthdays in September, and discovered that the ultra-conservative neighborhood of Highland Park, where I’d grown up, was filled with signs for James Talarico, I felt like I was hallucinating. In Austin, I drove by a new community-run Narcan vending machine and watched grassroots volunteers stand on street corners registering people to vote. I heard Ken Paxton and Greg Abbott publicly boo-ed. The Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders voted to unionize. I nearly gasped.

My childhood in Texas was surrounded by love, and that’s what I want for my nieces, my future children, and anybody else who makes my beautiful state their home. Today, that actually feels possible. The results of Tuesday’s elections—which amounted to a vote for a New Texas, or maybe a recognition of the Texas that has always been there, just beneath the surface (a Texas captured, presciently, by photographer Tyler Mitchell in Vogue only a few issues ago)—make me want to put on my mom’s cowboy boots, get in line for the queso fountain, and go line dancing in Dallas’s Gayborhood. I don’t want to push my luck here, but can I get a Super Bowl win for the Cowboys next?

#6636. The Best Teriyaki in Seattle

Who serves the best gorditas in Mexico City? Or Baltimore's can't-miss crab cakes? Welcome to Taste of the Town, where we call on a local expert to share the best versions of one of their city’s most iconic foods. Here, we explore Seattle’s take on teriyaki.

Seattle’s entire teriyaki universe exists because of one man, a pioneer of chargrilled chicken thighs. In 1976, Toshi Kasahara opened a restaurant serving lightly marinated and grilled chicken, glazed in a blend of soy sauce, ginger, garlic, and sugar. This wasn’t any teriyaki you’d find in Japan, but a cheap, filling, flavor-packed translation aimed at a working-class city still unaware of the tech boom on the horizon.

Kasahara established and sold about 30 shops over the years, and copycats began copycatting. Teriyaki became ubiquitous, the Japanese name concealing its hometown heritage. Some locals don’t even realize teriyaki joints are a Seattle thing—that is, until they move elsewhere and try to find one.

Kitchens with Vietnamese roots began dishing up teriyaki alongside steaming bowlfuls of pho. Many spots still specialize in a classic interpretation, typically served with scoops of rice, some fried gyoza, and iceberg lettuce bathed in a thin mayo dressing. Enterprising Korean immigrants embraced teriyaki and opened their own outfits, adding bulgogi to the menu and gochujang to the chicken’s marinade.

The forward march of time, trends, and real estate prices means there’s sadly no longer a teriyaki business every few blocks. Those that remain include a few clunkers: Many have succumbed to shortcuts, serving sad chicken in gloopy, way-too-sweet gravy, which obscure the dish’s appeal to outsiders. But find a place still making its own sauce and blasting thighs on high heat, delivering bits of caramelized char that balance its teriyaki sweetness. Then you’ll understand.

Local wisdom dictates the best shop is the one closest to you, but here are eight greats, new and old.

Toshi Kasahara’s original restaurant, now long shuttered, was the archetype of a Seattle-style teriyaki spot—a spare cafeteria-like space with a streamlined menu built around Kasahara’s iconic chicken. Just a sprinkling of these shops still exist, but today only one is the real deal: a take-out operation deep in a Mill Creek strip mall. It’s open just a few hours in the evenings, with the 77-year-old Kasahara at the grill. He’s tweaked his methods slightly over the years, but his chicken is just as juicy and smoky as ever. No one in Seattle does it exactly like Toshi, but his sons do farther afield. One runs a Toshi’s food truck in San Francisco; the other is opening a Toshi’s outpost this winter in his father’s hometown of Ashikaga, Japan.

Hawaii has its own relationship to teriyaki. When restaurateur Matthew Parker opened his ode to the teriyaki counters that fueled his first 20 years in Seattle, he looked to his family’s roots in Oahu—specifically to huli huli chicken. That dish inspires Grillbird’s glossy house sauce, sweetened just enough with pineapple juice and ketchup. There’s no iceberg salad here; sides include mac salad and marinated cucumbers, dishes standard to plate lunch, Hawaii’s answer to the meat-and-three. Purists can grouse about how teriyaki shops should be old-school in every sense, but I welcome Grillbird’s modern touches, like online ordering and a mostly gluten-free menu. Grillbird’s original West Seattle outfit occupies a former Pizza Hut, which feels just right for this utilitarian dish. A second location in Phinney Ridge operates alongside sister concept Salad Party, for those looking to get their greens in.

When the Lee family lost the lease on their longtime teriyaki restaurant, the new location they’d scouted came with a catch: The strip mall that housed it already had a teriyaki shop. So matriarch Yoo-Mi Lee camouflaged her teriyaki menu with dishes from her Korean heritage and influences from the years the family lived in Brazil. Be thankful for that other teriyaki business, because Tá Jóia’s highly specific Brazilian-Korean-teriyaki remix is so vibrant and delicious, it could (should!) be a national fast-casual restaurant chain. Feijoada, a hearty slow-cooked black bean stew made with pork, bacon, and sausage, fits right in next to bulgogi, while the kitchen’s spectacular teriyaki hides in plain sight under the moniker “spicy chicken bowl.” It’s the chicken teriyaki of your hottest, most chili-spiked dreams, brightened with a scoop of pico and a drizzle of creamy house cilantro sauce.

No matter which member of the Kim family is behind the counter here, chances are they will offer you tea while you wait for your order. If the hospitality is great, the food is even better. Chicken teriyaki looks like it came off a photo shoot, deeply juicy with properly charred edges. It’s chicken that needs no supporting cast, but with so many combos on the menu, it’s fun to compare how the gingery sauce hits different proteins including beef, pork, prawn, or tofu. (If you’re exceedingly hungry, go for the formidable triple combo, which delivers chicken and beef teriyaki, golden-fried gyoza with a flaky, blistered exterior, and fragrant mounds of fried rice.) Teriyaki lovers are especially protective of Rainier Teriyaki since its late owner, Hansoo Kim, was tragically killed during a 2023 attempted armed robbery; the family banded together and reopened the restaurant in his honor.

Most people show up at Fremont’s busy donburi shop craving its chirashi bowl, but the chicken teriyaki imagines what Seattle’s signature dish might have looked like if it actually hailed from Japan. Butterflied thighs with the lightest of marinades come straight off the grill to be dressed with a sauce that’s thin by Seattle standards, but nonetheless lands a careful balance of savory and sweet. I appreciate this subtler rendition of chicken teriyaki, which complements an otherwise traditionally Japanese menu of rice bowls. Granted, people don’t usually crave Seattle teriyaki for its subtlety; add a dose of the house chili oil for texture and kick. Fremont Bowl is a kiosk-driven take-out machine, but the dine-in vibes are friendly, provided you can find a free table.

Ask a local about their favorite teriyaki shop, and chances are high it’s this been-there-forever counter next to a laundromat not far from Lake Union’s north end—not to be confused with other very similarly named Seattle teriyaki practitioners, including one on this list. A high ratio of dark soy makes for a standout sauce, while the thin mayo-based salad dressing plays well against the crispness of the fresh iceberg lettuce. The kitchen even uses an old-school mold to press rice into a pleasing half-football shape. Many teriyaki shops also have chicken katsu and egg rolls on the menu, but the versions here are standouts for their nongreasy crispy exteriors. The tables are mostly waiting zones for people ordering takeout, destined for a lunch in Gas Works Park, the nearby brewery taprooms, or just back to the surrounding tech offices. Come hungry: Portions are huge, even by generous teriyaki shop standards.

Nikko is busy most of the day, feeding a bustling lunch rush, teenagers after school, and evening take-out crowds. That turnover means teriyaki that’s always fresh, swiped with sauce that’s more soy than sugar and thick without verging on gummy. Jong Kwon and his family have run this West Seattle staple with warmth for more than two decades. Step inside the narrow shop and you’re transported back to Seattle’s era of peak teriyaki, a simpler time when one ordered off pictures on the wall rather than QR codes and the cashier remembered your name.

Clamshell take-out containers are so inherent to the teriyaki experience that nobody asks if you want your food to go, they generally just assume you do. But visit this Georgetown favorite (no relation to I Love Teriyaki) and you’ll witness a rare sight: Diners eating off actual plates. After a three-year closure following a fire, owners Don and Eva Lo rebuilt the original building (once a KFC) into a shiny new space. Aromas of grilled meat hit you from the parking lot, and the cheerful dining room is usually full. Skip the newish teriyaki burritos, and run, don’t walk, to the short ribs teriyaki, so smoky and tender that you might almost be tempted to bypass the chicken altogether. Almost.

#6635. Schmaltzy Chicken and Stuffing Skillet

While you might think of instant stuffing as a once-a-year darling that makes an annual appearance like Punxsutawney Phil, this recipe is a case study of why this product should be put to use throughout the year. (Boxes of the dried mix can be found near the breadcrumbs any month.) Here, it’s called into action to prop up skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs in a bed of savory stuffing that’s bolstered by aromatics and sweet-tart dried cranberries. Starting with a cold pan ensures even rendering of the chicken fat and crispy skin. The lot gets baked together, allowing the savory drippings from the chicken to soak into the stuffing. Serve with a side of cranberry sauce, a fresh salad, or all by itself for a one-pan dinner that recalls Thanksgiving any night of the week.

More delicious skillet dinners this way: Chicken Thighs With Spiced Couscous and Carrots; Ruffled Mushroom Pot Pie; and One-Skillet Chicken Pot Pie.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Season 2 lb. skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs (about 4 medium) on both sides with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Pour 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil into a cold large stainless-steel skillet and swirl to coat bottom of pan. Arrange chicken, skin side down, in pan and place over medium-high heat. Cook undisturbed, rotating pan around on burner often to promote even browning, until skin is browned and chicken releases easily from pan, 7–10 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet or large plate and arrange skin side up.

Combine 1 large onion, finely chopped, 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, and 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan and cook over medium-high heat, stirring often, until onion is softened and just starting to turn golden, 8–12 minutes. Add one 6-oz. box instant stuffing mix, ½ cup unsweetened dried cranberries, and 1¼ cups water, then finely grate in zest from 1 lemon and set lemon aside. Mix until stuffing is hydrated. Remove pan from heat and push stuffing to sides to create wells for chicken to rest in. Nestle thighs, skin side up, into stuffing. Transfer pan to oven and bake until chicken is cooked through and top of stuffing is golden brown and crisp, 45–55 minutes.

Top chicken and stuffing with more dried cranberries and reserved celery leaves. Cut reserved lemon into wedges and serve alongside for squeezing over.

#6634. Chili’s Customers Suffered Chemical Burns From Margaritas Contaminated With Cleaning Product

A simple mistake behind the bar had some seriously frightening consequences.

A North Carolina Chili’s is facing questions after a margarita mix-up left customers and employees with chemical burns.

A group of customers stopped by Chili’s Grill & Bar in Forest City, North Carolina shortly after doors opened on October 28. After ordering a round of margaritas, three diners immediately experienced discomfort and chemical burns in and around their mouths.

According to a statement from the Foothills Health District, the customers notified Chili’s staff before leaving to seek medical attention. Public health officials immediately suspended the location’s food service permit while they investigated the incident.

Investigators soon identified the culprit behind the chemical burns: a granulated degreasing chemical.

Two days before the incident, a third-party contractor was power-washing the restaurant’s exterior when a Chili’s employee received some of the cleaning product. The employee placed it in an unlabeled container, which was then brought inside and left at the bar.

On the morning of October 28, an employee setting up the bar mistook the degreaser for sugar and used it to prepare the margarita station for lunch service.

The three customers weren't the only ones to suffer from chemical burns. After the guests reported their injuries, two Chili’s employees tasted the substance in the container and experienced similar symptoms.

The Foothills Health District completed its investigation on October 29 and reinstated the restaurant’s food service permit after officials confirmed it met applicable food safety requirements. While local health officials have closed their investigation, Chili’s is still conducting its own.

“We are aware of an isolated incident at our restaurant in Forest City, North Carolina, that resulted in injuries to two of our guests and Team Members,” a Chili’s spokesperson tells Delish. “Our team took immediate action to support those affected and avoid any further injuries. We are actively investigating the circumstances related to this incident as the health and wellbeing of our guests and Team Members remain our top priority.”

#6632. Georgia Governor-Elect Keisha Lance Bottoms Celebrated Her Historic Win in Full Fuchsia

Yesterday evening, amid the midterms’ historic blue sweep, former mayor of Atlanta Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected governor of Georgia—making her the first Democratic governor of Georgia in this millennium and the first Black woman elected governor in United States history.

To celebrate that momentous occasion, Bottoms donned a fuchsia pantsuit with a matching silk shirt underneath designed by Dedrick Thomas of Hideoki Bespoke in Georgia. It was a bright, joyous choice, marking a new chapter in Georgia’s gubernatorial record and reflecting the exuberant energy of the evening overall.

“This campaign was about every community and every corner of Georgia,” Bottoms said in her victory speech at the Marriott Marquis in downtown Atlanta. (She’d been introduced by her daughter, Lennox, wearing a matching pink ensemble.) “No matter who you voted for tonight, I will be a governor for all of Georgia.”

In the decades since Georgia last had a Democratic governor—Roy Barnes, who held the office from 1999 to 2003—monochrome pantsuits have become a working standard for women in government, as in many other professional environments. (And even that was controversial for a time: before 1993, women largely wore dresses or skirts with jackets on the Senate floor.)

As ever, however, fashion proves itself a powerful storytelling tool. The shocking shade, historically associated with girlhood, was immediately evocative of a new sensibility. In 2025, dozens of congresswomen, led by New Mexico representative and leader of the Democratic Women’s Caucus Teresa Leger Fernández, wore pink to protest policies of President Trump’s that were negatively impacting women across the country. Likewise, beginning in 2020, Florida Rep. Angie Nixon took to wearing the hue almost exclusively—to the point that pink became inextricably intertwined with her public image. The branding was effective: electric pink is shaping up to be the suffragette white of a new generation.

#6630. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

#6628. Montana’s Newest Congressman Dresses Like a Ralph Lauren Model

You couldn’t ask for a better embodiment of the blue wave than Sam Forstag, the 32-year-old rookie Montana Democrat who defeated his Republican rival in yesterday’s midterms to flip an important House seat. While unaffordability was a key issue in the midterms across the country, it’s especially noticeable in Montana, where an influx of billionaires and tech companies has sent the cost of living soaring. Like many of his compatriots, Forstag campaigned on promises of affordable housing, better healthcare, and getting money out of politics. Unlike his fellow Democratic challengers, however, he did it in a wardrobe that looked straight off a rack at the RRL store.

Last night, in front of a crowd of supporters in Missoula, Forstag delivered his victory speech dressed in a hickory-striped work shirt, jeans, a big western belt buckle, and a pair of weathered brown forestry boots. Forstag’s fit stands in contrast to the standard election night business-casual look favored by political hopefuls on both sides of the aisle, but he’s far from the first candidate to lean into the dress codes of blue-collar Americans. From Tim Walz’s camo hats and Filson Mackinaw jackets to John Fetterman’s Carhartt hoodie, workwear remains a potent symbol of working-class solidarity. In this case, however, it’s not just blue-collar cosplay.

Forstag at a student get-out-the-vote gathering at Montana State University in October.

Straight out of college and looking to pay off his student loans, Forstag joined the US Forest Service as a wildland firefighter and spent the next eight years battling blazes around the country, including four years as a smokejumper parachuting into fire zones. As a result, he comes by his love of Levi’s and sturdy, Goodyear-welted footwear honestly, and—Montana being a place where jeans and work shirts are considered business-casual for many—didn’t need to change his look for the campaign.

Forstag addressing voters at a town hall in August.

As authentic as Forstag’s election-night outfit was, he also appears to be a guy who understands the power of styling. While his shirt likely didn’t have Ralph Lauren’s initials on the tag (wildland firefighters only make $20 an hour), the way he wore it—half unbuttoned, layered over a red thermal henley, and tucked into his jeans—owes a debt to the romantic take on Western style Lauren has been trafficking in since the ’70s. Or, equally likely, the Montana cowboys who the designer borrowed it from. Either way, Forstag’s look, like the progressive politics he and his Democratic colleagues campaigned on, will be a welcome disruption to business as usual on Capitol Hill.

#6627. 8 Delicious Host Gifts That Aren’t Wine

“What should I bring?” When a guest asks this well-intentioned question, the knee-jerk answer is “Wine!” But it’s just as simple to source thoughtful bits and bobs to create a memorable start to the meal. This way the host can forget about hors d’oeuvres altogether. Pick up a bark-wrapped cheese, artfully marbled charcuterie, or some I-can’t-believe-it’s-store-bought spritzes—or better yet, all of the above—and your fellow diners will be asking where they can buy a box on the way home.

If you are looking to contribute an NA option to the bar, you can’t do better than Ghia’s most recent release, Le Spritz Blood Orange. It’s a bubbly mix of bitter and sweet that more than fills in for an Aperol spritz or predinner glass of prosecco.

The problem with baked Brie is you have to bake it. Instead, bring a soft-rind cheese that can hold its own weight. Set it out on a plate or board for up to an hour before serving; this variety is best eaten at room temp when it’s soft and spreadable and the flavors have bloomed. St. Stephen from Four Fat Fowl in upstate New York is a triple-cream so buttery that even kids will go for seconds. Rush Creek Reserve is a dippable fondue-like wheel wrapped in spruce bark from Uplands in Dodgeville, WI.

The thinly sliced Ibérico pork shoulder, aged for three years, is Hall of Fame charcuterie board fare. Or, double up on tinned ingredients by adding a layer of Row 7 Sweet Prince Tomatoes and you get a gussied-up pan con tomate.

Somewhere between the first holiday party invite and the moment you realize November is already a quarter of the way gone, your gift list starts growing on its own. The good news? Presents from the beauty category make it a lot more manageable. They’re easy to shop, they’re hard to get wrong, and everyone in your life could use a few more of them, whether they like to admit it or not.

It can be as simple as a lipstick in a case they’ll want to show off, or as big as the LED mask they’ve had in their shopping cart for months now. And there’s plenty to love in between, from skin care they’d never splurge on for themselves and makeup gift sets to a beauty tool or two that turn the bathroom into something close to a visit to the facialist.

Every year, the same people are the hardest to shop for: the mom who insists she doesn’t need anything, the sister with impossibly specific taste, the friend who has genuinely tried it all. This list has them covered, along with a few names you’ll probably add later. Keep scrolling to shop the best beauty gifts and thank yourself in mid-December when you’re crowned best gift giver ever.

The best makeup gifts are the ones most people wouldn’t buy for themselves, like a designer lipstick in a case nice enough to leave out on the vanity, or a set of minis that finally gets someone to try a brand they’ve been curious about. This year’s holiday sets lean right into that, with limited-edition shades and packaging that looks just as good on a dresser as it does wrapped under the tree. Whether the person on your list does a full face every morning or rarely gets past mascara, there’s something here for them.

It’s hard to go wrong with Chanel, and this set is all about the small details that make someone feel put=together. Tucked inside a limited-edition white pouch with a soft, knitlike texture, it includes the Rouge Coco Baume Satin tinted lip balm, which goes on sheer and builds to lipstick-like color with a few more swipes, plus one of the brand’s hand creams and a bottle of the Le Vernis nail polish in the classic shade Ballerina.

For the person who treats their makeup bag like an accessory, this one comes in a sleek metallic clutch that’s chic enough to carry on its own. Inside, there’s Prada’s Pradascope mascara for lifted, clump-free lashes; the refillable Monochrome lipstick in Tiepolo, a soft, diffused matte finish; plus two lip balm refills in Universal and Astral Pink that keep lips comfortable for up to 24 hours.

For the friend who always has their trusty lip liner handy, you can’t go wrong with this set. Makeup artist (and Vogue Beauty Board member) Fara Homidi’s Smudge & Contour pencils are a cult favorite, designed with a creamy, almost balmy feel, so they glide on without dragging, and can be smudged out with a fingertip or sculpted into perfection with a makeup brush. The brand’s holiday trio comes in three neutrals, a cool beige, a taupe, and a deep brown, covering everything from a barely-there line to a deeper, more defined lip.

If someone on your list always runs late to holiday parties, they’re in luck, because we’ve uncovered the perfect gift for them. Gucci Westman picked the four products she’d reach for with only a few minutes to get ready, and all four come in mini sizes that slip easily into an evening bag. A cherry red blush stick and a rosy-taupe highlighter take care of the cheeks, while a charcoal eye pencil and Westman’s buildable mascara handle the eyes, so the whole look comes together fast.

In our opinion, skin care is one of the easier things to gift, since almost everyone has a routine, and most people are quietly hoping someone will hand them the moisturizer or serum they’ve been too practical to buy for themselves. The best picks this season either upgrade a step someone already loves or introduce them to a brand they’ve been curious about, and a few come in packaging nice enough that the box doesn’t even need wrapping.

Sulwhasoo has built its name on ginseng, and this set is the easiest way to see why. It includes the brand’s full-size Concentrated Ginseng Rejuvenating Cream along with smaller sizes of the matching eye cream, serum, and cleansing foam, so the whole routine is covered from start to finish.

This is the moisturizer to give the person who has tried everything. Dr. Diamond’s HYDR/O is a sheer cream that sinks in quickly but delivers serious hydration, thanks to a long list of hyaluronic acids, ceramides, and squalane that help strengthen the skin barrier over time.

Dieux’s got loyal fans for a reason, and this kit pairs two of its most popular products in one, reusable and decorative tin. The full-size Deliverance Serum helps calm redness and soften the look of wrinkles and dark spots, while a mini Instant Angel Moisturizer locks in moisture and leaves skin dewy enough to wear under makeup. Both are fragrance-free and gentle enough for sensitive skin, so it’s an easy gift even if you’re not sure what someone’s routine looks like.

For the friend who loves a Sunday night face mask, this set is basically a week of spa nights in one box. It includes five of 111Skin’s sheet masks, each one targeting something different, from hydration and brightening to depuffing, plus a lifting mask for the neck. Each takes about 20 minutes, and at a $161 value, it’s a fun way to try the brand’s bestsellers and find out which one is best for you.

Beauty tools tend to be the gifts people secretly want most and are least likely to buy themselves, mostly because the price tags make it hard to justify. That’s exactly what makes them such a good present. This year’s picks bring the kind of treatments you’d normally book at a dermatologist’s office or a facialist into the bathroom at home, from LED masks and laser caps to a hydro-facial that takes about 10 minutes.

Currentbody’s LED masks already have a cult following, and the Series 3 is its most advanced yet. It packs 750 LED bulbs and six different wavelengths, including red and near-infrared light for firmness and fine lines, and blue light for breakouts. The brand’s MyDose technology works out the right treatment for your skin, and there are four preset modes if you’d rather not think about it. A touch-screen controller with a countdown timer makes it easy to stick with, which matters, since LED works best with consistent use.

For anyone dealing with thinning hair, this is one of the most serious tools you can give them. The Capillus Spectrum looks like a regular baseball cap, but inside, it uses red and infrared lasers to stimulate hair follicles, and it’s FDA-cleared to treat hereditary hair loss in both men and women. It only takes six minutes a day, and the cap shuts itself off when the session is done, so it’s easy to wear while you answer email or make coffee.

Think of this as a facialist that fits in your hand. HigherDose’s just-debuted wand pairs a cold laser with red, near-infrared, and blue LED light, so it can help firm and smooth fine lines on one setting and calm breakouts and redness on another. A cooling attachment swaps on to depuff under-eyes and sculpt along the jawline, and most sessions take 10 to 15 minutes. It even comes with a travel case, plus minis of the brand’s peptide serum and facial mist to prep skin first.

For the person on your list who splurges on a biweekly or monthly facial, the Shark Beauty FacialPro is most likely sitting high on their wish list. An easy way to unclog and clean pores plus infuse skin with powerful ingredients like hyaluronic acid, this gift takes its owner into the driver’s seat, giving them the power of visiting their favorite spa right at home.

Hair gifts are a safe bet for almost anyone, since even people who barely think about their routine still have a shampoo they’re loyal to or a styling tool they’ve been eyeing for months. From a splurge-worthy straightener that skips the hot plates entirely to travel-size sets that are perfect for stuffing into a carry-on, there’s something for the person who does their own personal blowout every morning and the one who simply wants their strands to feel soft.

Anyone who’s ever waited for their hair to dry before reaching for a flatiron will understand the appeal here. Dyson’s Airstrait dries and straightens at the same time, using airflow instead of hot plates, so you can go from towel-dried hair to a sleek, finished look with one tool. It has three heat settings and a separate mode for touching up dry hair, and the arms lock together so you can rough-dry your roots first. It’s a splurge, but it cuts out an entire step of the routine.

If holding a round brush and a dryer at the same time has never worked out for you, this is the fix. Wavytalk’s thermal brush works on dry hair, so you get the volume and bend of a blowout from a single tool, with five heat settings up to 420° F and a ceramic barrel that heats evenly. Negative ions help keep frizz down, and since it’s dual-voltage, it’s easy to pack for trips abroad.

As frustrating as it can be, you can’t reach your hair goals if you don’t repair damage first. If your giftee has been trying to assuage breakage, heat damage, or dry and brittle strands, Redken’s Acidic Bonding collection is like the golden ticket. Powered by Bonding Care Complex and citric acid, these products are formulated to reinforce weakened or broken bonds for smoother, stronger hair—and even protect hair color from fading.

For the person in your life who’s always on a plane, this set from RŌZ packs a full routine into carry-on-friendly sizes. The masterwork of celebrity hairstylist and Vogue Beauty Board member Mara Roszak, this set includes the Foundation Shampoo and Conditioner, the Santa Lucia Styling Oil for frizz and shine, and the Milk Hair Serum, a leave-in that works whether you air-dry or blow-dry. Plus, everything is sulfate-free and smells as good as it performs.

Yes, buying perfume for someone else can feel like a gamble, since what smells amazing on you might not work on them at all. There are two easy ways around that—you can go with a classic that almost everyone likes, or you can give a discovery set and let them find a favorite on their own time. We’ve rounded up a short list of both, so whether they’ve been wearing the same scent since college or still haven’t found their signature, there’s something here that’ll end up in their perfume collection.

If you’re shopping for someone who already loves Coco Mademoiselle, this set is a no-brainer. It pairs the full 3.4-ounce bottle with the Twist and Spray travel size, so there’s one for their vanity and one for their bag, all in limited-edition holiday packaging. The scent opens with bright orange, softens into jasmine and May rose, and settles into patchouli and vetiver. It’s easy to see why it’s become one of Chanel’s most recognizable fragrances.

For someone who loves fragrance but hasn’t found their signature yet, this set from Hermès makes the search a lot more fun. It includes minis of four of the house’s best-known scents: the warm, spicy Eau des Merveilles, the ginger-and-tuberose Twilly d’Hermès, the green, mango-tinged Un Jardin sur le Nil, and the luminous floral Jour d’Hermès.

If someone on your list loves a perfume that makes them stand out, put this one at the top. Merit’s New Wave is an extrait, made with nearly 30 percent fragrance oil, so it lasts a lot longer than most eaux de parfum. It starts out a little spicy from pink pepper and gets warmer and sweeter as it wears, with orange blossom and honey up front and vanilla and incense underneath.

Not sure whether they’d like something light or something a little more intense? This set lets them try both. It comes with four minis of Cartier’s La Panthère, an eau de toilette, two eaux de parfum, and the parfum, and they all share the same mix of gardenia and soft musk. The eau de toilette is the lightest of the bunch and works for daytime, while the parfum is deeper and better for a night out.

Some of the best gifts aren’t about what goes on your face but about how you feel day-to-day. Wellness picks make sense for the person who’s always trying to sleep better, drink more water, or finally figure out why they wake up tired, and they tend to get used every single day. These four are easy upgrades that will fit right into your giftee’s routine, whether they’re a total wellness devotee or just curious.

Most people filter their drinking water without thinking twice, but the water they shower in every day rarely gets the same attention. Jolie’s shower head swaps in for your regular one and filters out chlorine and heavy metals, which can leave hair dry and dull and skin feeling tight after a shower. Over time, they should notice softer hair and clear, glowing skin becoming the norm.

Oura’s new Ring 5 is about 40% smaller than the last one and made from lightweight titanium, so it’s easy to forget it’s on—perfect for the person who has been complaining about their sleep for years. Each morning, the app shows how well they slept, how stressed their body was, and how they’re recovering. The battery lasts up to nine days, and the charging case holds about a month of backup power, so there’s no need to pack a charger for a long weekend away.

If anyone you know is obsessed with their oral hygiene, getting them the Rolls-Royce of toothbrushes will keep you slated as the ultimate gift giver forever. Polish, prestige, and next-generation cleanliness make Philips’s latest in dental technology the ideal present for those who like to get five stars every time they visit the dentist.

For the person who needs a little bit of calm in their life and has getting bigger muscles on their resolution list, the vibration plate is the perfect contribution toward their 2027 health goals. This version from HexaPlate uses side-to-side oscillation to tamp down an active nervous system if you just want a little bit of relaxation or to challenge the body when doing squats, lunges, or push-ups.

La Mer is one of those brands people love but rarely buy for themselves, so this set is a smart way in. For under $100, you get four minis worth $250 in total: the brand’s lightweight Moisturizing Soft Cream; the Resurfacing Treatment, a gentle liquid exfoliator; the Renewal Oil; and The Concentrate, a serum made to calm stressed, irritated skin. Everything comes zipped inside a velveteen case, which works just as well for travel once the minis are gone.

This is a great gift for anyone who’s been eyeing red-light therapy but isn’t ready to spend hundreds on a mask. The set pairs True Botanicals’ Pure Radiance Supreme Eye Cream, made to firm and smooth the skin around the eyes, with a small red-light wand that you glide along the orbital bone after applying the cream. The wand shuts itself off after two minutes, so there’s no guessing how long to use it on each eye. Worth $215 in total, it’s another Nordstrom exclusive.

If you know someone who’s obsessed with anything vanilla-scented, this set from Summer Fridays will go straight into their bag. It includes the brand’s cult-favorite Lip Butter Balm in Vanilla in full size, plus travel sizes of the Body Butter Balm and the Sunlit Vanilla Eau de Parfum, which smells warm and a little like dessert. The perfume slides into an exclusive key-chain holder, so it can clip onto a purse or keys for touch-ups throughout the day.

Byredo’s Bal d’Afrique has a way of turning up on just about everyone’s vanity, and once you’ve smelled it, it’s easy to see why. If there’s a fellow fan in your life, this mini set lets you give them the whole ritual without the full-size price tag. It includes the fragrance, a body wash, and a body lotion, so the scent carries from the shower through the rest of the day, plus a tiny key chain filled with the perfume that clips right onto a bag for touch-ups on the go.

When winter hits, body care quickly becomes one of the most practical gifts you can give. Between the cold air outside and the heaters running inside, skin tends to feel tight and dry by mid-December, and most people don’t realize how much they need a good body oil or scrub until one is in their hands. These sets cover every step, from a scrub that buffs away dry patches to a rich cream afterward, and a few come with scents nice enough that they double as fragrance. They’re also an easy pick when you’re not sure what someone’s skin type is, since nearly everyone could use a little extra moisture this time of year.

For the friend who reads ingredient lists and actually wants to see results, Osea’s holiday set is a smart pick. It starts with the brand’s body scrub, which buffs away dry, dull skin and leaves it glowing, followed by its algae-infused body oil to lock in moisture and help skin look firmer and more elastic over time. And the dry brush, for daily lymphatic drainage and sloughing away dead skin, will remain useful long after the body-care products run out.

Fit for the king or queen in your life, Flamingo Estate’s Jasmine Damask Rose Bathroom Set takes the bathroom experience to the next level. It includes hand wash, a scented candle, and a bar of soap that indulge the senses in the rich and luxurious fragrance note that David Lynch himself deemed “intoxicating.”

If there’s a Salt & Stone fan on your list, this three-piece set is an easy way to stock them up for less. It comes with the brand’s bestselling scent in three minis—a fragrance, a body wash, and a deodorant—so they can layer it from the shower through the end of the day. The body wash is made with nourishing botanicals that keep skin from feeling dry, and the deodorant lasts up to 24 hours, which makes the set as practical as it is nice to smell.

Soft Services’ bestselling hand cream was made for the nightstand, and now there’s a version for the desk too. The new Lumelo Weightless Hydrator is a great pick for your office bestie or the friend who’s always applying hand cream between meetings. Instead of the rich texture of the original, it has a light, gel-like feel that sinks in fast, so it’s easy to work into a midday break without leaving fingerprints on your laptop.

#6624. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6622. Abdul El-Sayed Is Winning at Watches, Too

Michigan voters made history Tuesday night by electing Abdul El-Sayed to the US Senate, as part of a greater blue wave that swept the nation. The 44-year-old former epidemiologist is set to become America’s first Muslim senator—and, in a slightly more trivial milestone, might also be the first real-deal watch nerd to reach the Capitol.

During his victory speech, the senator-elect sported a Grand Seiko Spring Drive Chronograph (ref. SBGC249), a limited-edition piece from the Japanese watchmaker that pairs a GMT (which tracks the time across multiple time zones) and a chronograph (i.e. a stopwatch function). Politicians tend to go one of two ways with their timepieces: Either they’ll cosplay as a man of the people with an affordable Timex or Casio, or they’ll sport a luxury watch with historical pedigree—like the Rolex “President” Day-Date, worn by several commanders-in-chief—to make themselves appear ready for higher office. An obscure Grand Seiko fits neither of those categories.

Instead, El-Sayed’s Grand Seiko is a burly sport model made by one of the world’s most elegant watchmakers. At 43.5mm, it’s hefty, a good fit for the senator-elect’s beefed-up forearms. It’s quite complicated, with several different functions, and a dial as busy as Little Caesars Arena during a Detroit Pistons game. It costs $12,400, but you’d have to be very deep into the hobby to recognize its value.

What I find so compelling about El-Sayed’s choice is that it doesn’t appear to be masquerading as some political symbol. It’s simply the excellent wristwear of an honest-to-goodness collector. “Folks who know me know I’m a sucker for automatic watches and sort of classic watches,” El-Sayed said in an interview with LGBT Detroit in May.

Throughout his campaign, he’s worn a wide range of pieces. His recent go-to appears to be a Mühle-Glashütte S.A.R. Rescue-Timer, a great-looking and obscure German tool watch. He also owns the U-1 SE, a large dive watch from the German independent brand Sinn.

Not all of El-Sayed’s timepieces are devoid of political meaning, however. The senator-elect has worn an Omega Speedmaster, the watch worn by American astronauts Buzz Aldrin and Neil Armstrong when they first set foot on the moon. That’s about as patriotic as a watch can get without excerpting the Declaration of Independence on the dial. Naturally, he also owns a Shinola Runwell, from the brand based in El-Sayed’s native Detroit. El-Sayed is very aware of what a certain watch can signal about the wearer. In his 2020 book, Healing Politics: A Doctor’s Journey into the Heart of Our Political Epidemic, he wrote about how seeing Rolex billboards along a highway prompted him to reflect on income inequality: “How many people who drive this road can actually afford one of those?”

But when did I realize that El-Sayed was a true-blue watch guy? It wasn’t the dialed-in collection of interesting tool watches that did it, but his appearance at a rally on Sunday. He wasn’t wearing a timepiece at all, surprisingly. Which meant that there, on his wrist, was the mark of a true collector: a watch tan.

#6620. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6618. The Best Men’s Rain Boots Ranked From Drizzle to Downpour

The best rain boots for men aren’t a one-size-fits-all shoe. The chance of precipitation may be 100%, but you could be stepping out to a gentle mist, wading through cataclysmic flooding, or taking on sporadic showers—so your choice of shoes and outerwear should adapt to the weather. Popping up out for a quick coffee could require a pair of simple gardening shoes or tall wellingtons depending on whether you’re walking a few blocks or taking your car to a drive-thru.

There are many factors to consider but the most important is that your feet and socks remain dry, no matter the shoe or how heavy the rain is. So take into consideration how tall or short your rain boot ought to be, whether you need grippy soles to get you through some rough terrain or you might have to contend with slush and snow, which inevitably means you’ll need some boots with insulation. Your rain boots and shoes have to contend with a litany of different factors so we rounded up the best options for every kind of wet-weather situation from mild mists to ankle-deep downpours.

For the kind of mediocre rain that has you second-guessing whether you should open your umbrella or just stick it out, you’ll likely get by just fine with a pair of shoes built with a water-resistant or waterproof membrane. Think a slight spray or an annoying mist. Many outdoors-focused shoes and boots come with some type of Gore-tex lining or a coating that helps slough light water. In mild rain situations, your shoes don’t need to be very tall, either. Low-cut gardening shoes or rain-ready sneakers can manage the weather just so long as there’s a low risk of deep puddles along the way.

Norda's trail-ready slip-on runners are an iron-clad pick for any rocky terrain you might encounter, purposely or not. With their lightweight, tear- and water-resistant Dyneema uppers, and crag-grabbing Vibram lugged soles, these bad boys can handle more than a drizzle. Plus, the easy slip-on design is great for when you just need to jam out the door for a quick errand, not to mention for keeping water from sogging your socks.

If the precipitation falls anywhere between a drizzle to moderate showers, I can’t be arsed to bust out my heavier rain boots. I’m unlikely to wear my wellies in showers, too, if I know I won’t be outside for too long. For most situations, a good water-resistant boot will more than suffice. Save your brain cells and just get a pair of Blundstones—they’re tough as nails, reliably dry in the majority of rainy days, and look great with any pant. But if boots on the wellies-chelsea spectrum aren’t your speed, there are plenty of other shoes with rain-prepped details like Gore-tex linings and DWR coatings to keep water at bay.

It's hard to argue against a pair of Blundstones. The quality leather uppers age beautifully, the shape is ruggedly handsome and endlessly styleable, plus the hardy soles can handle most everyday situations regardless of the forecast. No wonder why you see everyone from your local barista to Hollywood's leading men rocking a pair. Their waterproof design is adept at traversing through medium rain, so long as you don't step into any deep puddles, and we like that they don't present as a full-on rubber boot which makes them easier to wear all year long.

What you’re probably imagining when you think of proper rain boots are the kind wrought entirely out of a block of rubber, reaching up to your calf, without any laces. Some people refer to these as Wellingtons—or wellies—whose origins go back to the Duke of Wellington, and though they were originally made of leather, are now mostly thought of as a rain-ready boot. Their seamless, monoblock design in conjunction with impermeable rubber makes them the right choice for heavy rain or if you plan on being outside for several hours in average rainfall conditions. Of course, they’re well-equipped for lighter precipitation as well.

Hunter's flagship boots are a textbook Wellington rain boot. Made entirely of waterproof (not water-resistant) rubber from sole to shaft, no amount of rain, sludge, or slush penetrates these boots. The carved rubber soles keep their grip amidst slippery sidewalks and slick metal grates, while the height is tall enough to stand nice and dry through calf-deep water, but isn't so tall to be a physical or stylistic burden. And at just under $200, they're a reasonable price for the quality.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6616. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

#6614. Pear Salad With Honey-Roasted Seeds

In the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake. Where lettuce splashed with vinaigrette can feel like an afterthought, a juicy, savory-slanting pear salad is worth making room for on a plate full of turkey and cornbread. This is the antithesis of the haphazardly chunked together fruit salads you find at the supermarket for a brunch or dessert spread. Keep the focus on crisp-tart pears—apples also work—and it’s a welcome accompaniment to the other hearty dishes. Sliced razor-thin (use a mandoline) and fanned out on a platter, the fruit acts as an edible canvas for wisps of cheese and clusters of honey-roasted seeds. Leftovers (if you have any, of course) are delightful spooned over a well-toasted and buttered slice of multigrain bread the next day.

Pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over. After slicing, have a taste: If they are very tart, add 1 tsp. honey to the dressing; if fairly sweet, skip it.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Preheat oven to 325°. Whisk 3 Tbsp. honey, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup raw sunflower seeds, pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or coarsely crushed raw nuts (such as walnuts, almonds, and/or hazelnuts) and stir to coat. Spread out in a single layer on a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet; reserve bowl.

Bake seed mixture until golden brown, 12–14 minutes. (Honey mixture will puff up a bit but will deflate when you stir.) Toss honey-roasted seeds, then let cool. Toss again just to break up.

Whisk 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, a pinch of kosher salt, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in reserved bowl. Add 2 lb. firm green pears (such as Bartlett and/or Anjou; about 4 large), cored, thinly sliced, to dressing and gently toss to coat.

Arrange pears on a large flat platter. Scatter honey-roasted seeds over and top with 2 oz. Parmesan, aged white cheddar, or Manchego cheese, shaved.

Do Ahead: Honey-roasted seeds can be made 6 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.
